title_en: China’s local officials feel financial stick long before seeing carrot
content_en:
The central government’s campaign to clean up local finances will not fade for lack of a stick, but it could stall in the absence of a carrot.
Officials from 105 countries and organisations attend an international seminar on understanding the fifth plenary session of the 20th Communist Party of China Central Committee in Beijing on November 6. Photo: Xinhua
Every Chinese New Year, a finance official in an eastern Chinese county braces for visitors. They run businesses to which his county owes money. When the county lacks the money to pay, he sometimes stops answering his phone. He described those visits to The Economic Observer, a business weekly.
Beijing has now taken his problem and made it his superiors’ problem. In a report to China’s legislature published on November 5, the State Council said the number of local government financing vehicles – investment companies formed by local governments to raise funds – had fallen 92 per cent since 2023. The rest must leave the official list by next June.
Days earlier, a decision by the Communist Party’s fifth plenum ordered a crackdown on officials who ignore inherited debt, abruptly reverse policies or take on illicit new hidden debt. For investors and suppliers, Hong Kong’s among them, who deal with mainland China’s local governments that matters more than the next stimulus package.
For decades, local officials were judged on growth and competed with cheap land, tax rebates and hidden borrowing. Provinces and cities have now scrapped or rewritten 833 rules and contract clauses promising tax rebates.
The central government’s stick is also personal. Wu Shenghua, a former party secretary of Bijie in Guizhou province, had asked publicly why he should repay his predecessors’ debts. He was expelled from the party in January on grounds that included bribery and failing to tackle local debt risk. A new party secretary now has more to answer for.
The stick reaches Hong Kong. Local financing vehicles sold more than US$46 billion of offshore bonds last year, mostly through Hong Kong and Macau. Beijing now lets these vehicles borrow offshore primarily to refinance. About US$40 billion of their offshore bonds fall due next year, the year they must leave the list. Once off the list, they will be ordinary companies. Holders should not assume a local government will stand behind every one.
[embedded media]
The money for industry has moved rather than disappeared. Guangdong, next door to Hong Kong, is building a strategic industries fund with a target of 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion), and Beijing’s policy banks fund national priorities. For Hong Kong investors, the counterparty that matters is shifting from the county to the province. It is still a government, so the old question of “who pays?” remains. It is the same ambition, just better organised.
Sceptics might argue that every Chinese campaign fades. This one will not fade for lack of a stick, but it could stall for lack of a carrot. The order is deliberate: discipline first so new money is not wasted. The risk is that the carrot arrives too late.
Beijing has issued 98 per cent of the bonds it set aside to swap hidden debt. That money mostly refinances what local governments owe banks and bondholders. Officials have received promises. The central government has pledged to provide local governments a share of consumption tax, but it has set no date for its disbursement.
[embedded media]
In 2018, the party promised to protect officials who make mistakes while trying new things. A scholar at a provincial party school wrote in August that those rules mostly stay on paper. The plenum has promised again. When a Jiangsu official was cleared, and even promoted, last year after approving a project before all its technical requirements were met, it was rare enough to make national news. Protection is news. Punishment is routine.
The test is whether suppliers get paid. A landscaping contractor from Nantong, Jiangsu province, was sued by his own suppliers because he still owed them for gardens he built six years ago at a public cultural centre.
An executive told The Economic Observer he overheard provincial finance officials describe the drill: delay the final inspection, then delay settlement, then delay payment. A Hong Kong supplier to a mainland county should ask at which stage its bill is stuck and which budget will pay it. A letter of support from the province is not payment.
Colourful vegetation covering Kaisha Island along the lower reaches of the Yangtze River on October 28, in Nantong, Jiangsu province. The Communist Party’s leadership has promised to protect officials who make mistakes while trying new things. Photo: VCG via Getty Images
The county finance official mentioned above has run into a flaw in the rules. After his county reported more of what it owed, he was notified that such arrears count as hidden debt. More hidden debt weighs against officials at performance review time and limits what the county can borrow. The county stood to be penalised for its candour. Others will learn to report less.
Two steps before the party congress next year would bring the carrot forward: protection for officials who report unpaid bills and a date for handing over the consumption tax. Without them, frightened officials will approve less, report less and declare debts settled that are not. The first checkpoint comes in June: whether the financing vehicles leave the list with their bonds paid.
Investors prize one thing above rebates: rules that outlast the officials who sign them. Beijing is right to push local governments in this direction. The verdict will come from that eastern county and whether its finance official can answer his phone next Chinese New Year.
The views here expressed are the author’s own.
By Robin Hu

title_en: Xi’s show of support should galvanise Greater Bay Area efforts
content_en:
The president’s speech during an inspection tour of Zhongshan should inspire the 11 cities of the development zone to work harder to achieve the initiative’s goals.
Chinese President Xi Jinping visits an artificial island that is part of the Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link, a project connecting the cities of Shenzhen, Zhongshan and Guangzhou, in southern China’s Guangdong province on November 16. Photo: Xinhua
President Xi Jinping has driven the planning and development of the Greater Bay Area (GBA) economic powerhouse from the start. Regular inspection visits reflect that. This week’s was his sixth since 2020. What set Xi’s visit apart was that it came just ahead of one of the biggest events in the history of Shenzhen, a core city of the GBA – the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting and CEO Summit.
The Apec meeting overshadows the domestic event but that is not to diminish the wider significance of the GBA. It will play a pivotal role in the future growth of the Asia-Pacific region.
Xi often delivers an important message on these visits. This time he called on the 11 southern Chinese cities – including Hong Kong – that make up the GBA to press on with the megacity cluster project, and talked about the significance of the Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link, a major infrastructure development.
During an inspection tour on Monday, the president said the Greater Bay Area was a “major strategic” programme from the Communist Party’s Central Committee. “Guangdong shoulders a crucial mission, and cities on both sides of the Pearl River Delta – including Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Dongguan and Zhongshan – must play a pioneering role,” state news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying.
Zhongshan is the western terminus of a major transport link with Shenzhen. Guangdong officials joined Xi on a visit to an artificial island on the link to see operations on the crossing. The road project linking the two sides of the Pearl River Delta opened to traffic in June 2024 after seven years of construction, boosting connectivity between nearby cities.
The link, which cut the travel time between Shenzhen and Zhongshan from at least two hours to as little as 25 minutes, forms part of the planned infrastructure to create a “one-hour traffic circle” within the GBA. Xi said the crossing had “played a pioneering role” in promoting the integrated development of the east and west banks of the Pearl River Delta.
The trip was Xi’s first domestic inspection tour after the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee, a key party meeting held in late October. He underlined the need to fully and faithfully implement the decisions and plans made at the session and better promote the integrated development of the east and west banks of the Pearl River Estuary.
The Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link is a cross-sea passage that includes two bridges, two artificial islands and an underwater tunnel. Spanning 24 kilometres, the link connects Zhongshan and the technology hub of Shenzhen, which lie on opposite sides of the Pearl River Estuary.
Xi sees the importance of closer integration of the whole area. The GBA and Apec share a common vision, reflected recently by Hong Kong’s and Macau’s hosting of related Apec meetings of finance and tourism officials respectively.
Meanwhile, at the Apec CEO summit in Shenzhen, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu told hundreds of business delegates that the GBA was a proven model of regional collaboration. He urged Apec delegates to “prosper and win together” in an increasingly complex global environment, positioning Hong Kong as a springboard for businesses seeking to enter the mainland Chinese market.
He said the bay area’s rapid growth demonstrated the importance of connectivity with the wider Asia-Pacific economy, bolstered by its unique institutional framework: the “one country, two systems” governing principle and three currencies working in synergy.
“Because nobody wins the future alone. The future is a team sport and the Asia-Pacific has always fielded a very strong side,” Lee said. “And nowhere is this spirit of collaboration more evident, or more vibrant, than in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area.”
Under its first five-year plan, Hong Kong is stepping up its efforts to integrate with other cities in the GBA, improving connectivity through infrastructure, rules, technology and people, and by putting in place healthcare and finance policies. The city recognises the importance of the GBA, and Xi’s show of support should galvanise efforts.
Ultimately the future of the GBA is also in our own hands. Different cities need to work together to promote exchange and smoother communication.
By SCMP Editorial
Sections: Opinion | Topics: Greater Bay Area, Xi Jinping, Zhongshan, China, Zhuhai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Dongguan, Guangzhou, Asia-Pacific Economics

title_en: Spy or not, Alice Huang was a useful pawn
content_en:
The alleged Chinese spy might have been more useful to Silicon Valley monopolists and Washington hardliners than Beijing.
Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang is seen with then Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after he delivered his keynote speech at Computex 2024 in Taipei on June 2, 2024. Photo: Reuters
She might not be a spy after all, but she could have been. That, apparently, is US intelligence’s current assessment of Alice Huang, the microchip siren blamed for bringing down AI titan Jensen Huang.
“The US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between a Chinese businesswoman who had an affair with [then] Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the Chinese government,” CNN reported, citing multiple sources.
“The intelligence collected on her to date,” it said, “does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing.” US officials also disagree about how strong the evidence is that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her to spy on Jensen Huang and, by extension, on US policymakers.
Now they tell us. How convenient!
Even The New York Times, which broke the story, appears to be backtracking a little. The unknowns around Huang, it said, have prompted questions about “what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role”.
What does it mean to be a Chinese spy? The Times reporters are getting positively philosophical. No wonder conspiracy theories about nefarious forces out to bring down Jensen Huang are spreading like wildfire online. Some now sound almost credible.
[embedded media]
We will probably never know what really happened. But we can at least apply the old Latin test of cui bono: who benefits?
Consider what Huang stood for. His ousting removes a singular voice that helped moderate the US-China rivalry over AI. He supported open-source models and defended “distillation” as common industry practice rather than intellectual property theft. He argued for giving China greater access to advanced US chips, on the basis that “addiction” to them would slow China’s own chip development and make its AI-related industry dependent on American tech.
Without that bridge with Huang, the artificial intelligence (AI) divide between the two rival superpowers is likely to deepen. The espionage allegations hand China hawks in Washington an excuse to press the Trump administration for tougher curbs. Just ahead of US-China AI safety talks, cooperation now looks hopeless.
Congress plans to pass tighter AI chip export rules. And the US Commerce Department is preparing to add seven countries – including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand – to the list requiring export licences for advanced AI chips. Small wonder Chinese AI stocks fell on Huang’s resignation.
[embedded media]
US start-ups and developers who rely on cheap, customisable open Chinese models could end up being forced to buy expensive tools monopolised by Silicon Valley giants.
Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have accused Chinese firms of unfairly copying their technology. One method is distillation, in which a “student” model is trained to replicate the outputs of a “teacher” model. It also means using a model to extract vast data from a source such as a newspaper’s digital archive or a publisher’s library, without paying for copyright. Yet all the AI giants in the US have practised distillation themselves and some have reached out-of-court settlements with IP holders affected.
Meanwhile, China hawks in Washington and congressional Republicans are blasting the Trump administration for being too soft on Beijing over AI and chip exports. A row within the White House surfaced when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for failing to restrict Megaspeed, the Singapore-based firm at the centre of the alleged scandal.
Critics say lax oversight let restricted chips reach Chinese buyers through intermediaries such as Megaspeed, whose Nvidia purchases are in the billions of dollars. John Moolenaar, the hardline Republican chair of the House Select Committee on China, argues that advanced chips aid Beijing’s military and surveillance systems. The disputes complicate Trump’s diplomacy with China and renew scrutiny of past conditional chip sales.
Jensen Huang is seen with Donald Trump after the US president presented him with the National Medal of Science at the US Institute of Peace in Washington on October 8. Photo: Reuters
Anthropic and OpenAI, for their part, have opposed open-source models, preferring to charge a premium for their own proprietary ones. So Huang stood against the political and commercial agendas of both the Washington and Silicon Valley establishments.
The two Huangs might have been the victims of infighting within the US government. But perhaps whether Alice Huang was a spy is moot, and not only because Jensen Huang has been neutralised. After all, every Chinese citizen is a potential spy.
That is what the CNN report says: “Under Chinese national security law, Chinese citizens can be compelled to help gather intelligence on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party. Even if she had not done so yet, given her access to Huang – and by extension, to Trump – some officials believe she posed a clear counter-intelligence risk.”
Guilty for being Chinese? That seems to be how Washington operates these days.
By Alex Lo
Sections: Opinion / China Opinion / News / China / Diplomacy | Topics: US-China relations, Nvidia, Jensen Huang, Espionage, United States, China

title_en: What does Trump want from Xi and Putin in Shenzhen?
content_en:
A US leader with a knack for showmanship becomes dangerous when he needs to prove relevance. A deal may be appealing for the headline alone.
Illustration: Mario Cameira
About two weeks after American voters delivered a devastating repudiation of Donald Trump and his Republican Party, the US president will re-emerge on the global stage later this week in Shenzhen.
For nearly two years, world leaders have courted Trump on the assumption that he has unilateral control of the American political apparatus. In January next year, Democrats will have substantial control of Congress and most American states.
World leaders can no longer assume Trump has a mandate from the American people on the same agenda he has swaggered around the world with since 2016.
This trip will give the first glimpse of what American foreign policy will look like in the final two years of the Trump era. It will test what leverage Trump still has, or whether his new position gives an advantage to an ascendant rival.
As Republicans sort through the rubble of a party that was just handed its most resounding defeat this century, they are beginning to consider jettisoning Trump to save the party. This summit will be Trump’s first opportunity on the world stage to convince his party that he can still deliver.
Should they want to avoid another wipeout in 2028, affordability will need to be the keyword among Republicans for the last two years of Trump’s time in office.
A person walks by large colourful signs encouraging people to vote and decrying the high cost of living on election day in Raleigh, North Carolina, on November 3. Photo: Reuters
Trump will be looking to use foreign policy, the area in which a president has the most unilateral control, to shift the conversation away from the election – and hopefully towards an agreement with other world leaders. Showmanship will not be enough any more. Trump will need to return with something that gives Republicans reason enough to stay in line with him.
In that context, Trump will meet his two primary counterparts on the global stage.
Xi Jinping is finishing a banner year of reshaping the world order, particularly around artificial intelligence (AI). Gone is his weak negotiating position of 2023, when he met then president Joe Biden in San Francisco as China’s economy flagged while the US’ roared. Xi now not only oversees an economy that is growing faster than the US’ but there is also increasing trust in the Chinese AI industry.
Xi has every reason to build a more stable relationship with Washington, as this would assist in China’s rise, but that isn’t the same as having a reason to rescue Trump from his own domestic political struggles.
The Chinese leader has to take the shifting winds in the United States into account. Starting in January, Congressional Democrats will mire the Trump administration in oversight hearings and investigations. Giving Trump a political lifeline now may not yield favourable policy next year, especially if it must go through Congress for approval.
Xi may prefer to see what the next part of a particularly turbulent era of American politics brings rather than try to make a deal that may not stick.
The most obvious route for Trump will be a trade deal with China. Many of the most surprising defeats for Republicans in these midterms came from states heavily affected by Trump’s trade wars
Vladimir Putin is playing a different game. After several years as a pariah, sitting alongside the American and Chinese leaders launders Putin’s image after his illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine that has also embarrassed Russia’s supposedly strong military.
Trump needs to emerge from Shenzhen with a deal. Neither Putin nor Xi has any reason to be particularly helpful.
The most obvious route for Trump will be a trade deal with China. Many of the most surprising defeats for Republicans in these midterms came from states heavily affected by Trump’s trade wars, shrinking international markets for both agriculture and manufactured goods.
That pain might be eased by a deal with China that combines tariff relief and more access for American exporters to Chinese markets. The simplest route would be to extend the current truce that runs out on January 10, one week after Democrats take control of Congress.
[embedded media]
A meeting between the three countries with the largest nuclear arsenals also gives Trump a reason to pursue a deal he has been interested in since the 1980s.
The last arms control agreement between the United States and Russia expired in February this year, leaving the two countries with no limits on how either builds or uses their stockpiles of over 5,000 warheads each.
The most likely outcome of an agreement between the three countries is one that limits the use of AI in nuclear command systems. This would build on the agreement to build a hotline between the US and China to address unintentional national security incidents caused by AI.
The domestic politics of that agreement would also benefit Trump in assuaging a country on edge after his administration wove AI into national air traffic control, only for the entire system to come to a nationwide halt three days later.
A man sits on a baggage carousel playing his harp at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, on November 13, after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop “due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety”. Photo: Reuters
The greatest danger for Trump is getting back to Washington with nothing in hand. It could tempt him into making riskier unilateral moves in an area where Congress, even a hostile one, has little authority. A president with a knack for showmanship becomes dangerous when he needs to demonstrate relevance and power. An agreement, regardless of its substance or who benefits from it, may become appealing for the headline alone.
What comes from Shenzhen will be a preview of the coming two years. Trump remains a powerful figure, but now he is only one part of an American political system that he no longer controls.
Trump faces a choice between changing his entire foreign policy outlook in response to the seismic jolt issued by his own voters or using foreign policy to escape the constraints he’ll soon face. We’ll have a hint soon as to which path he’ll take.
By Cory Alpert

title_display: What does Trump want from Xi and Putin in Shenzhen?
content_display:
A US leader with a knack for showmanship becomes dangerous when he needs to prove relevance. A deal may be appealing for the headline alone.
Illustration: Mario Cameira
About two weeks after American voters delivered a devastating repudiation of Donald Trump and his Republican Party, the US president will re-emerge on the global stage later this week in Shenzhen.
For nearly two years, world leaders have courted Trump on the assumption that he has unilateral control of the American political apparatus. In January next year, Democrats will have substantial control of Congress and most American states.
World leaders can no longer assume Trump has a mandate from the American people on the same agenda he has swaggered around the world with since 2016.
This trip will give the first glimpse of what American foreign policy will look like in the final two years of the Trump era. It will test what leverage Trump still has, or whether his new position gives an advantage to an ascendant rival.
As Republicans sort through the rubble of a party that was just handed its most resounding defeat this century, they are beginning to consider jettisoning Trump to save the party. This summit will be Trump’s first opportunity on the world stage to convince his party that he can still deliver.
Should they want to avoid another wipeout in 2028, affordability will need to be the keyword among Republicans for the last two years of Trump’s time in office.
A person walks by large colourful signs encouraging people to vote and decrying the high cost of living on election day in Raleigh, North Carolina, on November 3. Photo: Reuters
Trump will be looking to use foreign policy, the area in which a president has the most unilateral control, to shift the conversation away from the election – and hopefully towards an agreement with other world leaders. Showmanship will not be enough any more. Trump will need to return with something that gives Republicans reason enough to stay in line with him.
In that context, Trump will meet his two primary counterparts on the global stage.
Xi Jinping is finishing a banner year of reshaping the world order, particularly around artificial intelligence (AI). Gone is his weak negotiating position of 2023, when he met then president Joe Biden in San Francisco as China’s economy flagged while the US’ roared. Xi now not only oversees an economy that is growing faster than the US’ but there is also increasing trust in the Chinese AI industry.

Starting in January, Congressional Democrats will mire the Trump administration in oversight hearings and investigations. title_en: China, unlike the US, is investing in the right kind of engineering
content_en:
While the Western economic model focuses much on rewarding capital efficiency and shareholders, China focuses on industrial engineering.
Sun Kuan (left), founder and CEO of Hypershell, tests exoskeletons with his colleague at a park in Shenzhen on October 20. Hypershell is among companies transforming the once-bulky and expensive exoskeleton into a lightweight, affordable consumer product. In China, manufacturing itself is approached as a form of innovation. Photo: Xinhua
We live in the post-Bretton Woods Era. In this era, a nation’s economic progress is measured in gross domestic product, stock market valuations, corporate earnings and financial returns. Today, the Western economic model focuses much on rewarding capital efficiency and shareholders.
In the span of a few decades, the West has mastered the art of financial engineering through sophisticated financial products by investing in innovation, creating intellectual property and supporting it through venture capitalism. American capitalism has celebrated entrepreneurs, inventors and venture capitalists who invest in and finance the future. But one crucial factor is completely ignored: the ability to invent and finance the future has not always translated into the ability to manufacture it competitively at scale.
An economy can have the world’s most sophisticated financial markets and still struggle to build a transmission line. Similarly, it can lead in semiconductors yet lack sufficient electricity for data centres that run on those chips.
So, there is another way to measure a country’s economic progress: in factories, infrastructure, electricity generation, manufacturing capacity, supply chains and industrial scale. China has adopted this approach for decades. The West looks at growth on the books, while China considers growth on the ground; while the West focuses on financial engineering, China focuses on real engineering.
Today the world no longer sees the Chinese as imitators but as innovators, whether it is in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, solar panels and advanced manufacturing. But technology alone does not indicate China’s industrial strength.
Its greatest advantage lies in the ecosystem behind the technology. While innovation helps create possibilities, an ecosystem helps those possibilities reach the real economy. A company might develop a world-class product, but without an industrial system that is capable of producing millions of units, lowering costs and improving designs, the product cannot be delivered at scale.
Technicians work on an ultra-high-voltage power transmission project along the Yangtze River in Wuhu, east China’s Anhui province, on October 26. One such power line in China can carry more electricity than any transmission line in the US. Photo: Xinhua
In other words, economic competition is not simply about inventing the best technology, building the most powerful AI model or creating the most valuable company. China understood this decades ago.
Shenzhen is perhaps one of the best examples of how an ecosystem can become more powerful than any individual company operating in it.
In Shenzhen, an entrepreneur can easily turn an idea into a working prototype, find suppliers, source components and start manufacturing globally without having to build every capability in-house. In the manufacturing environment of any other country, chances of finding all the capabilities within such a small geographical area are close to zero.
The best way to understand Shenzhen is to examine the companies that emerged from it. One of them is DJI, which builds drones. Drone development requires a lot of complex equipment such as motors, batteries, sensors, cameras, flight control systems, software and electronic engineering. But the area easily provides access to all these capabilities. Another example is BYD, which makes EVs.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit to be held in Shenzhen this week highlights its importance.
Huang Xiaohua, who is in charge of the Industrial Development Centre at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, introduces a research “supermarket” in Shenzhen on October 19. Cutting-edge research results and contact information are displayed on shelves as cards with QR codes, to help entrepreneurs link up with scientists. Photo: Xinhua
There is no doubt that the United States and Europe remain among the world’s great innovation centres, and that American entrepreneurs have created some of the most influential companies in history.
But innovation and industrialisation are two different kettles of fish. For example, although it was the Americans who pioneered solar and EV technologies, it was the Chinese who scaled up these industries. Similarly, East Asian countries like Japan and South Korea made progress in electronics manufacturing earlier, but China has since caught up.
According to data from the International Energy Agency, China accounts for more than 80 per cent of all the stages of solar panel production globally, around 75 per cent of global EV production and more than 80 per cent of global battery cell production. These numbers suggest that China’s market position is not based on the success of one company but an entire ecosystem consisting of companies, suppliers, skilled workers, infrastructure, financing and distribution systems.
[embedded media]
One of the greatest strategic mistakes made by the Western economies was assuming that manufacturing could be outsourced to cheaper labour without compromising innovation capabilities. They ignored an important fact: manufacturing is not the last stage of innovation; it is a form of innovation.
An ecosystem where multiple companies are producing diverse products creates a learning loop conducive to improving materials, redesigning components, automating processes, optimising production and developing better technologies. Soon, the factory floor is not only a place of production but a laboratory.
Some in the West have been critical of China’s industrial model. They seem hardly aware that financial engineering may create wealth on paper, but industrial engineering builds the power to shape the future.
By Ravi Kant

title_en: Apec economies need predictable rules, not more walls
content_en:
Readers call on Asia-Pacific leaders to keep trade open, share a lesson of the Microsoft Outlook outage, and support the drive to expand job opportunities for Hong Kong youth.
Journalists work in the media center next to the logo of the 33rd Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen on November 16. Photo: Reuters
Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words.
As Apec leaders prepare to meet in Shenzhen, the Asia-Pacific faces increasingly turbulent waters. Trade disputes, technological competition and security concerns are prompting governments to reassess how much they rely on external markets and suppliers. Seeking shelter from uncertainty is understandable. But there is a difference between making a harbour safer and closing it altogether.
Trade across the Pacific has never depended on calm seas. When one route is disrupted, another may still be available. When a supplier falters, businesses can look elsewhere. The ability to change course is what makes interconnected economies resilient. Cutting too many connections may offer a sense of security, but it also leaves fewer options when the next disruption comes.
Of course, open ports still need rules, inspections and safeguards. Governments have legitimate reasons to protect sensitive technologies and critical supplies. The question is whether such measures address specific risks or become broad barriers to ordinary commerce. Smaller businesses, with fewer resources and alternatives, often have less room to adapt when trade rules change.
This is where the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum matters. Its 21 member economies will not agree on every question of trade or security. But they can work together to keep commerce moving: promoting the cross-border recognition of electronic trade documents, improving customs procedures and reducing unnecessary delays. These may seem like modest steps, but predictable rules matter when businesses must navigate uncertainty.
Shenzhen is a fitting place for this discussion. Its growth has been shaped by connections between manufacturing, technology and international markets, with its ports linking the city to the wider world. It is a reminder that prosperity depends not on the absence of storms, but on the ability to navigate through them.
The sea may be stormy, but it has no walls. The Asia-Pacific must keep it that way.
Maggie Le, Beijing
The sweet surprise of a digital disruption
The global disruption to Microsoft Outlook and Teams offered an unusual glimpse of how deeply digital communications have become embedded in working and domestic life. For many users, the interruption meant an abrupt inability to send or receive email, join scheduled meetings or respond to the steady stream of notifications that now structure the working day.
The immediate reaction may have been anxiety. Was an urgent message waiting? Had an important decision been made without us? Some users may have spent hours refreshing their screens, watching the small loading symbol circle without ever reaching its destination.
But I wonder what those same users felt when they logged in again. I found last Friday’s accumulated emails waiting, but did not feel that my work or personal life had been irreparably compromised. The backlog was real; the catastrophe I might have anticipated was not.
Perhaps others used the interruption to make a phone call, send a WhatsApp message or walk across an office to speak to a colleague. Maybe some rediscovered the efficiency and humanity of direct conversation. Others, of course, may have faced genuine operational problems, particularly where urgent decisions or time-critical services depended on these platforms.
The outage was not a voluntary digital detox. Nevertheless, it raises a worthwhile question: are we better connected, or simply more constantly connected? Perhaps a little less email ping-pong and fewer meetings would improve our working lives. A day of enforced silence may have given us a reason to find out.
Joseph Ting, adjunct professor, School of Public Health and Social Work, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane
City’s youth should look north for opportunities
The Hong Kong Youth Development Forum held this month did a good job presenting how young people in the city can seize the opportunities presented by “one country, two systems”. Hong Kong’s unique position linking mainland China to the world is a key advantage. Now a five-year plan that supports youth development will make it even easier for us to explore opportunities such as the Greater Bay Area Youth Employment Scheme. I look forward to these internship and exchange programmes to help us build mainland work experience in emerging industries such as fintech, aerospace and high-end research.
I was also struck by the encouragement that we should not limit ourselves to traditional career paths, but continue to explore new horizons. By taking initiative and using available policy support, we can link our personal goals with national development for a better future.
Yoyo Lee, Tsuen Wan
By Letters

title_en: Xi-Putin-Trump meeting in Shenzhen is no Yalta 2.0
content_en:
The world’s most consequential powers plan to meet in a spirit of pragmatic crisis management and calibrated cooperation, not to divide up the world.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
As leaders from across the Asia-Pacific converge on Shenzhen this week for the annual Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, global attention has zeroed in on a planned, unprecedented sideline gathering: a trilateral summit bringing together President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump.
At a moment when the international order is strained by protracted regional wars, supply chain fragmentation and eroding strategic trust, any direct engagement among Beijing, Moscow and Washington carries enormous weight. Even so, some Western commentary has continued to view the meeting through a distorted Cold War lens.
Some international media reports have invoked World War II-era imagery and dubbed the Shenzhen summit “Yalta 2.0”. That analogy is both analytically flawed and historically tone-deaf. Convened in February 1945 in Crimea, the original Yalta Conference saw Franklin D. Roosevelt, Joseph Stalin and Winston Churchill – the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom – coordinate the final defeat of fascism and sketch the architecture of the post-war order.
Over the decades, declassified archives have exposed Yalta’s darker legacy: an exercise in raw power politics defined by secret agreements and the unilateral carving up of spheres of influence. Worse still, the allies traded away the sovereign interests of nations absent from the table, including China, which was pushed into accepting territorial and strategic concessions without representation.
Equating a 21st century meeting in Shenzhen with Yalta misreads both the realities of modern diplomacy and China’s strategic posture. Beijing has been resistant to formal bloc politics and exclusionary geopolitical arrangements, offering only a tepid response to Trump advancing a “G2” concept which would have divided global management between two powers. Unlike the closed-door horse-trading of 1945, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum gathering in Shenzhen is anchored in open regionalism and multilateral economic integration.
[embedded media]
If Washington, Beijing and Moscow are not dividing the world between them, then what is driving them to sit down together now? The answer lies in distinct, pragmatic calculations.
For Russia, facing prolonged sanctions and diplomatic isolation over the war in Ukraine, sitting alongside Washington and Beijing in a high-profile trilateral format is an unmistakable demonstration that it remains an indispensable global player. It signals to the international community that Moscow cannot be sidelined from major Eurasian and global security arrangements.
For the US, domestic political headwinds are forcing a recalibration abroad. Following setbacks in this month’s midterm elections, Trump’s White House faces mounting pressure at home to curb inflation, avoid costly foreign entanglements and deliver tangible diplomatic results. Engaging directly with two primary strategic competitors offers Washington a practical avenue to manage crises and contain external volatility while tending to domestic priorities.
For China, hosting such a consequential dialogue reinforces its role as a diplomatic stabiliser and pragmatic convenor. The setting itself carries weight. In four decades, Shenzhen has transformed from a coastal border town into a global hub of technological innovation. Hosting direct talks among major powers here sends a clear message: Beijing favours economic connectivity over decoupling and diplomacy over confrontation.
Russian artist Alexey Sergienko unveils his new painting “Shenzhen 26” depicting US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, in St Petersburg in Russia, on November 12. Photo: AP
Beyond the immediate political calculus of each capital, a China-Russia-US trilateral meeting carries structural significance for the international system for three critical reasons.
First, it provides an essential guard rail against great power miscalculation. In the past decade, a steady erosion of strategic trust has prompted some observers to draw grim parallels between today’s geopolitical friction and the volatile European landscape leading up to 1914.
However, 2026 is not 1914. Unlike the rigid alliance systems that sleepwalked into World War I, direct communication among three permanent members of the UN Security Council creates a vital circuit-breaker. Candid dialogue at the highest level helps de-escalate flashpoints, reinforces the UN-centred international framework and prevents regional conflicts from spiralling into wider systemic confrontation.
Second, it is vital for stabilising global energy security and supply chains. Geopolitical ruptures have upended energy markets, disrupted maritime trade routes and fuelled global inflation, disproportionately hurting developing economies.
Together, Russia as a leading energy exporter, the US as a top producer and financial hub, and China as the world’s manufacturing powerhouse and largest energy consumer hold the keys to commodity stability. Even a tacit trilateral understanding to avoid further escalation in energy sanctions or maritime chokepoint disruptions would inject much-needed predictability into global markets and support a more orderly energy transition.
[embedded media]
Third, it creates a more constructive format for major-power interaction. For decades, relations among Washington, Moscow and Beijing were shaped by zero-sum triangular games, with two powers leveraging each other against the third. Bringing all three leaders to the same table breaks that cycle. It proves that nations with divergent political systems and competing interests do not have to lock themselves into rigid ideological camps.
By opening a direct channel to tackle shared transnational threats, from artificial intelligence governance to climate change, this format sets a practical precedent. Rival powers can still compete fiercely while coexisting and shouldering collective global responsibilities.
In a world pulled between economic integration and geopolitical fragmentation, the scepticism surrounding the Shenzhen trilateral meeting stems from an inability to imagine international politics beyond zero-sum rivalry. Yet as leaders gather in southern China, the real significance of this dialogue lies in its rejection of fatalism.
By choosing engagement over estrangement, the world’s most consequential powers have an opportunity to prove that global politics need not be dictated by the ghosts of Yalta or 1914 but by pragmatic crisis management and calibrated cooperation.

title_display: Xi-Putin-Trump meeting in Shenzhen is no Yalta 2.0
content_display:
The world’s most consequential powers plan to meet in a spirit of pragmatic crisis management and calibrated cooperation, not to divide up the world.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
As leaders from across the Asia-Pacific converge on Shenzhen this week for the annual Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, global attention has zeroed in on a planned, unprecedented sideline gathering: a trilateral summit bringing together President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump.
At a moment when the international order is strained by protracted regional wars, supply chain fragmentation and eroding strategic trust, any direct engagement among Beijing, Moscow and Washington carries enormous weight. title_en: China showcases value of openness rooted in a confident core
content_en:
The International Forum on Mutual Learning among Civilisations held in Macau underlined that Eastern traditions belong at the table as a complement to Western models.
Macau Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai speaks at the opening of the International Forum on Mutual Learning among Civilisations in Macau on November 9. Photo: Xinhua
For much of the modern era, the conversation about how nations should govern themselves, develop their economies and order their relations has been conducted largely in a Western idiom. A government-sponsored forum in Macau this month offered a timely reminder that this need not remain so, and that China’s growing civilisational voice is a net gain for a world that needs more, not fewer, sources of wisdom.
The second International Forum on Mutual Learning among Civilisations drew nearly 300 participants from more than 20 countries and regions, and covered subjects ranging from the ancient Silk Road to artificial intelligence and human values. Its premise was significant: cultures grow stronger by learning from one another, and Eastern traditions belong at the table as a complement to Western models, not as a rival seeking to unseat them.
Macau is a fitting host. Macau Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai invoked the city’s history on the Maritime Silk Road and pledged to keep promoting dialogue across cultures. The government describes the forum as a concrete measure to implement President Xi Jinping’s initiative, drawing on Macau’s role as “a base for exchange and cooperation where Chinese culture is the mainstream and diverse cultures coexist”. That formula, a confident core open to many influences, is what China can offer the wider world.
Xi has grounded the nation’s confidence in its own path, theory and system in more than 5,000 years of civilisation, describing traditional culture as part of the nation’s DNA. Critics may hear this as an assertion of exceptionalism. Yet confidence in one’s own heritage is the precondition for genuine exchange, not an obstacle to it. A civilisation unsure of itself has little to give; one secure in its roots can afford to listen.
Li Cheng, director of the Centre on Contemporary China at the University of Hong Kong, argued that Eastern civilisation’s ideal of “harmony without uniformity” deserves wider understanding. It is a principle the world could use.
In an age of polarisation, the notion that differences can coexist without being flattened into a single model is not a threat to pluralism but its fullest expression. Li also stressed people-centred development, which in the special administrative regions serves both economic growth and smoother global exchange.
China’s approach can also fill gaps others have left. Jasna Plevnik, president of the Croatian think tank Geoeconomic Forum Croatia, said that China’s global policy was “quite opposite” to today’s Western-led order. She cited artificial intelligence, where China seeks guardrails while American companies push to self-regulate, and lamented that the world lacks dialogue among civilisations and states.
A voice from Europe making precisely that case should give pause to those who view China’s rise as a zero-sum contest.
To many forum participants, current wars and conflicts seemed to signify the collapse or at least instability of the Western-led international order. One need not accept so stark a verdict to argue that mutual learning among civilisations should become a norm in tackling global problems.
For example, the “one country, two systems” principle was first conceived to let capitalism and socialism coexist. The two special administrative regions of Hong Kong and Macau, once showcases of the West’s most vibrant aspects, could now be where Western visitors first encounter China’s development.
Some will counter that such forums carry an official imprimatur and that claims made there, such as a broadcast commentator’s remark that young Chinese increasingly favour domestic brands, deserve scrutiny. They do. But the measure of China’s contribution lies less in rhetoric than in deeds, and here the forum delivered.
At its close, Macau’s Culture and Sports Bureau signed an agreement with a Brazilian university press to publish 20 Portuguese editions of Chinese classics, part of the China-Brazil Cultural Year.
That is what mutual learning looks like in practice: patient, reciprocal and open-handed. China’s rise, pursued in this spirit, does not diminish the world’s shared civilisational inheritance. It enlarges it. The task now is for others to meet that offer with equal curiosity.
By SCMP Editorial

title_en: World can’t afford to take freedom of navigation for granted
content_en:
Freedom of navigation is a foundation of global prosperity and every trading nation has a responsibility to protect it.
A ship manoeuvres at the Kwai Tsing Container Terminals on September 3. Disruptions to global trade stemming from the Strait of Hormuz crisis, and other events, illustrate the importance of global maritime shipping. Photo: Nora Tam
Hong Kong’s success rests on its connection to the world. Its position as one of Asia’s great maritime and trading centres reflects a simple principle: prosperity depends on moving goods, connecting markets and trading freely across borders.
That principle is as important today, during the 10th Hong Kong Maritime Week, as it was when Hong Kong first established itself as a major international port. At a time of growing geopolitical tensions, uncertainty over established trade routes and increasing fragmentation of the global economy, it is more important than ever.
China’s extraordinary development as a trading nation has helped reshape the global economy. This success has been aided by a stable international maritime legal system that protects freedom of navigation.
Around 90 per cent of global trade by volume is carried by sea. The ships moving between our ports transport the energy, food, raw materials and goods on which modern economies depend. Their ability to do so safely is not simply a shipping industry concern. It is a fundamental requirement of economic stability.
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea provides the essential legal framework. It establishes states’ rights and responsibilities at sea, including freedom of navigation and transit passage through international straits. These are neither privileges granted by individual countries nor principles to be applied selectively. They form part of an international framework benefiting all trading nations.
[embedded media]
Recent events have demonstrated just how much is at stake when that framework comes under pressure. The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the vulnerability of global supply chains to disruption. The war in Ukraine fundamentally altered established energy and commodity trading patterns, while attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea forced vessels to take longer routes around Africa.
The crisis around the Strait of Hormuz has provided an even starker illustration. A waterway through which around a fifth of the world’s oil consumption passes has become the focus of serious threats to commercial shipping, with direct consequences for energy markets, shipping operations and the safety of seafarers.
The economic consequences of these disruptions extend far beyond the immediate regions concerned. Longer voyages mean higher fuel consumption, increased insurance costs and delayed deliveries. Businesses face uncertainty over the arrival of essential components, while developing economies can be particularly exposed to increases in the cost of imported goods.
Disruption at one maritime chokepoint can ripple through the water and have consequences for economies thousands of kilometres away. This interconnected reality of global trade is precisely why freedom of navigation must be treated as a shared international interest.
A work crew using an excavator tries to dig out the Ever Given, a Panama-flagged cargo ship, that got wedged across the Suez Canal, blocking shipping traffic in the vital waterway, on March 25, 2021. Photo: AP
If different countries and regions begin to apply competing rules to international shipping, impose unilateral restrictions or challenge established navigational rights, the result will be greater uncertainty, higher costs and fewer reliable supply chains. In seeking greater national resilience, governments could inadvertently deliver the opposite: a more fragmented global economy that leaves businesses and ordinary people worse off.
As one of the world’s major trading nations, this is particularly significant for China. Its economic development and international commercial relationships are closely connected to reliable maritime routes. The same is true of Hong Kong, whose role as an international maritime centre depends on confidence in the movement of ships and cargoes between markets. Across Asia, from major manufacturing economies to smaller island and coastal states, the ability to access international shipping routes is essential to economic opportunity.
The challenges facing maritime commerce will not disappear. Geopolitical tensions will continue, trade patterns will evolve and new risks will emerge. However, we should not allow those developments to erode the principles that have enabled the world’s oceans to serve as highways for international trade.
Freedom of navigation is not simply a maritime principle. It is a foundation of global prosperity, and protecting it is a responsibility shared by every trading nation.
By John Denholm

title_en: The questions to ask before trying a ‘breakthrough’ skin treatment
content_en:
Readers discuss the seizure of unregistered injectables containing human tissue, fresh ways to engage young people, and support for workplace mental health.
Until a product has passed through a chain of safeguards, the honest description is not “breakthrough” but “unproven”. Photo: Getty Images
Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words.
I read with concern the reports of health authorities raiding beauty premises in Mong Kok, Tsim Sha Tsui, Tsuen Wan and Yuen Long, seizing vials of an unregistered injectable made from donated human skin – marketed to customers as an anti-ageing breakthrough (“What is the ‘cadaver skin jab’ beauty trend and does it really work?”, October 22).
As a reconstructive surgeon, I work with human dermal templates in the operating theatre. Used properly, a dermal template rebuilds breasts after mastectomy and covers burn and complex wounds that would not otherwise heal. But that work sits inside a chain of safeguards: screened donors, traceable batches, sterile handling, informed consent and a named surgeon who answers for the outcome.
Strip away that chain and the same material becomes something else entirely: a product with no local registration, no published safety data and no one accountable when something goes wrong. Registration is not red tape. It is the mechanism that forces a manufacturer to prove sterility, donor screening and benefit before a single paying customer is injected.
Novelty is not evidence. Until a product has passed that process, the honest description is not “breakthrough” but “unproven”.
Before any injection, consumers should ask three questions: Is this product registered in Hong Kong? Who is the doctor, and can I find that name on the Medical Council’s register? What exactly is in the syringe? If the answer to any of these questions is a shrug, the safest thing to do is to walk away.
Dr Wai Ming Yau, consultant plastic surgeon, Kwong Wah Hospital
City should rethink how it engages youth online
Scroll through the government’s social media accounts and there is no shortage of announcements and publicity materials, yet relatively little genuinely captures young people’s attention.
Elsewhere, politicians have found ways to bridge this gap. Take New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose creative, often humorous videos have attracted millions of views while making his policies more accessible to younger audiences. Or Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, who has found his own way of connecting with Singaporean youths by sharing everything from guitar performances to more personal moments on Instagram and TikTok.
Hong Kong doesn’t need to copy these approaches exactly, but there is certainly something to learn from them. More informal videos, a willingness to embrace social media trends and greater interaction with young people could make the government seem less distant and much more approachable.
Ultimately, the aim isn’t simply to gain more views or followers, but about building a stronger relationship and greater trust between the government and young Hongkongers.
Adam Wing Hoi Kwong, Sai Kung
Give workers protection, not just resilience training
A recent survey identified Hong Kong’s Generation Y, or those aged 30 to 45, as the city’s unhappiest age group. I welcome the health secretary’s written reply last week to a legislator’s questions about the government’s mental health strategy, but would like to point out the limitations of two of the measures he mentioned.
The first is resilience training. A Chinese University study funded by the government’s Mental Health Initiatives Funding Scheme examined an eight-week resilience programme involving 143 parents of autistic children. It found no significant improvement overall: only the moderately stressed benefited, while the most stressed did not. Training alone cannot remove the pressures people face.
The second is the Mental Health Workplace Charter, signed by more than 3,400 organisations by end-September. The charter is voluntary, its action items are mostly talks and information sharing, and it has no complaint channel, investigation procedure or outcome indicator.
When people describe being belittled at work, the response they need is not being told everyone is under pressure.
Generation Y’s unhappiness has many causes, but how people are treated at work is one that the law can address. Hong Kong’s anti-discrimination ordinances do not cover workplace bullying as a stand-alone category. Taiwan’s new legal provision on workplace bullying prevention, in force since July, requires employers to establish complaint and investigation mechanisms. A statutory obligation gives employers a reason to learn how to speak to people. Hong Kong should do the same for its workers. Employees need a way to report mistreatment and have it investigated, not another invitation to become more resilient.
Raymond Yang Sze-ngai, co-founder and executive director, Just Feel

When people describe being belittled at work, the response they need is not being told everyone is under pressure.
Generation Y’s unhappiness has many causes, but how people are treated at work is one that the law can address. Hong Kong’s anti-discrimination ordinances do not cover workplace bullying as a stand-alone category. Taiwan’s new legal provision on workplace bullying prevention, in force since July, requires employers to establish complaint and investigation mechanisms. A statutory obligation gives employers a reason to learn how to speak to people. Hong Kong should do the same for its workers. title_en: Xi’s speech affirms Beijing’s position on Taiwan reunification
content_en:
In his remarks marking Sun Yat-sen’s 160th birth anniversary, the president not only stressed the one-China principle but also pledged to give full consideration to Taiwan’s realities.
President Xi Jinping (centre) leads the commemoration of the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen’s birth, held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, on November 12. Photo: Xinhua
President Xi Jinping’s speech marking the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen’s birth was more than a commemoration of a revered revolutionary forefather. It was a timely affirmation of Beijing’s core position on a greater modern China and its readiness to engage with a wider non-separatist spectrum in the pursuit of peaceful reunification with Taiwan, an “essential requirement of China’s national rejuvenation”.
Coming days before the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, the remarks gave China an opportunity to project a message of continuity, determination and restraint to both domestic and international audiences. By invoking the revolutionary hero’s enduring commitment to national unity, modernisation and the revival of the Chinese nation, the commemoration placed the Taiwan question squarely within that historical context.
In the most unequivocal tone, Xi said reunification of the island with the mainland was an “unswerving historical mission” and an “essential requirement of China’s national rejuvenation”. Emphasising commitment to the policy of peaceful reunification and “one country, two systems”, he said that on the basis of upholding the one-China principle and the 1992 consensus, Beijing was willing to conduct dialogue and consultation on cross-strait relations and national reunification with “people of vision from all sectors in Taiwan”. “We will certainly take full account of Taiwan’s realities and fully accommodate the interests and feelings of Taiwan compatriots, but we will never leave any room for any form of Taiwan independence separatist activities,” Xi added.
Sun occupies a pivotal place in modern Chinese history. He led the movement that ended imperial rule in 1911 while also articulating a vision of a modern, unified and revitalised China. This effectively laid the foundation of a century-long national struggle to overcome weakness, division and external pressure, which resonates powerfully with Xi’s ideal of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
It is clear that the quest for a greater modern China cannot be accomplished when the Taiwan question remains unresolved. The assurance that Beijing would give full consideration to Taiwan’s realities and take account of the interests and feelings of Taiwan’s people is welcome. At the same time, a firm red line has been drawn that no room will be left for independence activities in any form. The position is not new. But at a moment of heightened concern over the local elections on the island, cross-strait relations and national unity understandably warrant attention.
The offer for more dialogue with “people of vision and insight from all sectors” is significant. It signals Beijing’s willingness to broaden the spectrum of engagement beyond existing protocol, creating more latitude for talks with the Kuomintang and other political groups, business leaders, academics, civic organisations and individuals who accept the one-China principle and the 1992 consensus.
It is reassuring that Beijing, which has never ruled out the use of force, remains committed to peaceful reunification as the best option. Xi’s remarks, notably without any explicit reference to military action, open the door for wider exchange while drawing a firm red line that distinguishes separatist forces from the wider Taiwan community. The timing of the speech gives it added diplomatic weight. Delivered shortly before the Apec summit in Shenzhen, where Xi is expected to meet US President Donald Trump, and ahead of Taiwan’s local elections, the dual-track approach of reaching out to the wider Taiwanese public to facilitate peaceful reunification while getting tougher on pro-independence activities sends the clearest message that the Taiwan issue is not up for external interference.
Meanwhile, the Hong Kong commemorations carry particular resonance. The city’s historical links to Sun’s revolutionary activities and its return to Chinese sovereignty under “one country, two systems” in 1997 have made Hong Kong especially relevant to the Taiwan issue. While the implementation of the unique formula has seen tough challenges, Xi’s reiteration of the model and reunification as the future of Taiwan shows Hong Kong will continue to be a reference point in the quest for one China. The challenge is to foster conditions for more constructive dialogue towards Taiwan’s peaceful reunification in due course.
By SCMP Editorial

title_en: 5 steps China, US and Russia could take at Apec to defuse nuclear risk
content_en:
Disarmament is still far away, yet the Shenzhen summit could kick-start efforts to contain the nuclear threat.
Illustration: Mario Rivera
Is a trilateral summit between China, Russia and the United States possible during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen? If so, it is striking that US President Donald Trump sees such a meeting focusing less on Ukraine, saying: “we would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation.”
How might this start? The US says China is the fastest-growing nuclear power in recent years. But even if Beijing’s warhead stockpile reached 600 by the end of 2025, as estimated by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, those of the US and Russia still account for almost 90 per cent of the world’s nuclear warheads. This is why Beijing insists Washington and Moscow should carry out substantive cuts before talking about nuclear disarmament.
Waiting for the US under President Donald Trump to lead nuclear disarmament is like waiting for Godot. The US has announced that it possesses on-orbit space control weapons and is building a “Golden Dome” system as a shield against missile attacks. Since the Biden administration, Washington has lumped Chinese and Russian missile capabilities together, arguing it faces a nuclear threat on two fronts. That raises a bizarre question: how is a coordinated nuclear strike by Beijing and Moscow against Washington possible?
Russia, which holds the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, has even less incentive to make nuclear cuts. Since 2025, Russian forces in eastern Donbas have advanced very little in many contested areas amid stiff Ukrainian resistance. History offers a clear pattern here: when a nuclear power enjoys conventional military superiority, it rarely resorts to nuclear sabre-rattling.
This is why, during the Cold War, Nato rejected proposals for a “no first use” nuclear policy, fearing that without nuclear deterrence, Soviet armour could surge across the North German Plain and pour into western Europe. This is also why, after the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia abandoned its own no-first-use commitment.
[embedded media]
Should the three parties decide to have a nuclear dialogue, the easiest thing to do is reaffirm the joint statement issued by the five nuclear-weapon states in January 2022: a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. If nuclear war is indeed unwinnable, what is the rationale for striking first?
This is in line with China’s long-standing no-first-use policy. It also helps improve Russia’s image. Although there is consistent speculation that Russia might use nuclear weapons at critical junctures, as some have suggested, President Vladimir Putin has never stated this overtly.
Another piece of low-hanging fruit would be for the three sides to pledge not to strike civilian nuclear power plants and exchange lists of nuclear facilities shielded from conventional attack. India and Pakistan have followed this model for decades under their Agreement on the Prohibition of Attack against Nuclear Installations and Facilities, swapping such lists every January. There is no clear reason why the same risk-reduction formula could not be adapted here.
A third agreement could be a joint announcement of a ban on anti-satellite weapons tests. China, the US, Russia and India have all demonstrated anti-satellite attack capabilities through live tests. Meanwhile, the world operates tens of thousands of satellites in crowded low Earth orbit, and the figure keeps climbing.
SpaceSail, developer of the Qianfan satellite constellation, plans to deploy more than 14,000 of these telecommunications devices in a global network. Photo: CCTV
No nation can yet fully disable another’s satellite network, but destroying only a few satellites would produce debris dangerous to all orbital assets. In this regard, an attack on one is an attack on all. The three nations should also put in place early-warning notification rules for high-risk incidents such as close satellite encounters, collision threats from debris and in-orbit directed-energy weapons testing.
A fourth step could be notification of missile launches. Washington and Moscow already operate such arrangements, as do Beijing and Moscow. A US-China deal would pave the way for a unified trilateral notification regime. In September and November 2024, China and the US exchanged advance warnings for their respective intercontinental ballistic missile tests. This was a rare, and positive, confidence-building milestone.
Such notifications only work when the advance notice is meant to prevent accidental scares, not to give an adversary the information needed to shoot down the missile. If Washington does build the Golden Dome with weapons in orbit, that understanding would break down. Trump’s Golden Dome is built around his delusion that the US can dominate outer space, yet US and Israeli missile defences have repeatedly proven far from invulnerable against Iranian missile and drone strikes.
[embedded media]
The final issue is how artificial intelligence (AI) might be unnecessarily involved in the nuclear domain. It makes one’s blood run cold to think that agentic AI might one day manipulate nuclear command-and-control systems. This is why President Xi Jinping and then US president Joe Biden agreed in 2024 to keep a human-in-the-loop requirement for nuclear command-and-control systems. China and the US have also agreed on regular talks on AI risks.
It would be desirable if Moscow could join this framework, and I see no reason why it would be reluctant to do so. Dialogue should build a consensus on three core rules: banning fully autonomous AI algorithms that trigger nuclear strikes; limiting AI to supporting threat assessment functions; and drawing up shared standards to guard against cyberattacks targeting nuclear command, control and communications infrastructure.
The three powers can also set a global example on instant hotline communications to defuse AI-induced nuclear false alarms and exchanges on the boundaries of military AI in nuclear operations. Nuclear disarmament is still far away, yet the Shenzhen summit could kick-start efforts to contain the nuclear risk before it contains us.
By Zhou Bo

title_en: A disastrous Iran war? The US is now a mover and shaker of oil markets
content_en:
All at once, the US finds it has levers over oil from the Middle East, Russia and Venezuela – influence possibly no less consequential than Opec’s.
The front page of the Iranian daily newspaper Javan features US President Donald Trump and the headline, “Scary oil in America voice”, seen in Tehran, on October 7. Photo: EPA
Many see the US war on Iran as a colossal geopolitical bungle, failing to secure its larger strategic objectives. Yet it has allowed the blundering Trump administration to move into an immensely powerful position – one it seems ready to embrace.
With its new-found sway over Venezuela’s oil reserves, degradation of Iranian exports and selective sanctions on Russian oil, Washington has unexpectedly acquired several important levers of the global petroleum trade.
Iran has worked hard to play spoiler in the Middle East. Its strategy of lashing out at its neighbours has sparked mayhem, roiled global energy markets and proven disastrous for America’s international standing. Yet every Iranian strike on oil depots, gas fields and tankers also strengthens the position of American energy producers.
History doesn’t quite repeat here. This is more of a Trump-era riff, shaded with dumb-luck opportunism.
The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (Opec) acquired its formidable influence through combined market power. Cartel producers can turn their massive collective spigot on or off, as they did notoriously during 1973 embargo. America’s emerging role works differently.
US President Donald Trump cannot simply command other nations to produce more or less oil. But America’s Gulf-based naval forces, air power, sanctions and diplomatic leverage give Washington considerable influence over who can sell petroleum, how much reaches international markets and at what cost.
[embedded media]
Washington can exert pressure on Israel to restrain attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure, for example, while threatening Tehran with devastating strikes. Conversely, the Pentagon can escalate its attacks and disrupt Iran’s capacity to export. Such decisions have consequences for global oil prices.
Meanwhile, the administration’s erratic gestures towards peace can temporarily calm markets and allow Gulf producers to resume shipments. Even the prospect of an agreement can move prices. Washington’s ability to alternate between threats, negotiations and military action has become an instrument of energy geopolitics.
Indeed, it may matter little who controls the Strait of Hormuz: whether Tehran can choke off tanker traffic or Washington imposes a blockade, sheer risk keeps commercial vessels away.
There is also a longer-term calculus at work. By allowing the confrontation to drag on, Washington may well be contributing to the lasting degradation of Iran’s ability to exploit its hydrocarbon patrimony. Damaged wells, neglected infrastructure and prolonged production interruptions can leave some oil and gas resources permanently unrecoverable.
Economically, this would weaken a dogged competitor in the energy market. Politically, it would diminish a vital source of Iran’s revenue and geopolitical influence. There might even be an environmental dividend if some fossil fuels remain underground.
[embedded media]
None of this means Trump holds command over international oil markets. Iran retains disruptive power. Global prices respond to myriad factors beyond Washington’s reach. But the United States increasingly finds itself able to benefit from circumstances that harm its competitors.
The Venezuela agreement adds another wrinkle. Although restoring that country’s decrepit petroleum infrastructure will take years, Washington has secured extraordinary influence over its potentially enormous reserves. This, combined with America’s prodigious oil production, strengthens the longer-term US bargaining position.
With ballooning energy prices, this arrangement is lucrative for major oil companies, many Trump allies and donors. Yet these benefits are unevenly distributed. Trump must juggle the interests of oil producers, consumers and his political survival.
His recent invocation of the Defence Production Act to support domestic refining and petroleum infrastructure illustrates the contradiction. Washington wants American producers to prosper from constrained global supplies while protecting American consumers from the fallout.
Fuel prices above US$7 a gallon for regular petrol and US$8 for diesel are displayed at a Mobil station in Los Angeles, US, on September 23. Photo: AFP
With the midterm elections past and an attack on Iran looming, that balancing act is particularly precarious. Trump’s ability to choose when and where to escalate against Iran gives him ample means of influencing market expectations. But military events can escape political timetables.
This makeshift system of petroleum leverage is neither an ingenious master plan nor a stable arrangement. It is an opportunistic response to a costly war.
Most troubling is what happens next. Even if Trump finds a face-saving way to declare “mission accomplished” and end the war, Washington may prove reluctant to relinquish its new-found influence over the world’s energy arteries.
The stakes extend beyond corporate profits. By restricting Iranian exports, shaping Venezuela’s petroleum future and selectively managing sanctions on Russia, Washington gains leverage over China, which remains heavily dependent on fossil fuel imports. China bought roughly 90 per cent of Iran’s pre-war oil exports.
[embedded media]
The resulting assemblage is neither a coherent grand strategy nor a stable geopolitical order. Rather, it is an improvised form of energy dominance born of pugnacious blundering and opportunism.
By squeezing China through constrained access to Middle Eastern oil, the White House hopes to compensate for its flawed and hastily conceived tariff roll-out and other largely unsuccessful attempts to pressure Beijing.
An otherwise disastrous war has generated perverse incentives for its perpetuation. Unlike Opec, America’s power is more diffuse, more coercive and potentially more volatile. But that may make it no less consequential.
Trump has stumbled into a position where military force, sanctions and an oil bonanza are increasingly intertwined. The danger is that the president may rediscover that prolonged instability can be profitable – even when peacemaking serves the world better.
By Peter Wynn Kirby
