title_en: The dollar’s reign endures not by merit but by default
content_en:
America’s rivals and allies alike are loath to live with the consequences of the monetary equivalent of a multipolar world.
An attendee holds a novelty US dollar bill featuring an image of US President Donald Trump during a rally at Guardian Centres in Perry, Georgia, on October 24. Photo: Reuters
Why is it so hard to replace the US dollar as the world’s dominant reserve and business currency? A long list of rivals, not least China, want its supremacy to end. Even some allies agree that dollar dominance is abused by Washington, such as when it is used for unilateral sanctions. Even so, rivals and allies alike are loath to live with the consequences of the monetary equivalent of a multipolar world.
Two new studies help clarify this dilemma. Economists Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad and Tony Zhang published their piece “The Paradox of Dollar Dominance: How Technology Is – and Isn’t – Changing the Global Economy” in Foreign Affairs last week. The authors set out to explain why the dollar should be losing ground but has not, at least not catastrophically.
Across administrations, Washington has imposed financial sanctions on rivals such as Iran and Russia, and its threat of secondary sanctions entangles allies too. In 2014, the French bank BNP Paribas was penalised for processing dollar payments on behalf of clients in Cuba, Iran and Sudan; the French government protested to no avail.
The US federal debt exceeds US$40 trillion, nearly 125 per cent of GDP. US President Donald Trump’s hostile approach to trade is prompting governments worldwide to consider “de-risking”, while his attacks on the US Federal Reserve’s independence and the weakening of political checks and balances erode the pillars of foreign investors’ confidence.
Signs of decline exist. The US dollar’s share of foreign central banks’ reserves has fallen from 71 per cent in 2000 to 57 per cent in the first quarter this year. In October, the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.3 per cent, the highest since 2002. Yet, excluding the euro zone, 60 per cent of cross-border transactions are still denominated in dollars. The euro accounts for about 13 per cent; the yuan, less than 3 per cent.
The reason is simple: other major currencies look even shakier. The euro, yen and sterling have been undermined by weak economies and political instability. The yuan is not realistically a rival, and it’s not clear that Beijing still has that goal in the near term.
An employee at China Construction Bank counts yuan notes in Haian City, Jiangsu province, on January 20. Photo: Getty Images
The prolonged property sector slump, high local government debt and tight state control over the economy mean capital controls are more important than allowing free foreign exchange rates and challenging the dollar.
For a while, technology was supposed to change this. Tokenisation and blockchain make it cheaper and quicker to move money across borders and to exchange currencies directly, rather than through the dollar. Brazil, China, India and Russia have been building and linking their own payment networks to trade in their own currencies, yet Liao, Prasad and Zhang argue that innovation could reinforce, not weaken, dollar dominance.
More than US$250 billion in stablecoins is in circulation, and more than 99 per cent of that value is tied to the dollar. Rising demand for dollar-backed stablecoins indirectly fuels demand for US Treasuries, easing the financing of US deficits. Innovation cannot make up for the weak economies and institutions behind other currencies.
A further shift favours the dollar. Foreign central banks accounted for 70 per cent of foreign-held Treasuries in 2010; that share has dropped to about 40 per cent as their demand has levelled off. But private investors are more than making up the loss, drawn by US markets’ unmatched combination of returns, low trading costs and legal protections. Net capital inflows into the US have been positive in practically every quarter this decade.
Passers-by in the capital Quito look at notes of Ecuador’s currency, the sucre, on its last day of official use on September 9, 2000. After 150 years, the sucre was replaced by the US dollar. Photo: Reuters
The authors warn that easier access to the dollar could spread “dollarisation”, long rampant in parts of Latin America, to other corners of the developing world, eroding monetary sovereignty and concentrating more of the world’s savings and risks in a single currency.
Of course, all is not rosy for the US dollar. The US is gradually losing its ability to borrow cheaply.
Robin Brooks, a senior fellow in Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution, wrote an article earlier this month in which he tracks the US “convenience yield”, or the yield markets forgo to hold Treasuries. He did so by comparing 10-year Treasury yields against a trade-weighted average for Germany, Japan, Britain, Canada, Switzerland, Sweden and Australia, hedged into dollars. The US once borrowed more than 10 basis points more cheaply than this average. The advantage eroded steadily and, in 2018, turned into a premium.
[embedded media]
After 2022, the premium stabilised at around 15 basis points, likely because fiscal stress abroad – with high-debt European countries such as France looking especially vulnerable – has made the US look better in relative terms. The erosion tracks the steady rise in US debt relative to its peers and, Brooks warns, could bring higher government borrowing costs and a weaker dollar. Still, he judges it “relatively contained and small”, which could explain why the dollar’s reserve status has stayed robust.
The dollar’s exorbitant privilege is fraying, but no successor is ready. A truly multipolar system – like the pre-1914 era of sterling, franc and mark, when central banks supported one another in crises – would be ideal. But the malaise afflicting China, Japan, Britain and the euro zone makes that unlikely. Should the dollar falter, it would be replaced not by a handful of strong currencies but by several weak ones, none with a central bank able and willing to act as lender of last resort. In 2008-09, even though the US was the epicentre of the global financial crisis, trust in the Fed helped prevent a terrible situation from becoming worse.
Washington will have even less incentive for fiscal discipline, and Fed decisions can whiplash others. That could cause emerging economies more frequent currency crises, capital flight and debt distress. The dollar’s comeuppance might be deserved, but even some of America’s adversaries have concluded the US currency is, for now, “the least bad option”.
By Alex Lo

title_en: Installing solar panels is easy, but keeping them running isn’t
content_en:
Readers discuss the challenge of providing longer-term climate finance, helping students bridge environmental knowledge with action, and protecting the city’s bamboo scaffolding heritage.
A resident installs an electric light inside a home in Kampung Bertang, Pahang, Malaysia, where solar power has brought electricity to the remote Orang Asli community. Photo: Handout
Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words.
Your report, “Southeast Asia’s green push brings solar power, but who pays to keep it on?” (November 8), asks the question climate finance prefers not to hear. A village like Kampung Bertang in Pahang gets its panels at a ribbon-cutting. The batteries, inverters and spare parts that keep the lights on arrive – if at all – without ceremony.
The green finance flowing through the Cop31 climate summit counts megawatts installed, not years of light delivered. That is backwards. Off-grid solar fails in ordinary ways, and in a remote Orang Asli village, an ordinary failure can mean a return to kerosene for want of a technician and an inexpensive part.
Three changes would fix the incentive. Fund maintenance endowments alongside installation, so every project carries its own upkeep. Pay for verified years of service, not megawatts on a plaque. And train and pay local technicians, which turns a donation into a local trade.
The energy transition will be judged in places like Kampung Bertang 20 years from now, not at the signing ceremonies this week. Finance that stops at the ribbon is not transition. It is photography.
Jackie Omotalade, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, US
Teach climate change – and help students act on it
At current rates, human-induced global warming will surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius around 2030, increasing risks to people and ecosystems, making adaptation harder and potentially causing irreversible damage. Thus, it is crucial we equip the young people who will inherit this future with the right skills to evaluate evidence, navigate uncertainty and participate in difficult decisions.
But knowledge is not enough; we must bridge knowledge with action.
Hong Kong has a strong foundation. Climate change, biodiversity and sustainable development are already covered in junior secondary subjects such as science and geography. The problem is not a lack of content, but a lack of connection. Students are not always given opportunities to link knowledge across subjects, relate it to their lives or apply it to real-world problems.
Our new report has found that, while the students surveyed generally embraced positive environmental values, 51 per cent identified hands-on activities as the most effective way to learn, yet 84 per cent did not feel prepared to respond to future climate challenges.
Teachers echoed this gap. They valued fieldwork and interdisciplinary projects, but limited curriculum time and practical resources meant such experiences remained occasional rather than routine.
The challenge is therefore not simply to teach more, but to help students use what they already know. Three priorities are essential: stronger curriculum integration, repeated experiential learning, and better support for teachers and schools.
Nature-based solutions offer a practical way forward. Students could investigate why parts of their school campus flood after heavy rain or overheat in summer, collect evidence and apply knowledge across subjects to design solutions. Through this process, they learn to investigate problems, make informed decisions and evaluate results. Successful approaches could then be scaled up through well-supported demonstration schools.
As societies navigate disruptive climate change, the question is no longer simply whether students know about climate change. Their ability to connect knowledge with judgment and action will be fundamental to society’s adaptive capacity. We cannot ask young people to repair choices made before them, but we can equip them to understand risks, evaluate responses and contribute confidently to a more resilient Hong Kong.
Peggy Cheung, senior community empowerment officer, Civic Exchange
Don’t let bamboo scaffolding disappear for good
The independent committee investigating the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po has recommended a review of the use of bamboo as scaffolding.
In view of this, I wonder if the government has considered submitting Hong Kong’s bamboo scaffolding history, traditional skills and practice to Unesco for inscription on its global intangible cultural heritage list. Inscription would reduce the risk of bamboo scaffolding being eliminated in its entirety and would protect the industry and even allow it to grow within a heritage envelope, while allowing alternatives to be explored.
Andrew Benton, Bristol, UK
By Letters

title_en: US President Trump casts doubt on spy claim at heart of Nvidia saga
content_en:
Speaking to reporters, Trump contradicts earlier reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed him on Alice Huang spying allegations.
US President Donald Trump speaks to members of the press before departing the White House for a trip to Asia on Monday. Photo: dpa
US President Donald Trump has cast fresh doubt on allegations that a Chinese businesswoman at the centre of a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, adding a new twist to the leadership crisis engulfing the chipmaker.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday before departing for a trip to Asia, Trump denied that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed him on US intelligence indicating that Alice Huang – a businesswoman reportedly involved in an extramarital affair with the Nvidia co-founder – was a Chinese operative.
When asked directly whether Rubio had shared intelligence showing she was a Chinese spy, Trump replied, “I haven’t heard,” contradicting earlier media reports that the top US diplomat had personally briefed him on the matter.
“Usually what happens with that is … a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” the president said.
Trump’s remarks came a day after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared to play down the espionage claims, underscoring mixed messaging within the administration over how to handle the Nvidia fallout.
In a Sunday interview with Fox News, Bessent dismissed the debate over whether Alice Huang was a Beijing intelligence asset as a “canard”, or false report, arguing that the real issue was corporate governance and potential export-control evasion.
[embedded media]
“It doesn’t matter to me whether she’s a spy or not,” Bessent said, questioning instead whether Nvidia had fostered a corporate culture that encouraged illicit chip sales to boost revenue and earnings.
The administration’s shifting tone comes amid lingering uncertainty over the credibility of the intelligence. Last week, US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang was a spy, according to Reuters.
Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based technology firm Megaspeed – a company suspected of helping divert Nvidia processors to China – is at the heart of the controversy.
While anonymous US intelligence officials were quoted in media reports, including in The New York Times, saying they suspected she worked as an intelligence asset for Beijing, the Chinese government has repeatedly dismissed the claims as “groundless” and a “smear campaign”.
She was also reported to be among the women with whom Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship. The former Nvidia chief, who admitted he was unfaithful to his wife and stepped down on Thursday after leading the company he co-founded 33 years ago, has not publicly identified anyone involved.
[embedded media]
Despite his resignation, the scrutiny in Washington continues. Both Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have voluntarily agreed to appear before three US House committees in early December for transcribed interviews regarding the company’s role in allowing Chinese entities to access advanced American chips.
Meanwhile, Huang broke his silence on Tuesday ahead of Nvidia’s first earnings call without him, expressing gratitude for the support he had received and signalling a willingness to return if the board deemed it in the best interests of shareholders, employees and the US.
“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a statement on social media.
The board, however, swiftly shut the door on a comeback.
“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” chairman Harvey Jones said during the firm’s third-quarter earnings call, adding that Nvidia had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent successor.
By Ben Jiang

title_en: How a Tsinghua spin-out became China’s first commercial AI safety watchdog
content_en:
The first in a three-part series profiles organisations at the forefront of efforts to balance innovation and safety in China’s AI industry.
Luke Li Xiaojian, CEO of Fangcun AI, is pictured at his office in Beijing, November 6, 2026. Photo: Simon Song
Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are set to meet this week in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Apec meeting, where the question of how to manage the risks of frontier AI systems is expected to be a major agenda item. In the first of a three-part series, we profile Chinese organisations at the forefront of efforts to ensure that innovation does not come at the expense of safety in China’s AI industry.
Launched in January, Fangcun AI is already larger than most Chinese start-ups at the same stage: over 40 employees, with plans to reach 100 by the end of next year.
It is not just the headcount that stands out. Spun out of Tsinghua University, China’s most prestigious higher-education institution and Chinese President Xi Jinping’s alma mater, Fangcun operates next to the university’s campus in Beijing’s Haidian district.
The company recruits heavily from Tsinghua’s legendary “Yao Class”, the elite undergraduate computer science programme founded by Turing Award winner Andrew Chi-Chih Yao, which is known for producing some of the country’s brightest AI talent including Tencent Holdings’ chief AI scientist Vinces Yao Shunyu.
As China’s first company dedicated to independent, third-party evaluation and research on frontier AI safety, Fangcun has seen its emergence coincide with surging investor interest in the sector.
According to Chinese database CVSource, seed and angel round financing in the AI security sector in the first three quarters of the year rose to 29 per cent of all sector deals, up from 16.7 per cent the same period last year. Series A and earlier financing proportions jumped from 52.7 per cent to 61.3 per cent.
But Fangcun’s Tsinghua ties and unique focus on frontier AI risks have set it apart from other new entrants. The start-up completed seed and angel funding rounds earlier this year, with investors including LinkX Capital, SEE Fund and the Tsinghua Alumni Seed Fund.
In many ways, the company’s rapid rise was not surprising given that it filled a glaring gap, according to CEO Luke Li Xiaojian. While high-profile rogue AI incidents and AI-enabled cyberattacks had triggered global alarm, the debate had largely been dominated by US firms, he said.
“This kind of cutting-edge technical research and model evaluation is quite common in the US now, but in China, fewer people have been doing it,” he said. “Chinese model companies are generally much smaller compared to the likes of Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic, yet the amount of work they need to tackle is by no means small.”
Beijing is also increasingly signalling its concerns with frontier AI risks. On Monday, an article in China’s top Communist Party journal, Qiushi, warned that frontier AI models were “showing signs of escaping human control … potentially creating major security risks that threaten human survival”. For Fangcun, the goal is to ensure that humans always remain in control in China’s AI industry.
Incidents such as OpenAI’s hacking of AI platform Hugging Face put the spotlight on AI model evaluation organisations. Photo: Reuters
Managing the frontier
AI model evaluation organisations have come under the global spotlight in recent months as they investigate high-profile incidents such as OpenAI’s hacking of AI platform Hugging Face, which also became headline news in China.
Following the incident, the US non-profit research outfits METR and Redwood Research conducted an independent investigation that uncovered more details than OpenAI had previously reported, spurring Washington policymakers to propose stricter regulations on AI model companies.
Li said one of the main reasons he decided to launch Fangcun was his growing concern that companies would not be able to manage the risks of AI by themselves. Both he and Dong Yinpeng, Fangcun’s chief scientist and an assistant professor at Tsinghua University’s College of AI, were full-time academics just a year ago.
After completing his master’s in engineering at UC Berkeley in 2023, Li returned to China to pursue a doctorate in AI at Tsinghua. Dong, meanwhile, had been researching AI safety and security issues since his undergraduate studies at Tsinghua a decade ago.
However, it became clear that academic research was not adequate for tackling the issues that were arising as AI continued to rapidly improve, said Li. Elite student researchers would be poached by Big Tech giants with offers of enormous salaries, while limited computational resources in academia also posed constraints for producing cutting-edge research.
Li therefore decided to launch Fangcun as a start-up. Part of the decision was the prediction that its services would be increasingly in demand in China. A recent report from research firm SemiAnalysis found that almost every frontier Chinese model released this year did not include any information about risks or safety evaluations.
Last month, a “rogue” AI incident involving third-party autonomous software agents operating on a cloud platform hosted by Chinese tech giant Tencent Holdings signalled that risks of AI escaping human control were not limited to the US.
A week later, Fangcun released its first major report, which concluded that DeepSeek’s latest model, V4.1 Flash-1017, matched top US models on key safety features, such as adherence to approval boundaries and obedience to human shutdown commands.
High-profile rogue AI incidents and AI-enabled cyberattacks have triggered global alarm. Photo: Shutterstock Images
However, it also revealed troubling anomalies, such as the model’s growing “evaluation awareness”, whereby the model recognised when it was being safety tested. Experts have warned that such evaluation awareness among AI models could compromise the integrity of safety evaluations, as test performance ceases to reliably predict real-world behaviour.
Fangcun’s research also identified a different but related phenomenon they called model “evaluation over-attribution”: where the model erroneously believed itself to be in an evaluation setting, rather than a real-world environment.
“Suppose a person suffers from hallucinations and mistakes the real world for a video game, might they casually rob a bank or gun down a pedestrian? The same logic applies to AI models,” said Li.
A Chinese approach
China’s third-party evaluation landscape is still much smaller and less well-funded than that of the US, said Li. He would not disclose how much Fangcun has raised so far, though he said investors were approaching him “every day”.
One advantage, he noted, was that China’s younger AI safety ecosystem did not necessarily have to follow the US template. US President Donald Trump, who has called AI safety concerns a “hoax”, has favoured a light-touch regulatory approach reliant on voluntary frameworks and industry self-regulation.
We don’t want to be in a position where we must wait until the model companies are willing to cooperate with us before we actFangcun AI CEO Luke Li Xiaojian
This means that US companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic are not obliged to open up their operations to third-party evaluators like METR but instead choose how much access to give them. Earlier this month, METR published another evaluation of Anthropic’s internal operations, though Anthropic redacted large parts of the final report, citing “confidentiality”.
In China, the prevalence of open-weight models means that Fangcun can evaluate the frontier models without formal partnerships with the model companies themselves, unlike its US counterparts.
“We don’t want to be in a position where we must wait until the model companies are willing to cooperate with us before we act,” said Li, noting that being a commercial entity also helps ensure the independence of their work.
Instead of monetising the model evaluations themselves, Fangcun targets downstream enterprise users of those models. One of its flagship products is the “Fangcun Observer”, which monitors the runtime security of the users’ AI agents and assigns responsibility when unexpected behaviours occur.
In turn, the real-world deployment experiences of these clients give Fangcun insights to refine its safety evaluation benchmarks. Notably, several clients are downstream hardware companies, reflecting China’s status as a world leader in “embodied AI” such as robots and drones.
According to Li, China can take important lessons from how AI safety has developed in the US. However, the country can also forge its own path: one that is less reliant on philanthropically funded non-profits and less narrowly focused on risks in the digital world instead of the physical.
“If a team lacks the ability to generate its own source of income, how can it sustainably conduct third-party evaluations?” said Li. “Establishing Fangcun, in large part, is about exploring a new way in China of maintaining independence while conducting AI evaluations.”
By Vincent Chow

title_display: How a Tsinghua spin-out became China’s first commercial AI safety watchdog
content_display:
The first in a three-part series profiles organisations at the forefront of efforts to balance innovation and safety in China’s AI industry.
Luke Li Xiaojian, CEO of Fangcun AI, is pictured at his office in Beijing, November 6, 2026. Photo: Simon Song
Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are set to meet this week in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Apec meeting, where the question of how to manage the risks of frontier AI systems is expected to be a major agenda item. In the first of a three-part series, we profile Chinese organisations at the forefront of efforts to ensure that innovation does not come at the expense of safety in China’s AI industry.
Launched in January, Fangcun AI is already larger than most Chinese start-ups at the same stage: over 40 employees, with plans to reach 100 by the end of next year.

Series A and earlier financing proportions jumped from 52.7 per cent to 61.3 per cent.

title_en: Hong Kong begins HarmonyOS adaptation of iAM Smart
content_en:
Representatives of the Digital Policy Office and Huawei Consumer Business Group at the launch ceremony for the HarmonyOS version of iAM Smart in Hong Kong on 9 November 2026.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Hong Kong's iAM Smart digital identity platform has begun adaptation for Huawei's HarmonyOS operating system, in a move aimed at giving residents another way to access online government services, particularly when travelling between Hong Kong and Mainland China.
The Digital Policy Office (DPO) and Huawei Consumer Business Group marked the start of the project at a ceremony on 9 November 2026. Once developed, iAM Smart is expected to become Hong Kong's first public services application available on HarmonyOS.
The milestone takes the government's core digital public services further into the HarmonyOS ecosystem while strengthening digital infrastructure connectivity across the Greater Bay Area.
Mr. Brian Sun Yue Man, Assistant Commissioner (Data Applications) of the DPO, officiated at the ceremony with senior Huawei representatives to formally launch the system development and adaptation work.
"Today, iAM Smart and Huawei are deepening their collaboration by commencing system development and adaptation for HarmonyOS,” Sun said at the ceremony.
“As a core piece of digital infrastructure supporting Hong Kong's smart city development, iAM Smart will become Hong Kong's first government services application to be adapted for HarmonyOS."
Promoted by the DPO as the government's one-stop personalised digital services platform, iAM Smart gives Hong Kong citizens a single digital identity along with personalised digital assistant services.
It allows residents to verify their identity and access more than 1,400 online services and electronic forms offered by government departments and public and private organisations.
Serving more than 4.9 million users in Hong Kong, the platform’s functions include digital identity authentication and digital signing, as well as services intended to reduce the need to enter personal details repeatedly when completing online transactions.
The platform received the Hong Kong E-Governance Project of the Year – Smart Government award at the GovMedia Conference & Awards 2026, in recognition of its use of technology in public services.
The HarmonyOS initiative is being introduced amid more frequent cross-boundary travel and business exchanges within the Greater Bay Area, where residents and commuters increasingly need access to digital services across different mobile platforms.
As the region's “one-hour living circle” takes shape, easier access to government services could prove useful to Hong Kong residents who regularly travel between the city and neighbouring Mainland cities.
Security will be a key consideration during development, particularly as iAM Smart handles identity authentication and electronic signatures. The move also reflects the government's pragmatic approach to adopting next-gen operating systems built to high security standards.
Technical teams will draw on HarmonyOS's encryption, key protection and permission management capabilities while working to meet requirements for privacy, data protection and information security.
The DPO and Huawei will also work on compatibility and user experience, including the processes used to verify identities and complete online government transactions on HarmonyOS devices.
Once available, the adapted application is intended to provide another means of accessing Hong Kong government services for HarmonyOS users, including residents based in Mainland and frequent cross-boundary travellers.
HarmonyOS is Huawei's proprietary operating system for smartphones and other connected devices. Its unified architecture is designed to allow applications and services to operate across different types of hardware, with strengths in all-scenario connectivity, microkernel security architecture and distributed cross-device collaboration.
According to Huawei, more than 90 million devices run HarmonyOS 6 and HarmonyOS 7. The company also reported more than 450,000 applications and services available within its ecosystem and over 11 million registered developers.
The project also demonstrates the government's forward-looking approach to innovation in government technology, and could provide a reference for other public utilities, financial institutions and consumer-service providers in Hong Kong and Macao considering HarmonyOS-compatible apps.
The rollout is expected to expand the range of devices through which residents can use iAM Smart, while giving government service providers experience in adapting identity verification and digital signing functions for another operating system.

title_en: Nvidia board rules out Jensen Huang return after ex-CEO says he’d gladly come back
content_en:
Chipmaker says not shipping Hopper data centre products, including H200 processors, to China and has formed national security committee.
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Photo: Reuters
Nvidia’s board has no plans to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, chairman Harvey Jones said on Tuesday, as interim CEO Colette Kress raised the chipmaker’s growth outlook and sought to reassure investors about its future without its long-time leader.
“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said at the start of the company’s first earnings call since Huang’s departure last week.
Hours earlier, in a post on X, Huang wrote that he “would be honoured” to return if the board decided that doing so served shareholders, employees, the company and America. He acknowledged serious mistakes in his personal life and pledged to cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.
Jones said Huang had voluntarily resigned following the disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.
Jones said the next CEO would need to navigate changes in advanced semiconductor technology and national security, adding that the board would prioritise finding the right person over rushing an appointment.
Kress, who continues to serve as chief financial officer, forecast around 75 per cent revenue growth for the 2028 financial year, up from the previous outlook of around 70 per cent. The increase would come off the back of a higher revenue base from the 2027 financial year, she said, citing growing demand and additional supply.
Nvidia reported revenue of US$115.8 billion for the quarter ended October 25, up 103 per cent from a year earlier. Adjusted earnings reached US$2.68 a share. Its data centre business generated US$107.6 billion, an increase of 110 per cent.
The results exceeded FactSet estimates of US$108.9 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of US$2.47 a share, which were cited in a note issued by Morgan Stanley on Monday. The bank had forecast 52 per cent revenue growth for next year and questioned whether Nvidia would provide annual guidance during the leadership transition.
We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100 per cent behind usColette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO
Nvidia forecast revenue of US$130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, for the current quarter, which includes an additional week. The outlook assumed no data centre compute revenue from China.
Nvidia shares rose more than 5 per cent in after-hours trading on Tuesday, after closing 0.4 per cent lower at US$155.46.
Kress stressed that customers and suppliers continued to support Nvidia following Huang’s departure, describing operations as “business as usual”.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100 per cent behind us,” she said.
The leadership of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, had visited Nvidia’s offices this week and remained engaged in helping the company, Kress said, adding that Nvidia had secured memory and advanced packaging capacity.
Kress also said Nvidia would continue considering financing assistance and guarantees for selected customers, while closely examining their financial strength and data centre plans.
The company’s written commentary disclosed maximum gross exposure of US$118 billion under guarantees as of October 25. Separately, it specified that commitments to specialist AI cloud providers took effect only after they secured financing to purchase infrastructure and the related computing capacity was deployed, made operational and accepted by Nvidia.
Kress said the disclosure clarified existing arrangements. “Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said.
On China, Kress said Nvidia was no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre products to the country – including the H200 processors that were approved to be sold to China under a US licensing scheme. Those shipments amounted to US$2.4 billion in the third quarter, according to the filing.
Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia announced the establishment of a new national security and export control oversight committee, giving directors dedicated oversight of national security policies, export compliance and global trade risks. It said Nvidia’s national security and global trade compliance teams would report directly to the committee and to Kress on day-to-day operations.
The moves come as Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter prepare to appear for closed-door, transcribed interviews with three US House committees early next month.
By Howard Liu

title_en: China’s ‘token export’ ambitions take shape with new Huawei-powered data centre
content_en:
China has opened first AI computing cluster powered by Huawei’s latest Ascend chip that specifically targets overseas markets.
Huawei Technologies’ latest artificial intelligence chips are rapidly being rolled out commercially as China looks to become technologically self-sufficient. Photo: Shutterstock
China has set its sights on becoming an export hub for artificial intelligence computing power, as the country launches its first AI computing cluster powered by Huawei Technologies’ latest Ascend 950DT chips that specifically targets overseas customers.
The facility, which is based in the southern coastal city of Shantou, runs on the home-grown Ascend 950DT chip and is designed for a “token export” business model, according to local media reports. It started operations last week.
The 1 billion yuan (US$150 million) project is a collaboration between Huawei and several other Chinese companies. It is located at state telecoms giant China Telecom’s submarine cable landing station and is operated by IT services firm Guangdong Tianyima Information Industry.
The cluster processes AI queries from foreign users locally, with only the generated tokens transmitted back across the border, local media reported.
The project marks the latest step in China’s efforts to build out cutting-edge AI infrastructure using home-grown technology and become a global exporter of AI tokens – units of data consumed by AI models.
Huawei’s Ascend AI chips, seen as China’s best hope for cutting reliance on US semiconductors, are playing a critical role in this initiative.
The project comes as the US Commerce Department moves to tighten restrictions on Chinese companies’ access to advanced chips via overseas data centres, which is adding urgency to China’s need to boost self-sufficiency in chip technology.
Officials announce the new facility in Shantou, southern China’s Guangdong province. Photo: Handout
Chinese AI developers have seen rapid growth in overseas demand for their models this year, as they capitalise on their lower prices compared with their Western rivals. MiniMax, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, StepFun, DeepSeek and Xiaomi have all intermittently ranked near the top of the global league table for token usage.
The new data centre also underscores Huawei’s accelerating commercial deployment of its supernode computing clusters.
The Ascend 950DT, which was launched earlier this year, features an independent architecture boasting 144 gigabytes of in-house high-bandwidth memory, delivering 1 petaflop of FP8 computing power per card.

title_display: China’s ‘token export’ ambitions take shape with new Huawei-powered data centre
content_display:
China has opened first AI computing cluster powered by Huawei’s latest Ascend chip that specifically targets overseas markets.
Huawei Technologies’ latest artificial intelligence chips are rapidly being rolled out commercially as China looks to become technologically self-sufficient. Photo: Shutterstock
China has set its sights on becoming an export hub for artificial intelligence computing power, as the country launches its first AI computing cluster powered by Huawei Technologies’ latest Ascend 950DT chips that specifically targets overseas customers.
The facility, which is based in the southern coastal city of Shantou, runs on the home-grown Ascend 950DT chip and is designed for a “token export” business model, according to local media reports. It started operations last week.
The 1 billion yuan (US$150 million) project is a collaboration between Huawei and several other Chinese companies. It is located at state telecoms giant China Telecom’s submarine cable landing station and is operated by IT services firm Guangdong Tianyima Information Industry.
The cluster processes AI queries from foreign users locally, with only the generated tokens transmitted back across the border, local media reported.
The project marks the latest step in China’s efforts to build out cutting-edge AI infrastructure using home-grown technology and become a global exporter of AI tokens – units of data consumed by AI models.
Huawei’s Ascend AI chips, seen as China’s best hope for cutting reliance on US semiconductors, are playing a critical role in this initiative.
The project comes as the US Commerce Department moves to tighten restrictions on Chinese companies’ access to advanced chips via overseas data centres, which is adding urgency to China’s need to boost self-sufficiency in chip technology.
Officials announce the new facility in Shantou, southern China’s Guangdong province. Photo: Handout
Chinese AI developers have seen rapid growth in overseas demand for their models this year, as they capitalise on their lower prices compared with their Western rivals. MiniMax, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, StepFun, DeepSeek and Xiaomi have all intermittently ranked near the top of the global league table for token usage.

title_en: Nvidia results beat expectations, as ousted CEO Huang told no way back
content_en:
The chip giant’s revenue doubled to more than US$115 billion, amid a crisis over Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Nvidia’s interim CEO forecast stronger revenue growth of 75 per cent in next financial year, up from 70 per cent. Photo illustration: Reuters
US chip giant Nvidia doubled revenue in the third quarter to more than US$115 billion, the company reported on Tuesday while ruling out any return for ousted CEO Jensen Huang after a Chinese spy scandal.
The results, which beat expectations, came hours after Huang said he wanted his job back in the latest twist for the company at the centre of an AI boom that has propelled markets to record highs and boosted global economic growth.
Huang, a leading promoter of AI, stepped down last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a spy for Beijing.
Investors scoured the upbeat results for evidence that the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.
“Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” interim CEO Colette Kress said in a statement, her first since being appointed by the board last week.
Nvidia’s Colette Kress poses for a photo. Photo: Nvidia via Reuters
She forecast stronger revenue growth of 75 per cent in next financial year, up from 70 per cent.
The recent upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia – which has lost US$700 billion in market value since the scandal broke – and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.
But his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and others for his return, and even US President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the espionage allegations.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in his first statement since his resignation.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
But Harvey Jones, the chair of the company’s board, slapped down the move, saying in an earnings call that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.
[embedded media]
As the scandal deepened, Washington on Monday announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing.
The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.
The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.
The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.
His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Huang on Tuesday sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying: “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.”
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Shenzhen – once a fishing village, now China’s ‘Robot Valley’ – takes the Apec stage
content_en:
With global attention turning to the summit, Shenzhen highlights its booming robotics industry and hardware supply chain.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
Standing on a 53rd-floor balcony overlooking the Yangtai and Tanglang Mountains in Shenzhen’s Nanshan district, Liu Tuo finally managed to catch his breath.
He had spent the entire day leading back-to-back foreign delegations on tours around his robotics showroom, which features calligraphy-writing humanoids, kickboxing bipedal bots and motorised exoskeletons.
Recent visitors to his showroom in Shenzhen’s so-called Robot Valley included old-money European hoteliers browsing cleaning robots, a park manager from Melbourne in search of robotic lawnmowers, and other foreign executives curious to witness China’s booming robotics industry first-hand.
Liu is the founder and CEO of Robotuo, an open-source robotics platform that connects international firms with China’s robotics supply chain.
The Robotuo account has 10,000 followers on the social media platform X, and its inbox was full of investors and Silicon Valley founders inquiring about tours and potential collaborations with Shenzhen hardware suppliers, Liu said.
Looking over his shoulder, he pointed to Liuxian Boulevard, which alone has over 200 robotics firms and suppliers.
“In San Francisco, building a physical AI system could take two months,” Liu said. “Here, you can source more than 90 per cent of the components in less than an hour.”
Hosting Apec here sends a clear signal: China is showing how a former assembly workshop can reinvent itself into an innovation engine driven by green, high-end industrialisationGuo Wanda, China Development Institute
The unmatched speed and density of innovation are precisely what Beijing wishes to showcase as the world turns its attention to the southern China technology hub for the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
As leaders and executives of the 21 member economies gather this week in Shenzhen, a metropolis where airborne food delivery drones and driverless robotaxis have become a routine part of daily life, they will see a city that is adding hi-tech innovation to its long-held status as a manufacturing hub.
“Apec advocates openness, innovation and shared prosperity, and Shenzhen is the living embodiment of that philosophy,” said Guo Wanda, executive vice-president of the Shenzhen-based think tank China Development Institute, which was founded in 1989 to support China’s reform and opening-up policy, with Shenzhen at its forefront.
“Hosting Apec here sends a clear signal: China is showing how a former assembly workshop can reinvent itself into an innovation engine driven by green, high-end industrialisation,” he added.
From ‘shanzhai’ knock-offs to innovation hub
Shenzhen’s transformation did not happen overnight. The city was a low-margin manufacturing base geared for export just a few decades ago, attracting contract assemblers such as Taiwan’s Foxconn to employ large numbers of migrant workers to produce circuit boards and electronic devices designed outside the country.
That rapid boom drastically brought down the barriers to electronics manufacturing, making it easier for small workshops to quickly churn out knock-offs of popular Nokia, Sony and BlackBerry devices. This earned the city a notorious reputation as “the capital of shanzhai” in the early 2000s, a term referring both to the copycat products themselves and to a broader business philosophy, one defined by iterative speed and entrepreneurial tenacity.
“Shenzhen famously didn’t have any state-owned enterprises, which was one of the secret sauces behind its success,” said Martin Sebena, a lecturer at the University of Hong Kong who researches global value chains.
[embedded media]
The city has largely retained its private-sector prowess in the decades since, with private firms now contributing nearly three-quarters of the foreign trade in a city with a gross domestic product of 3.87 trillion yuan (US$580.6 billion), similar to that of Belgium and Thailand.
Crucially, these private firms have been the main drivers of Shenzhen’s innovative capacity. Of the 245 billion yuan Shenzhen spent on research and development in 2024 – the highest in China as a proportion of GDP at 6.67 per cent – its companies accounted for over 93 per cent of the spending. Much of this came from the numerous tech giants that call the city home, including telecoms equipment and smartphone maker Huawei Technologies, electric vehicle leader BYD, video game and social giant Tencent Holdings and the world’s largest consumer drone developer, DJI.
This has helped Shenzhen steadily climb global innovation rankings over the years. In 2025, the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster overtook Tokyo-Yokohama for the first time to rank as the world’s top innovation hub, according to the World Intellectual Property Organization – a crown it retained this year.
Today, Shenzhen is targeting breakthroughs in core sectors, including semiconductors, robotics and artificial intelligence – strategic areas that Beijing considers vital to the country’s technological self-reliance amid deepening geopolitical tensions with Washington.
“For Shenzhen, navigating geopolitical and supply chain friction boils down to three things: conquering critical core technologies, deepening digital and smart industrial integration, and accelerating the integration of manufacturing with advanced services,” Guo said.
Applications for AI
Like most other Chinese cities, Shenzhen has made AI a centrepiece of its development strategy. However, it differs from Silicon Valley and other Chinese tech hubs in that it has not seen a major AI model from a start-up launch locally; instead, it focuses on the many industrial “scenarios” in which AI can be deployed.
“Shenzhen is very well positioned for applied AI: you can put it into cars, drones, whatever,” said Sebena, who compared the city to Japan and Germany, which also do not have stand-out foundation model companies.
[embedded media]
Unlike Beijing, which boasts Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, and Moonshot AI, or Hangzhou, which has DeepSeek, Shenzhen’s AI strength lies in its rich array of industries that can serve as a testbed for AI.
The strategy is expressed in Shenzhen’s latest five-year plan, which sets out ambitious targets for the adoption of AI.
The plan, unveiled in May, saw the city set a target to achieve “full-suite, full-time” adoption of AI across every household and business by 2030, targeting key established industries such as smart devices, manufacturing and robotics.
“While this might not be the sexiest topic, it’s very important because eventually these [industrial application] companies might be the biggest beneficiaries of AI if generative AI does end up having limits to what it can do,” Sebena said.
Embodied AI, or the integration of AI models with robots, has also emerged as one of Shenzhen’s cornerstone strategies. Last year, the city government unveiled an action plan that laid out concrete targets for growing the embodied AI industry to a value of 100 billion yuan by 2027, with over 1,200 companies in the sector.
Shenzhen’s poster child for AI is Hy, previously known as Hunyuan, the flagship model by Tencent. The company is increasingly positioning itself as an AI-native company, recruiting star researcher Vinces Yao Shunyu from OpenAI last year to lead its AI efforts.
Yao, 29, has since helped Tencent catch up with domestic peers, with its latest Hy4 model ranking as one of China’s best, according to third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis. As the strategic partner of Apec, Tencent will also offer its AI capabilities to support media with content production and volunteers with instant translation during the conference.
Favourable and targeted policies play a key role in nurturing industrial clusters and innovative ecosystemsVivian Jiang, Deloitte China
A unique model
Beijing has framed Shenzhen’s transformation over a matter of decades – from fishing village to manufacturing base to hi-tech hub – as a template for other Apec economies looking to quickly move their industries up the value chain. However, experts warned that the “Shenzhen model” may not be so easily replicated.
One unique element was Shenzhen’s geography, Guo said, referring to its proximity to Hong Kong.
“In the early days, Shenzhen relied on industrial relocation and service spillovers from Hong Kong, a global financial, trade and shipping centre,” Guo said.
Vivian Jiang, the chair of Deloitte’s China board, noted that the speed-to-market advantage was also unique to Shenzhen.
“This velocity is powered by having R&D talent, prototyping capabilities and specialised manufacturing networks co-located within the region, shaped by years of regional development.”
However, she pointed out that there were several practical elements in the Shenzhen model that could support efforts by other economies to upgrade their industries.
“Favourable and targeted policies play a key role in nurturing industrial clusters and innovative ecosystems, while developing a strong advanced manufacturing base can enable commercialisation,” she said.
[embedded media]
There is also heightened global attention on what the Apec summit and the hotly anticipated meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump will mean for AI governance. This year’s summit will be the first time the two leaders meet since agreeing to launch a bilateral AI dialogue in Washington in September, amid growing concerns about AI cyberattacks and biological misuse.
While details about the talks remain scarce, one of their chief proponents, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, said on November 10, US time, that they would include an exchange of “best practices” for evaluating and testing advanced AI models before their release – one of the most contentious questions in the global AI industry – for the purpose of avoiding a “misunderstanding between our two systems”.
Still, expectations about concrete deliverables regarding AI risks were lower than those present during the September summit in Washington, said Mark Witzke, a non-resident scholar at the UC San Diego 21st Century China Centre.
“Not enough groundwork has been laid for a substantive agreement yet, but maybe Apec is where they can at least keep the ball rolling,” he said.
The price of innovation
Showcasing Shenzhen’s ambitions as a venue for international diplomacy is the Apec meeting’s venue itself: the Shenzhen International Exchange Centre, a purpose-built conference centre in the Xiangmi Lake area of Futian district that began construction in 2021.
Like many other parts of the city, this area was once home to a mix of residences and businesses that sprang up in the 2010s, following the closure of a nearby resort. The local government commenced a major campaign in 2019 against the city’s many illegal temporary constructions, demolishing the Baishizhou “urban village” in Nanshan district that once housed 150,000 tenants, mainly migrant workers.
According to Sebena, Shenzhen’s urban villages were often the first landing places for Chinese entrepreneurs migrating to Shenzhen, making them pivotal in promoting grass roots entrepreneurship in the city by offering cheap accommodation and amenities.
[embedded media]
While the city remains one of the most attractive destinations for Chinese internal migrants – its population reached 18.25 million last year with an annual increase of 259,000, the largest among Chinese cities – there are now concerns that the growing gentrification of the city may hurt its capacity for innovation.
“Now that Shenzhen is clearly a rich and, by extension, expensive city, the question is whether it will retain its experimental edge because it’s getting more expensive to do business in Shenzhen, especially for start-ups,” Sebena said. Shenzhen today has one of the highest house price-to-income ratios in China, with prices even higher than those in Beijing and Shanghai.
“If you’re in your 20s and you want to do new things, I don’t think Shenzhen is the place to be any more.”
Robotuo’s Liu disagrees. Both of his parents are entrepreneurs from Hunan who moved to Shenzhen. After a decade studying and working in the US, Liu relocated back to the city in 2024 to start his own business.
Despite the cost-of-living issues, exacerbated by growing numbers of Hong Kong residents visiting the city on weekends, Liu said that Shenzhen’s mature ecosystem of hardware suppliers, tech giants, robotics start-ups and elite higher education institutions, such as branches of both Tsinghua University and Peking University, offered a complete “closed loop for innovation”.
“I believe after Apec, we will have more international clients come to Shenzhen,” he said.
“There will only be more companies, innovators, entrepreneurs and business leaders coming here and collaborating with local companies to build better products for the world.”
By Iris Deng, Vincent Chow

However, experts warned that the “Shenzhen model” may not be so easily replicated.
One unique element was Shenzhen’s geography, Guo said, referring to its proximity to Hong Kong.
“In the early days, Shenzhen relied on industrial relocation and service spillovers from Hong Kong, a global financial, trade and shipping centre,” Guo said.
Vivian Jiang, the chair of Deloitte’s China board, noted that the speed-to-market advantage was also unique to Shenzhen.
“This velocity is powered by having R&D talent, prototyping capabilities and specialised manufacturing networks co-located within the region, shaped by years of regional development.”
However, she pointed out that there were several practical elements in the Shenzhen model that could support efforts by other economies to upgrade their industries.
“Favourable and targeted policies play a key role in nurturing industrial clusters and innovative ecosystems, while developing a strong advanced manufacturing base can enable commercialisation,” she said.
[embedded media]
There is also heightened global attention on what the Apec summit and the hotly anticipated meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump will mean for AI governance. This year’s summit will be the first time the two leaders meet since agreeing to launch a bilateral AI dialogue in Washington in September, amid growing concerns about AI cyberattacks and biological misuse.
While details about the talks remain scarce, one of their chief proponents, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, said on November 10, US time, that they would include an exchange of “best practices” for evaluating and testing advanced AI models before their release – one of the most contentious questions in the global AI industry – for the purpose of avoiding a “misunderstanding between our two systems”.
Still, expectations about concrete deliverables regarding AI risks were lower than those present during the September summit in Washington, said Mark Witzke, a non-resident scholar at the UC San Diego 21st Century China Centre.
“Not enough groundwork has been laid for a substantive agreement yet, but maybe Apec is where they can at least keep the ball rolling,” he said.
The price of innovation
Showcasing Shenzhen’s ambitions as a venue for international diplomacy is the Apec meeting’s venue itself: the Shenzhen International Exchange Centre, a purpose-built conference centre in the Xiangmi Lake area of Futian district that began construction in 2021.
Like many other parts of the city, this area was once home to a mix of residences and businesses that sprang up in the 2010s, following the closure of a nearby resort. The local government commenced a major campaign in 2019 against the city’s many illegal temporary constructions, demolishing the Baishizhou “urban village” in Nanshan district that once housed 150,000 tenants, mainly migrant workers.
According to Sebena, Shenzhen’s urban villages were often the first landing places for Chinese entrepreneurs migrating to Shenzhen, making them pivotal in promoting grass roots entrepreneurship in the city by offering cheap accommodation and amenities.
[embedded media]
While the city remains one of the most attractive destinations for Chinese internal migrants – its population reached 18.25 million last year with an annual increase of 259,000, the largest among Chinese cities – there are now concerns that the growing gentrification of the city may hurt its capacity for innovation.
“Now that Shenzhen is clearly a rich and, by extension, expensive city, the question is whether it will retain its experimental edge because it’s getting more expensive to do business in Shenzhen, especially for start-ups,” Sebena said. Shenzhen today has one of the highest house price-to-income ratios in China, with prices even higher than those in Beijing and Shanghai.
“If you’re in your 20s and you want to do new things, I don’t think Shenzhen is the place to be any more.”
Robotuo’s Liu disagrees. Both of his parents are entrepreneurs from Hunan who moved to Shenzhen. After a decade studying and working in the US, Liu relocated back to the city in 2024 to start his own business.
Despite the cost-of-living issues, exacerbated by growing numbers of Hong Kong residents visiting the city on weekends, Liu said that Shenzhen’s mature ecosystem of hardware suppliers, tech giants, robotics start-ups and elite higher education institutions, such as branches of both Tsinghua University and Peking University, offered a complete “closed loop for innovation”.
“I believe after Apec, we will have more international clients come to Shenzhen,” he said.
“There will only be more companies, innovators, entrepreneurs and business leaders coming here and collaborating with local companies to build better products for the world.”

title_en: ‘China question’: Nvidia crisis and new US chip curbs split Washington and Silicon Valley
content_en:
Beijing condemned the new remote cloud rules as ‘economic coercion’, accusing Washington of interfering in normal trade and tech cooperation.
In this file photo taken in Beijing on May 14, 2026, Chinese President Xi Jinping greets US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang looks on. Huang resigned as CEO last week. Photo: Reuters
A leadership crisis at Nvidia and a fresh round of US chip curbs have highlighted fractures inside the Trump administration and Silicon Valley over how to maintain America’s artificial intelligence lead over China, according to analysts.
The turmoil escalated after the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) extended export controls to remote cloud access on Monday, closing a major loophole that had allowed Chinese firms to tap advanced Nvidia chips via third-country data centres.
Beijing condemned the new rules on Tuesday as “economic coercion” and “long-arm jurisdiction”, accusing Washington of interfering in normal trade and technology cooperation.
Speaking at a regular press briefing, foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China would take necessary measures to defend its legitimate interests. The commerce ministry said the move “runs counter to the important consensus reached by the two countries’ leaders” and “disrupts the stability of the global semiconductor industry and supply chains”.
The BIS crackdown follows the abrupt resignation of Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, a vocal opponent of tighter export controls.
Huang stepped down amid controversy over extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom US intelligence agencies suspect of gathering information for Beijing – an allegation China has repeatedly denied.
Analysts said the corporate and regulatory battles reflected how tightly Nvidia’s fate has become bound to US national security.
Both the White House and Silicon Valley viewed “Nvidia as the single most important American asset in the AI arms race with China, and Jensen as the reason it exists”, analysts led by Dan Ives at merchant bank Yorkville Ives & Co wrote in a client note on Monday.
Nvidia, which was reportedly among more than two dozen firms slated to be named US “national champions” next week under a White House initiative, had effectively become a “China question”, Ives wrote.
Jensen Huang, the former CEO of Nvidia, is seen giving a keynote address at CES in Las Vegas, Nevada, in this file photo dated January 7, 2018. Photo: Reuters
“That a CEO succession at one company is being argued between the president and his treasury secretary … is the clearest signal yet of how central AI and the chips that power it have become to US policy and the global economy,” Ives said.
“And this global story is just beginning.”
In Washington, the fallout has laid bare an unusual public rift at the highest levels of the administration. While US President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang return, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent demanded a “dramatic shake-up” at Nvidia and blamed the Commerce Department for failing to enforce existing chip restrictions.
In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Bessent dismissed debate over whether Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence operative as a “canard”, arguing that the real issue was corporate governance and potential export-control evasion.
“It doesn’t matter to me whether she’s a spy or not,” Bessent said. “Jensen’s foibles are his foibles … But, again, I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?”
That inter-agency friction was also visible in Monday’s BIS filing. The bureau noted in its press release that the cloud-access regulation was drafted by the Treasury Department and the National Security Council rather than by Commerce officials.
“It’s unprecedented for BIS to essentially disavow responsibility for a regulation issued in its name and under its legal authority,” Christopher Padilla, a former US undersecretary of commerce for international trade, the South China Morning Post reported on Monday.
He added that the Commerce Department appeared to have issued the rule “almost under protest”, signalling that “inter-agency coordination on export control has broken down”.
The BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Huang’s exit from Nvidia has sparked an intense backlash across the US tech sector, with an online “Stand with Jensen” petition gathering more than 123,000 signatures from purported Nvidia employees, partners and shareholders by Tuesday.
The campaign urges the board to reinstate Huang “while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
Tech billionaire Elon Musk, among the petition’s most prominent signatories, cautioned that many of Nvidia’s supply chain agreements were “a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract”, underscoring the acute key man risk facing the US chipmaker, which sits at the centre of the global AI boom.
By Ben Jiang

title_en: What to watch for in Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned
content_en:
Interim CEO Colette Kress faces pressure to reassure investors the chipmaker can meet growth forecasts amid supply chain, financing concerns.
An undated photo shows Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Photo: Xinhua
Nvidia faces its biggest investor test since the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang when it reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday US time, with interim CEO Colette Kress under pressure to prove the chipmaker can scale up its next-generation hardware and keep customer orders flowing without its long-time visionary at the helm.
Wall Street expects Nvidia to post financial third-quarter revenue of US$108.9 billion, up about 91 per cent from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of US$2.47 a share, according to FactSet estimates cited in a Monday note by Morgan Stanley. Nvidia’s guidance in August was US$108 billion, plus or minus 2 per cent.
The results are due at 5.20am on Wednesday in Hong Kong, followed by an earnings call at 6am. Nvidia shares fell 4.1 per cent to US$156.14 on Monday.
Can Nvidia stick to its growth outlook?
A central question for Kress is whether Nvidia can stand by its August forecast of around 70 per cent revenue growth for the financial year ending in January 2028.
Morgan Stanley analysts are modelling 52 per cent growth after trimming their forecast last week. While demand from major cloud providers remained robust, the bank flagged tight memory supply and increasingly restrictive China-related export rules as key headwinds, adding that it was unclear whether Kress would update the full-year outlook during the call.
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress. Photo: Via Reuters
For a more immediate benchmark, investors can look to Nvidia’s guidance for the January quarter. Morgan Stanley projected US$120 billion in revenue for the quarter, trailing the US$125.1 billion FactSet consensus cited in its note.
Meeting those expectations hinges largely on how quickly Nvidia can ramp up Vera Rubin, the artificial intelligence computing platform it began shipping in August.
Morgan Stanley estimated Rubin would generate around US$20 billion – about a fifth of data centre revenue – in the October quarter, before contributing a larger share over the next two quarters.
Can Nvidia keep rivals and supply chain delays at bay?
With Nvidia’s board searching for a permanent CEO, business stability has become a focal point on Wall Street and beyond.
Chairman Harvey Jones said last week that the company expected to honour its customer commitments and stick to its product road map.
“A clean quarter and guide” would be a crucial stabilising step for the company, said Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at US merchant bank Yorkville Ives & Co, in a note on Monday.
But reassigning decisions that were formerly concentrated in Huang’s hands could slow pricing approvals and manufacturing capacity commitments, said Arthur Lai, head of Asia technology research at Macquarie Capital.
While Rubin production was far enough along to insulate near-term deliveries, Lai said that cloud providers could accelerate efforts to qualify rival chips from Advanced Micro Devices or lean into custom processors, which could give them more control over specifications and deployment costs.
[embedded media]
Any delays to future platform upgrades could eventually hurt Taiwan’s hardware suppliers from 2028, said Citi analyst Laura Chen.
However, she said Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest contract chipmaker, would remain relatively resilient because competing AI accelerators relied on the same advanced foundry nodes.
Will tighter financing and export hurdles slow AI orders?
Beyond execution and governance, Kress would face mounting scrutiny over how Nvidia funds customer demand and navigates tightening US trade restrictions, according to analysts.
In August, Kress indicated that AI companies backed by Nvidia’s own balance sheet could account for roughly a quarter of its business in the next financial year. JPMorgan credit analysts said Nvidia was likely to continue financing customers, though new deals could take longer or become costlier if lenders sought fresh assurances about the chipmaker’s role.
Export controls represent another hurdle. On Monday, Washington announced new licensing requirements for advanced chip shipments to overseas data centres that grant China-headquartered firms remote access to significant computing power.
Nvidia’s August outlook assumed no data centre computing sales to China.
The US also imposed licensing rules on shipments to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, subject to exceptions.
Meanwhile, broader industry expectations are cooling.
In a report on Friday, research firm SemiAnalysis slashed its 2028 forecast for global AI accelerator spending by 28 per cent to US$758 billion and cut its estimate of Nvidia’s computing revenue for that year by 39 per cent, citing tighter financing, lower expected shipments and softer chip prices.
Even so, its revised projection put 2028 industry spending well above the US$392 billion expected this year.
By Howard Liu

title_en: Baidu, Xiaomi CEOs warn of growing gap between AI hype and returns
content_en:
Practical applications, not more powerful models, will determine AI’s value, tech leaders say.
Baidu’s Robin Li, right, speaks as Robin Zeng of CATL, left, and Simon Trott of Rio Tinto listen at the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday. Photo: AP
Amid mounting concerns of an artificial intelligence bubble and fresh market jitters following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the leaders of two of China’s biggest tech giants have urged the industry to focus on building practical applications, warning that massive investments in the technology are outpacing commercial returns.
Speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday, Baidu founder and CEO Robin Li Yanhong and Xiaomi founder and CEO Lei Jun both flagged a widening gap between heavy capital expenditure and profitable AI adoption.
“The most pressing task is to identify and develop the right, high-value applications for AI models,” Li said during a panel on regional AI development, a day after Baidu reported its sixth straight quarterly revenue drop.
“If we fail to address this, the common fear that AI might be a bubble could well become a reality.”
Lei, who spoke on a separate panel, voiced similar concerns.
“The investment in AI has been extremely huge, yet the scenarios where the technology can actually be implemented are very limited,” he said, adding that very few companies had succeeded in closing the “commercial loop” needed to turn the technology into profits.
Despite rapid advances in recent years, Lei noted a lack of “truly revolutionary” AI products. He expressed optimism, however, that combining AI with hardware and the physical world could unlock greater value.
Great products would emerge in fields like AI smartphones and vehicles in the coming years, Lei predicted, while humanoid robots could bring far-reaching changes to manufacturing.
Xiaomi’s Lei Jun uses his mobile phone during a session at the Apec CEO Summit. Photo: AP
Li likewise argued that AI’s greatest economic value lay in the application layer rather than in foundation models themselves, saying industry-wide adoption was still “falling short of expectations”.
He questioned whether the fierce US-China race to build more advanced AI models justified the massive costs involved.
Comparing the situation to the Industrial Revolution, Li said electricity did not deliver widespread economic benefits immediately after it was harnessed, only decades later when factories were completely reorganised around the technology.
“The same applies to AI today: while large language models possess immense power, the question is still whether small and medium-sized enterprises can truly benefit from them,” he said.
“Beyond simply adopting the technology, you need an organisational structure that aligns with AI’s capabilities to derive real value.”
Li’s remarks came after Baidu reported a 46 per cent drop in adjusted net profit for the September quarter to 1.4 billion yuan (US$210 million), as AI-related gains failed to offset sliding advertising revenue. Its Hong Kong-listed shares fell 5.8 per cent on Tuesday.
Although AI generated 53 per cent of Baidu’s core revenue, the company’s early lead with Ernie Bot in 2023 – one of China’s first generative AI chatbots – has faded.
Start-ups DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, along with rivals Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding, have since overtaken its foundation models. The gap remains even after the release of its latest model, Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview, last week. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
Rather than competing solely on general-purpose models, Li said domain-specific AI agents were more likely to generate measurable economic benefits.
He cited Baidu’s partnership with the Port of Qingdao, where AI agents trained on specialised data identify the most efficient way to load shipping containers onto vessels, delivering “immediate and measurable gains”.
The two executives’ remarks also land as investors question whether AI capital expenditure can continue at its current pace. Market concerns have intensified following the recent US midterm elections and the resignation of Nvidia’s Huang.
Despite those concerns, Li maintained that Baidu and the broader tech industry still faced a “most urgent” shortage of computational power.
To ease that constraint, the company plans to launch a Tianchi 1024-chip supernode next year, powered by proprietary processors from its in-house semiconductor unit, Kunlunxin.
By Vincent Chow, Iris Deng
