title_en: US details criminal probe into Nvidia customer Megaspeed over potential chip diversion
content_en:
The departments cited the ‘significant public attention’ on the Megaspeed case as the reason for releasing details of their investigation.
The Nvidia logo and decreasing stock graph are seen in this illustration taken on November 16, 2026. Photo: Reuters
The US Justice Department is leading a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, over possible violations of US chip export controls, US authorities said on Monday.
The Commerce Department opened its investigation in 2024 after officials detected suspicious activity while monitoring for possible diversion of sensitive semiconductors, the Commerce and Justice departments said in a joint statement. Investigators requested records from Nvidia in May 2025 on direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Nvidia placed the company on its “no sell” list the following month, the departments said.
US export-control officials worked with Singaporean law enforcement to conduct an on-site check that June, when then-CEO Alice Huang was interviewed, according to the statement. The Justice Department took the lead in the criminal investigation after the visit.
The departments said they rarely comment on ongoing investigations. They cited the “significant public attention” on the Megaspeed case in the past week as the reason for releasing details to “provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting”.
The disclosure comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his reported relationship with Alice Huang. Singapore’s own investigation into possible false declarations involving server purchases began in February 2025 and remains open, its Ministry of Home Affairs said last week.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the joint statement on Tuesday.
In a statement to the South China Morning Post on Sunday, the company said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and had hired outside lawyers to carry out an internal investigation. It said Alice Huang left on August 30, 2025, and no longer had a role there.
By Howard Liu

title_en: Apec CEOs seek common AI safeguards as adoption accelerates: Deloitte
content_en:
Executives back shared cybersecurity and risk frameworks as AI becomes central to regional trade, survey finds.
A robot patrols outside the venue of the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen during a tech demonstration. Photo: Reuters
As Beijing pushes for artificial intelligence cooperation with Washington ahead of this week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, Deloitte’s Asia-Pacific CEO Robert Hillard is urging regional governments to agree on common AI rules and cybersecurity guard rails to boost trade.
The call for cross-border alignment comes as China seeks to make AI collaboration with the United States a major agenda item at the gathering, after President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump agreed to launch a bilateral AI dialogue during their meeting in Washington in September.
With more than 70 per cent of global trade originating, ending or taking place within the Asia-Pacific region, cross-border coordination was vital as AI reshaped industries, Hillard said in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Monday.
“AI, and indeed digital technology more generally, is only effective in enhancing trade when there’s collaboration across borders, and that requires common standards,” Hillard said, adding that regional economies needed to agree on “at least some commonality of regulation”.
His remarks coincided with the release of Deloitte’s latest report on AI leadership in Apec economies on Monday. Based on a survey of 1,278 CEOs and other executives across 18 Apec economies and India, the study found that around half of respondents viewed cybersecurity, risk and resilience frameworks as the top priority for regional cooperation.
About 44 per cent also called for greater collaborative investment in regional digital infrastructure, according to the report.
Deloitte’s Asia-Pacific CEO Robert Hillard. Photo: Handout
“One of the things that we hope is that CEOs play a lead role in working with governments across the region to make sure that [AI] evolves in an appropriate way that meets everyone’s needs,” Hillard said.
More than 100 major global enterprises and over a dozen national leaders are expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday and Wednesday, immediately preceding the main leaders’ meeting on Wednesday and Thursday.
Speaking in an interview on Monday, Deloitte China CEO Dora Liu said other Apec economies could learn from Shenzhen’s approach by bringing innovation and production closer together, treating institutional reform as being just as important as technology, and integrating AI with real-world industrial capabilities.
Across the wider region, more than half of executives surveyed ranked AI as their top priority, ahead of revenue and profit growth.
Chinese firms are leading that adoption curve. Around 78 per cent of enterprises in China had deployed AI across multiple functions or embedded it in their core workflows, outpacing the 71 per cent average across surveyed economies, the report showed.
Hillard said Chinese companies were moving faster than their regional peers, with physical AI emerging as a leading driver of value as the technology became more deeply integrated into the country’s vast manufacturing sector.
By Iris Deng

title_en: Baidu quarterly profit plunges 46% as ad slump overshadows AI growth
content_en:
Revenue from Baidu’s AI-powered businesses rose 37 per cent from a year earlier, while legacy business profits declined 24 per cent.
Robin Li, CEO of Chinese search giant Baidu, speaks during the Baidu World conference in Beijing on Thursday. Photo: AP Photo
Baidu’s push into artificial intelligence failed to offset a downturn in its traditional search advertising business, dragging the Chinese tech giant’s third-quarter net profit down 46 per cent.
Net profit came in at 1.4 billion yuan (US$208 million) for the September quarter, down from 2.6 billion yuan a year earlier on an adjusted basis that excluded a prior-year asset writedown, Baidu said in a filing on Monday.
Quarterly revenue dipped 1 per cent to 30.8 billion yuan from 31.2 billion yuan a year earlier, in line with market expectations.
“This quarter, AI Cloud [infrastructure] emerged as a major driver of Baidu … revenue expansion,” founder and CEO Robin Li Yanhong said in the earnings release.
This quarter, AI Cloud [infrastructure] emerged as a major driver of Baidu … revenue expansionBaidu CEO Robin Li Yanhong
The results come as Baidu, operator of China’s long-dominant internet search engine, accelerates its transformation into an AI-focused company, betting on AI cloud services, foundation models, autonomous driving and home-grown AI chips to drive future growth as its traditional advertising business faces mounting pressure.
Revenue from its AI-powered businesses – spanning cloud services, applications and marketing services – reached 13.2 billion yuan during the quarter, up 37 per cent from a year earlier.
These AI-powered business segments now accounted for 53 per cent of Baidu’s core business revenue, Li said in the earnings statement, adding that this “further reinforced AI’s position at the core of our business”.
Meanwhile, the legacy business category, including traditional online marketing services, declined 24 per cent to 9.4 billion yuan.
Baidu’s growing AI cloud business is helping offset persistent weakness in its traditional search advertising operations, said Cathy Chan, analyst at securities firm CCB International (CCBI), in a research note ahead of the earnings announcement.
Baidu was seeing robust demand for enterprise computing power, as AI-generated search answers were increasingly displacing traditional advertising placements, Chan said in the note.
Shen Dou, Baidu’s executive vice-president and head of the company’s cloud business, said during an earnings call that the company was optimistic its AI cloud infrastructure business could sustain its growth momentum, citing accelerating demand for AI computing across training and inference workloads, a growingly diversified customer base and revenue mix, and buoyant adoption of AI across different industries.
“We are encouraged to see more customers choosing longer contract terms and making prepayments,” Shen said.
The earnings announcement came days after the company showcased its latest AI progress and computing infrastructure at its annual Baidu World conference.
At the event, the company touted how its adoption of AI agents had streamlined internal operations, with the number of AI agents deployed to assist employees surging over the past year to automate their work.
“Many of our [staff] are helping prepare for the [event] on-site today, but their AI agents are working on assignments non-stop, not missing a single task they are supposed to deliver,” Li said during the event.
Baidu unveiled the latest iteration of its model series at the event. Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview featured a larger parameter size and general improvements, it said.
Baidu’s Tianchi 512 Supernode system seen at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 18. Photo: Reuters
The model could generate more than 200 tokens – around 150 English words – per second while reducing computing and memory requirements through architectural improvements, the company said, making it one of the speediest Chinese models in generating responses.
The efficiency-focused model was available to developers through Baidu’s cloud platform, priced as low as 1 yuan (US$0.15) for every million input tokens.
Baidu also flexed its AI hardware muscle at Thursday’s event, previewing its Tianchi 1024-chip supernode, set for release next year, which the company said could be scaled up to support 500,000 chips, providing the massive computing power needed to run increasingly complex AI models.
The company’s chip unit Kunlunxin also pledged to maintain heavy investment in research and development and launch new AI processors annually in the next few years, seeking to deliver higher computing performance at lower costs per token.
Li said the company was moving forward with a planned initial public offering for Kunlunxin, without providing a timeline for the listing. He also highlighted the chip unit during the earnings call, describing it as a key part of Baidu’s AI infrastructure that allowed the company to better integrate and optimise its computing stack while gradually lowering costs as deployment scaled up.
In autonomous driving, Baidu’s Apollo Go robotaxi service expanded its global footprint to 30 cities worldwide. In Dubai, it added to its fully driverless commercial fleet while in London, Apollo Go continued open-road testing in partnership with Uber and Lyft, progressively expanding its testing areas.
Baidu said that as of October 31 this year, its Apollo Go fleet had accumulated more than 390 million autonomous kilometres.
Baidu’s Hong Kong-listed shares closed up 1.42 per cent at HK$75.25 ahead of the earnings announcement on Monday.
By Ben Jiang

title_en: China’s Moonshot AI puts Kimi models into race for scientific discoveries
content_en:
Company explores applications that demand more advanced reasoning, pushing into biology, chemistry and pharmaceutical research.
People visit the Moonshot AI booth during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 18. Photo: AFP
Chinese artificial intelligence start-up Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi models, is setting its sights on scientific discovery, joining US rivals in the race to turn AI into a research engine.
The Beijing-based company is increasingly exploring applications that demand more advanced AI reasoning capabilities, pushing into the realms of biology, chemistry and pharmaceutical research.
“The real excitement is … science,” said Giacomo Ficari, Moonshot’s director of international, during a keynote address at the Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon late last week. “While finance and legal are [at] the same level of intelligence [as] coding, science is actually bringing the level of intelligence even higher.”
Ficari said coding, which had driven much of the recent demand for advanced AI models, was approaching saturation in terms of technological progress, prompting Moonshot to explore applications in domains like scientific and pharmaceutical research.
“You see OpenAI focusing a lot on mathematics,” he said. “We are focusing a lot on biology and chemistry. Think about what we can do with pharma and all the technological advancement.”
The company has begun putting its ambitions into practice. On Thursday, DP Technology – a Beijing-based AI-for-science start-up – announced a collaboration with Moonshot to integrate the Kimi K3.1 Pro model into its research agent for biomedical applications.
DP Technology said that in an internal evaluation of AI models for biological research tasks, Kimi K3.1 Pro paired with its coding tool achieved the highest score, relative to other undisclosed model combinations.
In one demonstration, BioMaster, DP Technology’s research agent, and Kimi analysed gene-expression data from 3,696 mouse pancreatic cells, identifying 100 candidate genes for further investigation in about 90 minutes, compared with an estimated four hours of human work.
While the results highlight how advanced models can automate time-consuming data analysis, they stop short of showing an ability to make autonomous scientific breakthroughs.
[embedded media]
That distinction was underscored earlier this month in a paper co-authored by Moonshot founder Yang Zhilin and Turing Award-winning computer scientist Andrew Yao, which examined whether leading AI models could contribute to original mathematical research.
The study introduced a benchmark comprising 100 tasks spanning mathematical theorem proving, algorithm development and attempts to solve long-standing unsolved problems in theoretical computer science.
The researchers found that while frontier models could produce verifiable results and assist with complex research tasks, none could independently solve the benchmark’s open mathematical conjectures – highlighting both the promise and current limits of AI in autonomous research.
Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
The company’s push comes amid rival claims of scientific milestones from US peers.
Last month, OpenAI claimed in a blog post that its models had made three new discoveries across mathematics, computer science and physics, generating proofs for long-standing problems. However, its results drew pushback from the scientific community, particularly mathematicians.
In September, Anthropic said its researchers had used its Claude model to discover a new enzyme system.
Still, industry insiders remain cautious about AI’s near-term impact on pharmaceutical research and development.
A survey of 50 US-based pharmaceutical R&D executives by Citi in June found that only 24 per cent expected AI to significantly improve the probability of drug success, even though 72 per cent said their firms were “scaling” or had “fully scaled” the technology across research operations.
By Chong Ming Lee

title_en: Alibaba says new flagship AI model cuts task costs by 60% while tightening cyber guardrails
content_en:
The company says its next-generation model, Qwen 5, will be scaled up to between 5 trillion and 10 trillion parameters.
Alibaba’s Max series of models had always been closed-source until Qwen 3.8, which was made available as open source in August. Photo: Shutterstock
Alibaba Group Holding has launched its most advanced artificial intelligence model to date, Qwen4-Max, with strict cybersecurity guardrails, as the tech giant balances safety with a continued commitment to open sourcing amid growing global concerns over AI-enabled cyberattacks.
The release highlights a growing focus on safety in China’s AI industry as Alibaba said it intentionally filtered the model’s training data to remove offensive cyberattack capabilities while retaining capabilities useful for cyber defence such as vulnerability detection.
The Hangzhou-based company also introduced dedicated data sets and post-training enhancements to mitigate chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) risks, it said on Monday.
Alibaba also highlighted the model’s improvements in scientific research, including the completion of a continuous 48-hour run to discover an experimentally validated coolant molecule for next-generation semiconductor chips, as well as autonomous research on Alzheimer’s disease.
There is heated debate about whether open-weight models, which are favoured by Chinese companies, could heighten CBRN risks more than the closed-source models championed by their US rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
Some experts have warned that AI systems could eventually be powerful enough to enable malicious actors or states to develop CBRN weapons.
While Qwen4-Max is a closed model, Alibaba reaffirmed its open-source strategy by noting that smaller-scale, open-weight versions of the Qwen4 series would be released to global developers soon.
Alibaba’s Max series of models had always been closed-source until Qwen 3.8, which was made available as open source in August. The Max series is also the company’s largest model by parameter size. However, the company highlighted its achievements in making its latest model more cost-efficient when served to users.
Qwen4-Max boasts 2.4 trillion parameters, the same size as its previous Qwen3.8-Max, though it activates only 71 billion parameters per token – 25 per cent less than its predecessor.
[embedded media]
That allows it to deliver superior reasoning capabilities while bringing down inference costs, cutting the average cost per task by 60 per cent, according to Alibaba, citing an internal benchmark called Work360, which evaluates model performance on various work tasks.
The model is currently available via QwenCloud, with input pricing set at about 8 US cents per 1 million tokens.
Alibaba’s AI efforts have focused heavily on capturing the enterprise AI market and cultivating an open-source community to outpace local rivals like DeepSeek and Z.ai, as well as US competitors.
Liu Dayiheng, head of Alibaba’s Qwen large language model team, presented a road map outlining plans for the Qwen 4, Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 series in September, while stressing the team’s commitment to the open-source community earlier this month at the World Internet Conference in Wuzhen.
The company has said that its next-generation model, Qwen 5, would be scaled up to between 5 trillion and 10 trillion parameters.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
Separately, Shenzhen-based Tencent Holdings rolled out Hy4 Flash on Monday, a lightweight and low-cost model with 224 billion parameters priced at 7 US cents per million input tokens.
Described as the most cost-effective Hy model to date, the flash variant comes less than two weeks after the launch of Tencent’s latest flagship model Hy4, which the company ranks among the world’s first-tier open-weights models.
Tencent said the flash model only cost one-twentieth as much per task as the flagship Hy4, and one-eighth as much as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 from Hangzhou-based rival DeepSeek.
By Ann Cao, Iris Deng

title_en: Could Jensen Huang make a comeback? Musk, other tech heavyweights pressure Nvidia board
content_en:
Online petition tops 136,000 signatures as supporters warn Nvidia risks losing key business ties built around former CEO’s leadership.
Jensen Huang attends a luncheon for tech leaders hosted by US President Donald Trump at the White House on September 29, 2026. Photo: Reuters
Support has continued to build across the tech industry for Jensen Huang, with figures including Elon Musk rallying behind the former Nvidia CEO and an unverified online petition calling on the board to reinstate the company’s founder.
Organisers of the “Stand with Jensen” campaign, who describe themselves as Nvidia employees, partners and shareholders, urged the board to “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”, according to an open letter on the initiative’s website.
As of 2pm on Sunday, the petition had attracted more than 136,000 signatures, including entries claiming to represent over 6,800 current Nvidia employees and 73,000 shareholders, as well as Tesla and SpaceX head Musk and other global tech leaders.
The petition does not include identity-verification measures, allowing users to submit names and titles without proof.
[embedded media]
However, several prominent industry figures, including YouTube co-founder Steve Chen and Atreides Management managing partner Gavin Baker, have publicly endorsed the campaign on X.
Musk, who has repeatedly voiced support for Huang since the controversy erupted, said on social media on Saturday that a “petition is under way to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too”.
The post came in response to a Tesla engineer who urged Nvidia employees to resign in an effort to pressure the board, drawing comparisons with the staff revolt that helped reinstate Sam Altman as OpenAI CEO in 2023.
Altman returned as OpenAI CEO four days after being abruptly dismissed by the company’s board in November 2023, following an intense backlash from investors and employees.
Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contractElon Musk, Tesla
In a separate post on Sunday, Musk warned that Nvidia could struggle to maintain some key business relationships without Huang.
“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” he wrote.
Support for Huang has gathered momentum since he resigned on Thursday amid media reports of alleged extramarital affairs, ending a 33-year tenure during which he transformed Nvidia into a US$4 trillion artificial intelligence chip powerhouse.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress has assumed the role of interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.
Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Baker, both major Nvidia investors, also urged the board to keep its options open, including “the potential return of Jensen Huang”, in an open letter.
They called on directors to “pursue a slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia”.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang embraces Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang after delivering his keynote speech at Computex 2024 in Taiwan in June 2024. Photo: Reuters
Gerstner and Baker said they believed the board “should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders”.
Some employees have voiced opposition to the board’s handling of Huang’s departure. Robotics engineer Darrell Dai said in a widely shared social media post on Sunday that he planned to leave the company, citing frustration that employees were excluded from the process that led to Huang’s resignation.
“I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here,” he said. “On this decision, I have not felt heard.”
By Iris Deng

title_en: Key takeaways from speeches at Apec CEO Summit, including Xi and Putin addresses
content_en:
Several world leaders spoke at the gathering, with technological innovation and regional partnership common subjects.
President Xi Jinping (centre) and leaders gather for a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: AP
Global leaders addressed a crowd of business figures at Wednesday’s Apec CEO Summit, sharing their perspectives on the most pressing issues affecting the world economy and trade relations.
Here are our summaries of the speeches, including the major points covered by each address.
President Xi Jinping
Xi described the current geopolitical situation as “complex and volatile”, citing rising protectionism, weak growth momentum and new challenges from emerging technologies.
Xi said “innovation is crucial for progress” in the Asia-Pacific region, as unicorn companies and large language models have “emerged in large numbers”. He praised China as a vast testing ground for innovation, where cutting-edge technologies could be tested and refined through real-world application.
Xi said China was accelerating the development of a big domestic consumption market and more diverse sources of demand would be unleashed. He vowed that China would not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also carry out reforms in trading rules and regulation, fostering a more stable and predictable environment for all companies to invest and do business.
Xi emphasised Shenzhen’s status as a part of China’s Greater Bay Area – which comprises Guangdong province, Hong Kong and Macau. He said China supported the establishment of an association for bay areas across the world to deepen exchanges.
Russian President Vladimir Putin
Putin said sanctions, tariffs and export limitations could hold back development, but were not capable of fully stopping growth or destroying economies. Europe and the US had “punished themselves” with such measures, he said.
The Russian leader said European nations, by halting the supply of Russian energy resources that fuelled the continent’s prosperity for decades, have caused their own decline, lost their industrial capacity and raised deficits and inflation.
He noted the share of the dollar and the euro in Russia’s exports has slumped due to sanctions from banks and other financial organisations, but Russia had established networks to continue making transactions.
He said Russia is moving full speed ahead – faster than expected – and was committed to cooperation with the Asia-Pacific region. He called for the build-up of logistical links within Apec.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney
Carney noted economic ties between China and Canada were getting closer, and said China had restored market access for more than 90 per cent of the Canadian trade that had faced tariffs. Canadian businesses already enjoyed tariff-free access to 1.5 billion consumers, and the country aimed to double that soon, he said.
Carney said Canada had signed over 50 critical minerals agreements with more than 15 countries in the past year, diversifying its sourcing for crucial supply chains. He also urged economies to take steps to diversify away from single payment channels.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim
Anwar said developing economies needed a breath of “new life” by using platforms like Asean and Apec to promote trade and investment. They should engage with global superpowers like the US, the European Union and China, which play an important role in multilateral mechanisms, and be treated with respect, dignity and equality, he urged.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul
Anutin stressed Thailand was working with global partners and extending cooperation beyond the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to tackle online scams, which he called a shared threat affecting many countries in the region. He also talked up Thailand’s economic transformation, including upgrading its automotive manufacturing and developing capabilities in semiconductors, AI and advanced medical technologies.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese
Albanese pledged to create conditions across the Asia-Pacific region to deploy AI safely and responsibly, bringing investments, research and businesses together to build new capabilities and create secure jobs. He said Australia was setting its own terms and developing AI standards to shape the technology’s future.
By Mandy Zuo

title_en: Putin says Western sanctions are backfiring as he pitches Russia as Asia-Pacific trade hub
content_en:
The Russian leader, set to join Xi Jinping and Donald Trump for a trilateral meeting on Thursday, also promoted Moscow’s bid to host Apec in 2035.
Putin delivers a speech at Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, on Wednesday. Photo: Reuters
Russian President Vladimir Putin has argued that Western economic sanctions are losing their effectiveness and harming the countries that impose them, saying Moscow’s reduced reliance on the US dollar and euro shows it has adapted to the restrictions.
Speaking at the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday morning, Putin said the European Union, one of the main enforcers of sanctions against Russia, was losing industrial capacity and falling behind in global competition. He cited the bloc’s deficits and inflation as signs of weakness, while saying external pressure had pushed Russia to strengthen its technological sovereignty and increase industrial production.
Traditional tools of economic dominance and coercion were now a thing of the past, Putin said. Sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions could constrain development but were no longer capable of fully halting growth or destroying national economies, he added.
“Any artificial barriers, in any links of the supply chain, result in damage to all participants,” Putin said, adding that countries that had imposed sanctions or other embargoes on Russia were also suffering costs.
European countries, he said, had caused their own decline by ending imports of Russian energy, which he said had supported the continent’s prosperity for decades.
Since Russia invaded Ukraine, the EU has sought to dramatically reduce its reliance on Russian energy, banning most seaborne oil imports from late 2022 as Europe grappled with an energy crisis marked by soaring gas prices and inflation.
The EU and the US have also imposed sweeping economic and financial sanctions on Moscow, including freezing Russian central bank assets and restricting banks’ access to the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, commonly referred to as Swift.
Putin said the share of the US dollar and euro in Russia’s export payments had fallen from 85 per cent in 2021 to about 9 per cent today, adding that Moscow had built alternative networks to sustain global financial transactions.
“Let me emphasise: we have never rejected the euro or the dollar,” Putin said, adding that it was the holders of those currencies who had cut off their use. “And by doing so, they have punished themselves.”
With the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Israel war on Iran disrupting global transport and trade routes, Putin said Russia could offer “wide opportunities” for land and maritime transit. Moscow was upgrading its eastern rail links, including the Trans-Siberian network, and expanding the capacity of border checkpoints, he said.
The Russian leader called for greater investment in logistics links and transport infrastructure to reflect shifts in the global economy and help Asia-Pacific economies expand their exports.
Russia, he said, had applied to host Apec in 2035 and was confident its bid would win the support of member economies.
Putin’s speech was followed by a meeting with President Xi Jinping, their fourth this year. The two leaders are set to join US President Donald Trump for a trilateral meeting on Thursday, according to the People’s Daily.
By Mia Nurmamat

title_en: China’s youth unemployment rate down as tide of fresh graduates continues to ebb
content_en:
National Bureau of Statistics says jobless rate for those aged 16 to 24, excluding students, fell to 17.2 per cent in October.
A worker on a smart technology-powered spinning production line at a textile factory in Yudu county, Jiangxi province, on Tuesday. Photo: Xinhua
China’s youth unemployment rate fell in October as the seasonal impact of university students’ summer graduations continued to ease.
The unemployment rate among people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, declined to 17.2 per cent last month from 18 per cent in September and 18.9 per cent in August, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday.
The October rate was 0.1 percentage points lower than the same month last year.
August’s figure and the identical number from the same month of last year were the highest readings since Beijing revised its calculation methodology to exclude students after the youth unemployment rate hit 21.3 per cent in June 2023.
The unemployment rate for those aged 25 to 29, also excluding students, was 7.3 per cent last month, compared with 7.4 per cent in September and 7.5 per cent in August.
The improvement in youth unemployment came as other economic indicators remained weak. Retail sales rose 0.4 per cent year on year in October, down from year-on-year growth of 1.1 per cent year in September, while industrial output growth slowed to 4.8 per cent from 5.5 per cent, according to the bureau.
Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1 per cent in the first 10 months of the year compared with the same period last year.
A report last month by the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (Merics) said fresh graduates in China faced fierce competition for entry-level positions within a growing pool of educated jobseekers, as Beijing’s preference for hi-tech industries restricted overall jobs growth.
Job growth in some advanced manufacturing sectors had not been sufficient to offset employment declines in traditional industries such as textiles and coal mining, Merics found, while weak consumption had limited hiring in services.
Despite China’s growing trade surplus, the overall number of industrial sector jobs had remained basically flat since the end of the zero-Covid policy in December 2022, the report added. It said more workers were relying on “flexible employment” for income, with the gig economy workforce set to hit 320 million, or roughly 40 per cent of urban employment, this year.
The overall surveyed urban unemployment rate fell to 5.1 per cent in October from 5.2 per cent in September, according to bureau data.
Meanwhile, average weekly working hours of employees in enterprises remained high at 48.3 hours last month, unchanged from September and compared with 48.2 in August, July and June.

title_display: China’s youth unemployment rate down as tide of fresh graduates continues to ebb
content_display:
National Bureau of Statistics says jobless rate for those aged 16 to 24, excluding students, fell to 17.2 per cent in October.
A worker on a smart technology-powered spinning production line at a textile factory in Yudu county, Jiangxi province, on Tuesday. Photo: Xinhua
China’s youth unemployment rate fell in October as the seasonal impact of university students’ summer graduations continued to ease.
The unemployment rate among people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, declined to 17.2 per cent last month from 18 per cent in September and 18.9 per cent in August, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday.
The October rate was 0.1 percentage points lower than the same month last year.
August’s figure and the identical number from the same month of last year were the highest readings since Beijing revised its calculation methodology to exclude students after the youth unemployment rate hit 21.3 per cent in June 2023.
The unemployment rate for those aged 25 to 29, also excluding students, was 7.3 per cent last month, compared with 7.4 per cent in September and 7.5 per cent in August.

title_en: As caution grips consumer spending, China’s jewellery sales tumble
content_en:
Sliding marriage rates and falling gold prices are also weighing on the sector.
A customer tries on lab-grown diamond jewellery at the Jiaruifu Diamond showroom in Henan, China, in September. Photo: Reuters
Tang Fang used to buy herself one or two pieces of jewellery, such as rings or bracelets, every year. But this year, with her third son starting primary school and fewer orders coming in for her sales business, she has put those purchases on hold.
“I really wanted to, because I love bright, shiny things,” the 46-year-old said. “But I’m under a lot of financial pressure now. My two youngest sons are in primary and middle school, and I need to spend more on their education.”
Tang is among a growing number of consumers cutting back on discretionary spending as economic uncertainty pushes households to prioritise more practical purchases. Combined with a decline in marriage registrations and rising competition from lower-priced lab-grown diamonds, that trend is adding pressure to China’s jewellery market.
The slowdown is reflected in sales data. China’s jewellery sales plunged 28.7 per cent year on year to 25.5 billion yuan (US$3.8 billion) in October, following a 9.6 per cent decline in September, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday.
Sales also edged down from 25.8 billion yuan in September, despite the National Day holiday in October, a week-long break that is traditionally a peak period for shopping and weddings.
For the first 10 months of the year, jewellery sales fell by 5.4 per cent from a year earlier.
The pullback is not limited to middle-aged consumers facing household financial pressures. Younger shoppers are also reassessing whether jewellery is worth the expense.
Xu Tianqi, who bought his first ring from Monaco-based brand APM in June, said he recently spent considerable time weighing whether to buy another ring to mark the start of his first job. In the end, he decided against it and instead set aside part of his salary for unexpected expenses.
“I bought my first ring when I was still in graduate school,” he said. “But now I have to earn money and think more practically, so jewellery has become less of a priority.”
[embedded media]
The slowdown in demand also extends beyond individual purchases to the wedding market, traditionally an important source of jewellery sales in China.
China witnessed a nearly 10 per cent drop in the number of marriages in the first three quarters of the year, recording 4.648 million marriage registrations during the period, official data released in early November showed.
Many Chinese brides traditionally receive “five golds” – earrings, a necklace, a ring, a bangle and an anklet, with regional variations – as wedding gifts from the groom’s family.
Meanwhile, the natural diamond market is facing a different kind of pressure from the growing availability of lower-priced lab-grown alternatives. Natural diamonds have traditionally commanded a premium because of their rarity and perceived value, but lab-grown stones are giving consumers another option.
China is the world’s largest producer of lab-grown diamonds, with the central province of Henan serving as a major production hub, according to state-owned news outlet China News earlier this month.
The decline in jewellery sales also “partly reflects lower gold prices”, according to note by investment bank and financial services company Macquarie on Monday.
Spot gold traded at about 828 yuan a gram on the Shanghai Gold Exchange on Monday, more than 30 per cent below its all-time high in late January.
Amid weakening jewellery demand, retailers have been scaling back their store networks. Major brands including Chow Tai Seng, Lao Feng Xiang and Chow Tai Fook have each reportedly closed hundreds of outlets this year.
By Alice Li

content_en:

President Xi Jinping (centre) and world leaders pose for a group photo during the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: Reuters

President Xi Jinping and other world leaders spoke at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) CEO Summit on Wednesday in Shenzhen.
China’s first Apec summit since 2014, this year’s edition saw a host of business figures in attendance, including several high-profile executives in tech and other emerging industries.

title_en: Chile and Mexico, caught in US-China rivalry, pitch industrial upgrades at Apec
content_en:
The two countries are pushing separate economic agendas as Washington’s effort to limit China’s regional influence reshapes landscape.
Mexico President Claudia Sheinbaum attends the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters
The presidents of two Latin American nations have used the Apec summit in Shenzhen to court foreign investment, setting out plans to expand domestic industry and secure greater economic benefits from global trade.
“Those of us who are resource-rich countries do not want to merely be a place where raw materials are extracted,” said Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast, making his first visit to China since taking office in March, during a speech on Tuesday afternoon.
“We want processing, research and innovation to happen there as well,” he said at the forum’s CEO Summit, which was attended by executives including Wang Chuanfu, chairman of electric car maker BYD.
Minerals, Kast said, would be essential to a clean-energy future, noting that electric cars required several times more copper than conventional vehicles and many batteries needed lithium.
Chile is the world’s leading copper producer and holds one of the largest lithium reserves on the planet, he added.
“No one can do things alone. Some hold the resources, others hold the technology and others the capital – and all of us need open markets,” Kast said.
Chile was the first Latin American country to sign a free-trade agreement with China, which took effect 20 years ago. China is now its largest trading partner, export market and source of imports globally, according to Xinhua.
Chile is also China’s third-largest trading partner in Latin America and its largest source of imported copper, the state news agency reported.
Earlier on Tuesday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum presented her “Plan Mexico” initiative to business leaders from Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies, highlighting opportunities to improve infrastructure and expand domestic manufacturing.
[embedded media]
“Over six years, from 2024 to 2030, Plan Mexico thus envisions US$432 billion in public, mixed and private infrastructure investment,” Sheinbaum said.
Mexico planned to expand power generation by 32,000 megawatts, with a growing share coming from renewable energy, she stated. It also aimed to build nearly 2,500 kilometres (1,553 miles) of passenger and freight railways, including a freight rail line along the Interoceanic Corridor between the Pacific and the Gulf of Mexico. The corridor could become an alternative to the Panama Canal, she said.
Sheinbaum met President Xi Jinping on Tuesday afternoon, also pitching Plan Mexico and saying her government sought to strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, technology, manufacturing and artificial intelligence, according to a Chinese readout.
Xi said China and Mexico must treat each other with sincerity, deepen political mutual trust, keep bilateral relations steadily on the right track and intensify exchanges and cooperation across all fields and at all levels, according to the readout. He also met with the Chilean president in the afternoon.
Mexico became a popular investment destination for Chinese companies venturing overseas after the US-China trade war began in 2018, largely because of its proximity to the American market. But that enthusiasm has cooled over the past two years as Washington pressed the Mexican government to scrutinise Chinese investment and widen tariffs on the country’s goods.
Mexico already imposes duties on many of those goods under a package Congress approved in December. The tariffs, which took effect on January 1, range from 5 to 50 per cent and apply to 1,463 products from countries without trade agreements with Mexico, including China.
Latin America has become a growing point of contention between the US, long the region’s dominant power, and China, whose economic presence has expanded. Chinese investors have become more cautious this year amid heightened geopolitical tensions, including a US raid that ousted the then-Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and a Panama Supreme Court ruling that annulled contracts allowing a Hong Kong-based company to operate container ports along the Panama Canal.
By Ji Siqi

title_en: Can Xi-Trump talks at Apec turn China’s pledge to buy 200 Boeing jets into firm orders?
content_en:
The company’s executive in charge of global business welcomes regional connectivity and trade, but questions remain over Chinese airlines placing new orders.
President of Boeing Global Brendan Nelson attends a session at the 2026 Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen, southern China’s Guangdong province, on Tuesday. Photo: ap
China’s expanding air links, a proposed Asia-Pacific free-trade agreement and an expected meeting between the US and Chinese presidents are creating a more favourable backdrop for regional business, a top Boeing executive said. But he offered no update on China’s pledge to buy the company’s aircraft.
“Over the last 10 years, airlines within Apec economies have established 5,000 city-to-city links, with a third of them in Asia and almost every one includes a Chinese city,” said Brendan Nelson, president of Boeing Global, at the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday.
He pointed to rising demand for air travel in China on the back of the country’s growing middle class, describing the changes as a “revolution”. The event he addressed brought together business leaders from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies ahead of the Apec leaders’ summit on Wednesday and Thursday.
Nelson, who oversees global strategy and operations outside the United States, cited routes linking Chinese cities to destinations across the Pacific and elsewhere on the continent.
“Hainan Airlines does a flight from Beijing to Mexico City. China Southern flies from Guangzhou to Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea. These are a reflection of the connectivity being achieved and the proud role that [Boeing airliners] play in it,” he said.
Nelson also revealed that he had discussed with senior Chinese ministers how Boeing could help deepen China’s connections with the rest of the world, though he stopped short of addressing the country’s plans to buy aircraft from the American firm.
In May, China agreed to buy at least 200 Boeing aircraft following a meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Beijing. The pledge raised hopes that Boeing could regain market share in the world’s second-largest aviation market following a decade-long drought, but progress has since appeared to stall with no orders finalised.
There is anticipation that the two countries could make progress on business deals when Xi and Trump sit down for talks in Shenzhen – and Nelson underscored the significance of the two leaders meeting for the third time this year.
“One of the great achievements, if you’re sitting here looking at the sea of men and women from 21 Apec economies in a world of disorder, is when the presidents of the US and China meet,” he told the event. “That, in itself, is a significant achievement here in Shenzhen.”
Nelson added that a proposed free-trade area spanning the Pacific could support business. “Air cargo, driven in part by AI and e-commerce in a broader FTA, has and will allow us to navigate geopolitical challenges,” he said.
Beijing is pushing to establish an action framework for the long-discussed Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP), which first appeared on the agenda in 2006. Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation members are negotiating a statement that could be agreed at this week’s leaders’ meeting.
Wang Jian, a retired fleet management chief engineer at China Southern’s bases in Guangzhou and Zhuhai, said Boeing would be hoping that China’s hosting of Apec could reduce trade frictions to bolster its prospects.
“Trade disputes have a knock-on impact on high-profile jet purchases between China and the US, which are usually used as bargaining chips. A senior Boeing executive attending Apec in China ahead of Xi-Trump talks is a good sign, even if no specific order has been finalised yet,” he said.
For the 200-jet pledge to become binding contracts, Wang said central procurement agencies, including the Civil Aviation Administration of China, would need to allocate slots across major airlines. He assessed that Boeing was still involved in a “complex, multistep order conversion and allocation process”.
In September, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer suggested China was in the process of placing firm orders for 150 Boeing planes. However, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said specific allocations would be announced by individual Chinese carriers at their own pace, rather than as a single group order.
The last time China placed a major Boeing order came in 2017 during Trump’s visit to Beijing. Since then, trade tensions and geopolitical frictions have left the aerospace giant’s business in China on the tarmac.
By contrast, European aircraft manufacturer Airbus has since gained orders in the world’s second-largest economy, while China’s domestically developed C919 passenger jet has been in commercial service since 2023.
By Frank Chen

By contrast, European aircraft manufacturer Airbus has since gained orders in the world’s second-largest economy, while China’s domestically developed C919 passenger jet has been in commercial service since 2023.

title_en: China and Canada agree tariff, currency deal to boost ‘strategic partnership’
content_en:
Nations agree to revive bilateral currency swap and lower trade barriers in several sectors after Xi-Carney meeting in Shenzhen.
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney (left) meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday. Photo: Canadian Press via ZUMA Press/dpa
China and Canada have agreed a basket of measures to deepen their economic and trade relationship – including tariff reductions and a revived bilateral currency swap arrangement – following a meeting between President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Shenzhen on Tuesday.
Canada will expand the scope of tariff exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminium products as part of the deal, while China will lower trade barriers targeting certain Canadian agricultural and seafood products, according to an announcement by China’s Ministry of Commerce.
The two countries will also renew operational testing for a bilateral currency swap between the Chinese and Canadian central banks, which has been on ice for nine years, according to China’s Ministry of Finance. An operational rehearsal would be conducted by the end of 2026, with a test draw slated for 2027, it said.
Talks on reviving the currency swap took place during the second China-Canada Economic and Financial Strategic Dialogue in Vancouver on November 8 and 9, according to a joint outcome document released by the finance ministry on Tuesday afternoon.
Leaders from both sides reviewed the deliverables from the dialogue during their meeting on Tuesday, Carney’s office said.
The swap was first launched in 2014 and lapsed in 2017, around the time US President Donald Trump began his first term. The People’s Bank of China said earlier this year that the revived agreement would run for five years, up from the initial three-year term, with a quota of 200 billion yuan (US$30 billion).
“Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral economic and financial relations and advancing the China-Canada new strategic partnership through practical cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” the joint outcome document said.
Alongside the currency swap arrangement, China is also seeking wider adoption of the yuan for cross-border investment.
The agreement said that China would welcome long-term Canadian investors including pensions through the Qualified Foreign Investor (QFI) scheme and would encourage foreign institutions to issue panda bonds – yuan-denominated bonds issued by foreign entities – in China’s interbank bond market.
China’s Ministry of Finance on November 9 printed its first green sovereign bond marketed in Canada. The 4 billion yuan offering garnered strong international investor appetite, attracting 54.04 billion yuan of subscriptions, equivalent to 13.5 times the amount on offer. Canada voiced support for the issuance in the joint outcome document.
Canada raised tariffs on Chinese steel and aluminium products in 2024 and introduced further duties the following year. But the country has since introduced exemptions for products in areas where Canada faces supply shortages.
Canada has agreed to extend those exemptions for two years and also widen the scope of those waivers, according to China’s Ministry of Commerce.
Washington levied additional 50 per cent duties on a selected roster of Canadian imports in August.
By Emma Ma

title_en: Rio Tinto CEO flags historic copper, lithium demand, urges supply-chain cooperation
content_en:
Head of mining behemoth tells Apec summit annual demand for lithium could soon equal total amount mined to date.
Rio Tinto CEO Simon Trott at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters
With global demand for key minerals such as copper and lithium shortly expected to surpass the total quantities mined since ancient times, British-Australian mining behemoth Rio Tinto has warned of mounting supply pressures and called for greater supply-chain cooperation.
“We’re going to need more copper between now and 2050 than has been mined since the time of the Phoenicians,” Rio Tinto CEO Simon Trott said at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday.
He added that the world’s annual demand for lithium could soon equal the total amount mined to date, attributing the surging need for minerals to long-term trends such as electrification and the growth of artificial intelligence.
Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange remain roughly 20 per cent higher than a year ago after retreating from a record high in September. Meanwhile, demand for lithium, a key raw material for electric vehicle (EV) batteries, is expected to grow as the global green transition gathers pace.
“To be able to deliver that at a time when it’s getting harder and harder to develop projects, we’re going to need all of the innovations,” Trott said.
He said the mining industry had probably adopted more technology in the past five years than in the previous 50, while noting that innovation in integrating supply chains would be even more important in meeting future demand.
If you don’t have supply chains that are integrated … and businesses and governments collaborating, you’re going to see much higher pricesSimon Trott, Rio Tinto
“It’s either going to express itself as economic growth or it’s going to express itself as higher prices,” Trott said, referring to the coming wave of demand for minerals.
“If you don’t have supply chains that are integrated, that are working together, and businesses and governments collaborating, you’re going to see much higher prices than we would otherwise.”
Trott cited the Simandou iron ore project in Guinea, involving the African country’s government, Chinese partners and Rio Tinto, as an example of a partnership that could reshape supply chains.
Simandou, the world’s largest known undeveloped reserve of high-grade iron ore, is strategically important to China, which is seeking to diversify its iron ore supply away from Australia and Brazil, which together account for the bulk of China’s imports.
The project has begun delivering iron ore to China, with the first shipment of about 200,000 tonnes (220,462 short tons) arriving at a port in Zhejiang province in January.
“That consortium, if you’d asked me probably 10 years ago, I would have struggled to imagine how that could be put together,” Trott said, adding that such collaboration could reshape supply chains and help deliver the raw materials needed by industries undergoing rapid technological change.
By Sylvia Ma

title_en: China’s GPS rival BeiDou expands commercial reach with 27% rise in compatible devices
content_en:
Beijing is pushing to turn the satellite navigation system into a bigger commercial force at home and internationally.
A model of the Beidou satellite navigation system captured in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, China, on May 15. Photo: Getty Images
China is stepping up efforts to expand the commercial and industrial reach of its BeiDou satellite navigation system, with the number of devices and units equipped to use it surging 27 per cent in a year.
Excluding consumer electronics, 42 million equipment units supported BeiDou at the end of June, up by 9 million from a year before, state news agency Xinhua reported on Tuesday. The system is widely regarded as China’s home-grown alternative to the United States-run Global Positioning System, better known as GPS.
The growth underscores BeiDou’s expanding presence in China’s consumer and industrial markets, from smartphones and automobiles to shipping.
More than 98 per cent of the 124 million smartphones released domestically in the first six months of the year supported BeiDou positioning, according to Xinhua, citing data from the Global Navigation Satellite System and Location Based Services Association of China.
About 10 million passenger cars made in China and equipped with BeiDou terminals were also sold in the first half of the year, while the number of electric bicycles featuring the technology reached 26 million, Xinhua reported.
In its 15th five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, Beijing pledged to accelerate the use of BeiDou across major industries and consumer markets, as well as promote the technology globally.
The system is already deeply embedded in the Chinese market where it is used to track shipping fleets and guide automated agricultural machinery among other industrial uses.
China’s market regulator recently issued six national technical standards for maritime BeiDou equipment, covering integrated bridge systems, short-message communications and data management.
“These standards ... can provide strong technical support for the large-scale application of BeiDou on waterways,” state broadcaster CCTV reported on Monday.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said in August that BeiDou had been adopted in about 90 per cent of critical industry applications nationwide. The National Development and Reform Commission, China’s top economic planner, said earlier this year that the system would be worth 1 trillion yuan (US$145 billion) within the next five years.
By Xinyi Wu

title_en: Hong Kong firms count on supply chains and AI to offset rising costs, HSBC survey finds
content_en:
Four in five local executives are using AI to mitigate supply chain shocks, but oversight frameworks may be lagging behind.
About 40 per cent of Hong Kong firms say shipping and freight are affecting their costs, according to the HSBC survey. Photo: Felix Wong
Hong Kong businesses are resorting to regional diversification and artificial intelligence to weather rising costs and geopolitical uncertainties, HSBC said on Tuesday in its annual Global Trade Pulse Survey Report.
About 40 per cent of Hong Kong businesses surveyed identified shipping and freight as a factor affecting their cost base over the past six months, ahead of tariffs and currency fluctuations, according to the poll of 500 business leaders in the city.
The results are based on a survey of 10,000 senior executives across 26 markets.
These headwinds were expected to linger. The HSBC report found 64 per cent of Hong Kong business leaders were already grappling with higher overall costs, 70 per cent expected costs to rise further over the next two years and 50 per cent reported higher working capital requirements since last year.
Despite continued uncertainty, 72 per cent of Hong Kong business leaders remained confident they could grow their international trade over the next two years, a modest uptick from a year earlier.
“Hong Kong businesses are showing that resilience is more than absorbing disruption. It’s using change as a catalyst to evolve,” said Frank Fang, HSBC’s head of commercial banking in Hong Kong and Macau.
A general view of Kwai Tsing Container Terminals. Photo: Eugene Lee
“Companies are revising pricing strategies, strengthening supply chains and exploring AI to improve how they operate.”
Four out of five respondents said they had either adopted or were considering using AI tools to improve efficiency or competitiveness. AI joined pricing changes, risk planning and organisational adjustments among the methods businesses were using to mitigate trade disruption.
While 69 per cent of respondents said wider disruption was pushing them to rethink their long-term business models, uncertainty was also creating momentum for transformation, Fang added.
Meanwhile, companies expected AI infrastructure investments to unlock new sources of demand. More than half – 52 per cent – of Hong Kong respondents anticipated that investments in AI and supporting power infrastructure would increase demand for their products and services over the next two years.
AI was also reshaping the way businesses operate and trade, according to HSBC. Sixty-nine per cent of respondents said they had deployed AI in at least one trade-related function, with customer service and demand forecasting as the most common use cases.
The survey, however, indicated that AI adoption may be outpacing the governance frameworks required to support it. While businesses were deploying AI across a range of trade-related functions, they reported uneven levels of testing, accountability and formal oversight.
By Zhu Wenqian

title_en: Indonesia eyes bigger slice of its mineral wealth. Are Chinese investors at risk?
content_en:
The presidential order could reshape foreign investment in the mining sector but implementation remains uncertain, analysts say.
A worker in a protective suit pokes a metal rod to tap slag from a smelting furnace at PT Vale Indonesia’s nickel processing plant in Sorowako, South Sulawesi, Indonesia, on September 12, 2023. Photo: AP
Indonesia, home to the world’s largest nickel reserves, is considering a new rule that would ensure the state receives at least 70 per cent of the benefits from mining permits. The proposal could strengthen Jakarta’s negotiating position with foreign investors, including Chinese companies, but may prove hard to implement given past precedent, analysts said.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto announced the policy in his opening speech at the 2026 Muhammadiyah Tanwir, a major forum of Muhammadiyah, the country’s largest modernist Islamic organisation.
Prabowo said the country’s mineral resources belonged to its people and should be managed in line with the “national interest”. He instructed government ministries, including the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, to ensure that at least 70 per cent of the proceeds from mining permits went to the state, according to a statement published on the Presidential Secretariat’s official website.
“For hundreds of years, nations have come to our archipelago. Do they come here for picnics, for tourism? They come here because we are rich in mineral resources,” Prabowo said during the speech on Saturday.
Analysts said for now, the proposal’s precise terms remained uncertain. “The denominator behind the 70 per cent is undefined – it is still unclear whether the calculation draws on revenue, gross margin or dead rent,” said Zhang Hang, an independent analyst based in Shanghai who specialises in non-ferrous metals. “Whether it applies to existing contracts also remains an open question.”
Indonesia already collects royalties from mining companies at tiered rates across different minerals. For nickel ore, the level ranges from 14 per cent to 19 per cent, depending on the benchmark price.
Even so, Chinese analysts said Prabowo’s public remarks often take a “hawkish” tone while policies tend to be softened following negotiations.
Earlier this year, Indonesian media reported that officials were considering a separate revenue-sharing arrangement for the minerals and coal industries. Under the proposed gross-split scheme, the government would receive 70 per cent of production while mining operators retained 30 per cent, according to reports citing Yuliot Tanjung, vice-minister of Energy and Mineral Resources.
[embedded media]
Then, in June, Bahlil Lahadalia, the Indonesian energy minister, said the government had scrapped the proposal following discussions involving Prabowo.
The global nickel benchmark was largely steady following Prabowo’s announcement on Saturday.
China’s Zhejiang-based Tsingshan Group, the world’s leading stainless-steel manufacturer, ranks among the largest foreign investors in Indonesia’s nickel industry. The company holds a majority stake in Weda Bay Nickel, a joint venture home to one of the world’s largest nickel deposits.
Wang Yanqing, an analyst at Chongqing-based China Futures, agreed that Jakarta’s latest proposal was short on details. “Capturing 70 per cent of a mine’s revenue looks unfeasible to me,” he said.
Beyond the proposed revenue-sharing arrangement, Prabowo also called for stronger oversight of exports. Authorities would aim to verify that shipment volumes were accurately reported, allowing for “more optimal oversight of national wealth management,” the Presidential Secretariat’s website said.
Analysts said Indonesia already exercised tight oversight of nickel output. Indonesian media reported that authorities had approved an updated work plan and budget for 2026, known as the RKAB, which set the nickel ore quota at about 290 million tonnes. Output last year stood at about 320 million tonnes, according to official data.
“Indonesia will keep managing RKAB limits to prevent oversupply and stabilise the international benchmark,” wrote Li Ting, an analyst at Shanghai-based Tongguan Jinyuan Futures, in a November 9 research note.
“It has told domestic producers to curb output when surplus emerges, so Indonesian nickel is not purchased and stockpiled by other countries at depressed prices,” she added.
By Emma Ma

title_en: Nvidia saga making some US CEOs reluctant to attend Apec summit in China: sources
content_en:
Jensen Huang controversy has put off some US executives from attending summit in Shenzhen, for fear of being seen as close to China: sources.
US President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after presenting him with the National Medal of Science at a ceremony in early October. Photo: Reuters
The Nvidia saga that has unfolded over recent weeks has played a role in discouraging some American business leaders from attending this week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, as they worry about being perceived as close to China, according to three people familiar with the matter.
“The recent scandal absolutely impacts executives’ calculus on coming to Apec,” said Zak Dychtwald, the founder of Young China Group, a Shanghai-based consultancy that advises American companies operating in China.
“CEOs had spent the last 18 months returning to China with more confidence, and this sets that back,” added Dychtwald, who is in Shenzhen attending Apec-related activities.
“Some are hesitating, some are sending someone more junior and some are coming quietly.”
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia last week amid reports that he had an extramarital affair with a businesswoman suspected of allegedly engaging in espionage for Beijing. China has strongly denied the allegations, calling them “smears” against China.
“When affiliation with China is once again being discussed in national security terms, simply being seen at Apec becomes a calculated risk,” Dychtwald said.
Executives from more than 100 major global enterprises will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday and Wednesday, which immediately precedes the leaders’ meeting later this week that Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are both set to attend.
[embedded media]
The organiser announced over the weekend that representatives from US companies would make up the largest foreign contingent at the CEO Summit, accounting for nearly 20 per cent of participating firms.
Yet that proportion remains relatively modest, considering American businesses make up nearly 30 per cent of this year’s Fortune Global 500.
While Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, was expected to accompany Trump to Shenzhen, he was not expected to participate in the CEO sessions, sources said.
“[American executives] now appear reluctant to attend the summit and engage in discussions, wary that saying too much could result in a misstep,” said one source on condition of anonymity.
The confirmed US business delegation includes Boeing Global president Brendan Nelson, Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, Mastercard CEO Michael Miebach, PayPal CEO Enrique Lores and United Parcel Service CEO Carol Tome, according to a summit agenda seen by the South China Morning Post.
Google’s head of global government affairs and public policy, Karan Bhatia, will also attend, the agenda showed.
Executives from other countries, such as the United Kingdom and Canada, appeared to be more proactive in attending, the source added.
Another source said the Nvidia issue might have affected some American tech companies’ willingness to attend, but the impact on US firms in other sectors remained limited.
Meanwhile, a third source said logistical challenges remained the key obstacle to attracting more American CEOs to participate.
Some CEOs had decided against attending because the agenda was not clear and the focus would likely be on the trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin scheduled for later this week, the person said.
By Ji Siqi, Frank Chen

title_en: China seeks Apec road map for long-envisioned Asia-Pacific free trade area
content_en:
The push comes as leaders of China, the US and Russia gather in Shenzhen for this week’s summit.
Li Chenggang, China’s vice minister of commerce, speaks at a news conference on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, on Monday. Photo: Reuters
China is pushing to establish an action framework for the long-envisioned Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP), with Apec economies negotiating a statement that could be agreed at this week’s leaders’ meeting.
Li Chenggang, China’s international trade representative and vice-commerce minister, said on Monday that the proposed document would seek to “build a systematic and practical action framework” for the next stage of FTAAP work while encouraging stronger coordination on economic policies and trade rules.
“All parties are stepping up consultations on the statement, which is expected to be reached during the leaders’ meeting,” he said at a press conference in Shenzhen.
First put on the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation agenda in 2006, the FTAAP has long been envisioned as a region-wide free-trade area spanning economies including China, the United States and Russia as well as other major regional trading powers. The ambition has yet to be realised, however, amid geopolitical tensions and competing arrangements.
The leaders of China, Russia and the United States are set to meet on the sidelines of the Apec leaders’ summit on Thursday, China’s foreign ministry confirmed on Monday. The meeting will mark the first time the leaders of the world’s three foremost nuclear and geopolitical powers sit down together in a three-way format.
“We are working with other Apec economies on an outcome document related to the FTAAP and encouraging members to pursue pilot initiatives through the Pathfinder approach and other flexible and pragmatic means,” said Chen Chao, head of the international trade and economic affairs department at the Ministry of Commerce, on Monday.
These efforts could include reducing barriers to trade and investment and improving the FTAAP’s development pathways, action framework and institutional arrangements, Chen said.
Digital trade and artificial intelligence are also featuring prominently in this year’s Apec discussions, according to officials. The two areas accounted for about half of the nearly 50 trade and economic outcomes delivered during the Apec China Year, they added.
Chen said China was leading efforts to develop an Apec framework for digital trade cooperation, aimed at “providing practical and actionable guidelines tailored to the Asia-Pacific region”, with consultations in their final stages.
He added that members have also called for greater capacity to negotiate and implement AI-related trade rules, and to share best practices for applying the technology to trade documentation, logistics and customs clearance.
On Sunday, Li Qingshuang, vice-chairperson of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, said the leaders’ meeting would be preceded by the Apec CEO Summit held on Tuesday and Wednesday, which is expected to draw more than 2,000 participants from business, government and media.
Representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies are expected to take part, with US companies making up the largest foreign contingent and accounting for nearly 20 per cent of participating firms.
On Friday, China and the United States also held the inaugural meeting of their bilateral Board of Trade. The two sides had “candid, deep and constructive” discussions on tariffs, reciprocal tariff cuts and agricultural trade, China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a brief statement on Saturday.
By Sylvia Ma
