title_en: China economy misses expectations in weak start to fourth quarter
content_en:
October’s data release provided little cheer ahead of key economic meeting, with retail sales and industrial production heading a roll-call of disappointments.
Shoppers at a mall in Beijing. Photo: EPA
China’s October retail sales and industrial output both trailed expectations, and other economic measures worsened, as limited stimulus measures failed to revive lacklustre growth.
Consumer spending growth slumped to 0.4 per cent, missing expectations for no change from September’s 1.1 per cent pace based on estimates compiled by Chinese financial data provider Wind. Industrial output growth slowed more than expected to 4.8 per cent from 5.5 per cent in September.
The decline in property investment worsened to 21.6 per cent in the first 10 months of the year from 20.6 per cent between January and September as new mortgage subsidies and other measures did little to ease a five-year real estate market slump. Policymakers announced the support in late September as weak domestic demand cooled third-quarter growth to the bottom end of the government’s 4.5 per cent to 5.0 per cent full-year growth target.
“There are still unstable and uncertain factors in the international environment, and the domestic imbalance between strong supply and weak demand is acute,” Fu Linghui, a spokesman for the statistics bureau, said at a briefing on Monday following the data release.
Still, the economy was “generally stable” during the month, and on track to hit its annual goal, said bureau spokeswoman Wang Guanhua. This year’s earlier Mid-Autumn Festival also pulled some consumer spending into September, she said.
The slowdown in overall fixed-asset investment worsened to 8.1 per cent in the year to October, missing expectations for a 6.9 per cent decline. The drop in construction spending accelerated from 7.2 per cent in the first nine months of the year.
[embedded media]
Related news:
New-home prices fell by 0.15 per cent last month, little changed from September’s 0.14 per cent decline, according to statistics bureau data tracking 70 Chinese cities. The pace of decline for existing-home prices was also little changed at 0.24 per cent in October versus 0.26 per cent in September. The government granted an annual interest subsidy of 1 percentage point to qualified first-time homebuyers from October 1 in a bid to revive the housing market and the wider economy.
The US-China Board of Trade held its first meeting on Friday ahead of a summit this week between President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump. The two sides held “candid, deep and constructive” exchanges on tariffs, arrangements for reciprocal tariff cuts and agricultural trade during the online meeting, according to a Chinese government statement. Both countries intend to cut tariffs on US$30 billion of imports from the other under the Board of Trade framework. Trump and Xi will meet this week at an Apec summit in Shenzhen. They will also have a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. Separately, an upgraded free- trade pact between China and Asean will take effect on December 1.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang pledged to accelerate efforts to address gaps in the social security system amid demographic changes as he chaired a meeting of the State Council on Thursday. During the meeting of China’s cabinet, Li outlined steps including broadening access to supplementary workplace pensions, making voluntary retirement savings more attractive and supporting the development of private health insurance. Guo Shuqing, a former chairman of the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission, earlier called for new tax sources and greater transfers of state-owned capital to social security funds as he highlighted forecasts that the pension system may run short of funds in the next 20 years.
How others reported it
Policy response: China remains on track to meet its annual growth target despite Monday’s weak data, but the abrupt loss of momentum calls for an urgent policy response. We continue to expect a policy rate cut in the coming months, though the window for meaningful intervention this year is closing fast … The next key policy signals will come in December, when the Politburo meeting and Central Economic Work Conference will set the tone for 2027. (Bloomberg Economics)
Worrying start: Lynn Song, ING chief economist for greater China, described the [data] falls as a “worrying start to the fourth quarter”, adding that the domestic economy “would benefit from more policy support”. (Financial Times)
Subsidising the world: “An export-dependent model essentially means Chinese households are subsidising global consumers,” Alicia Garcia Herrero, a senior fellow at Bruegel, a Brussels-based think tank, told Al Jazeera. “High precautionary savings – driven by falling property wealth and thin social safety nets – leave families with weaker wage growth, deflationary pressures at home, and a smaller share of the country’s economic gains.” (Al Jazeera)
AI driver: “Artificial intelligence has become the most important driver of China’s export growth,” Larry Hu, chief China economist at Macquarie, wrote in a research note last week. He added that chips, computers and related parts are the country’s largest export categories by volume. “While AI has supercharged China’s exports, it has also reduced the need for policy support, and even prompted fiscal tightening, putting further pressure on domestic demand.” (Nikkei Asian Review)
Lopsided growth: The increasingly lopsided growth comes as major trading partners have ramped up calls for the economy to rebalance. Headwinds on China’s export engine could intensify next year, with further trade restrictions from the European Union posing a critical downside risk, Citi Research analysts said. “More EU trade measures targeting China look plausible to us, potentially adding to tensions ahead,” the bank said, though Beijing is likely to be open to negotiating “reasonable, practical concessions”, such as import pledges, sector-specific deals and value-added tax rebate cuts. (CNBC)
The SCMP Plus takeaway
Chinese policymakers gather next month for the most important economic meeting of the year. October’s lacklustre numbers will give them much to think about as they draw up plans for 2027.
The Central Economic Work Conference takes place in mid-December each year, and it is the key forum for drawing up priorities for the 12 months ahead. The meeting sets the tone for potential stimulus measures and helps to shape the annual growth target, which is usually announced in early March.
October’s economic data will ensure plenty of discussion about possible stimulus measures and domestic reforms in the run-up to the meeting, as there were few positives to be found in the statistics bureau’s release.
Factory output fell short of economist expectations. Retail sales also disappointed, with growth of less than 1 per cent for the third month in four. The shorter National Day holidays and earlier Mid-Autumn Festival certainly didn’t help the October numbers. Still, it’s clear that China’s consumers are showing no appetite for opening their wallets.
Elsewhere, the decline in fixed-asset investment accelerated, signalling further erosion in business confidence. The five-year real estate crash also showed no signs of improvement. The slump in new-home sales in terms of floor area worsened to 13.7 per cent in the year to October from 13.2 per cent between January and September.
Coal production slid for a seventh straight month in October as mines came under government scrutiny for safety in the wake of a disaster in May. Power generation fell 2.1 per cent, as a slowdown worsened.
Weak domestic demand means that China is increasingly reliant on exports to fuel growth in what has been described as a K-shaped economy. A boom in outbound shipments means that the trade surplus for the year has already surpassed US$1 trillion.
The risk for China now is overseas markets raising trade barriers to slow the flood of imports and protect domestic industries. That could hurt Chinese producers’ overseas sales and either lead to lower production or more profit-destroying price wars in the saturated domestic market.
Notably, China’s October car production only rose 0.9 per cent, the slowest pace since 2022’s Covid-19 lockdowns, according to Bloomberg News. The slowdown came as China agreed to limit electric-vehicle shipments to Europe and as the nation’s carmaker industry group said that “supercharged” exports would slow due to overseas tariffs and quotas.
Other industries face similar pressures, meaning that China’s policymakers will next month face an unappetising choice – maintain export growth and worsen trade tensions, or cool shipments and stoke domestic economic strains.
Risks on the global stage include higher food costs. The World Bank sees prices rising by 18 per cent across this year and next because of wars, the El Nino weather phenomenon and higher costs for fuel and fertiliser. That’s just the baseline forecast. In a worst-case scenario, food commodity prices could be 12 per cent higher than expected, the institution said in a report last month.
On a brighter note, it expects the price of Brent crude oil to ease to US$79 per barrel in 2027 after surging to US$91 this year from US$69 in 2025. That assumes “no major intensification of conflicts affecting global commodity supplies”. If things go wrong, Brent crude may average US$105 next year, the World Bank said.
China’s policymakers have shown limited appetite for stimulus measures this year, even as growth slows. In January, the central bank cut relending rates to encourage business loans. In August, the Ministry of Finance launched steps to boost consumer spending on big-ticket items like car purchases and home renovations. In September, first-time homebuyers were granted mortgage subsidies, while policy banks got a rate cut for supporting infrastructure projects. Last month, the central bank launched a liquidity backstop for non-bank financial institutions to stabilise the bond market.
Authorities are tending towards doing “just enough” to keep things on track provided export growth remains strong, Macquarie Group said in a note last month.
It’s probably fair to say that the central and local governments will be able to squeeze enough juice out of the fourth quarter for annual growth to limp into the government’s target range. The statistics bureau certainly thinks so.
The question at December’s Central Economic Work Conference meeting will be how much government support is needed to ensure that growth makes a strong start in 2027.
By Brian Rhoads, Raymond Ma

It’s probably fair to say that the central and local governments will be able to squeeze enough juice out of the fourth quarter for annual growth to limp into the government’s target range. The statistics bureau certainly thinks so.
The question at December’s Central Economic Work Conference meeting will be how much government support is needed to ensure that growth makes a strong start in 2027.

title_en: China still has ‘catching up to do’ to become biotech powerhouse, JPMorgan says
content_en:
China has big ambitions in biotech, but a lack of foundational research and geopolitical risks could hold it back, JPMorgan research head says.
China still has ‘catching up to do’ in foundational biopharmaceutical research, according to JPMorgan’s head of China healthcare research. Photo: Shutterstock
A lag in foundational research and looming geopolitical risks will weigh on China’s bid to build a world-class biotechnology innovation ecosystem, even as the sector’s overseas momentum remains strong, according to JPMorgan.
“In China, there is still some catching up to do in basic research, particularly in biological and pharmaceutical research,” said Yang Huang, head of China healthcare research at JPMorgan, during an interview on Wednesday.
To meet the “ambitious goal” set in the country’s new five-year plan for the biopharmaceutical industry, China will need to focus on basic research that pushes the scientific frontier, according to Huang, who was speaking on the sidelines of the investment bank’s APAC Technology, Innovation and Growth conference in Hong Kong.
Beijing said the country should “firmly rank at the global forefront” for biopharmaceutical innovation by 2030 in the plan released in September, with China-originated first-in-class innovative drugs accounting for at least one-quarter of the global total.
Producing these drugs would require “significant investment” and “continued work” from Chinese universities and labs to advance basic research, Huang said.
China’s role as a biotech innovation hub has grown rapidly in recent years, with global pharmaceutical giants increasingly sourcing drug assets from the country. The value of out-licensing deals involving China-developed innovative drugs had reached US$130 billion so far this year, approaching the full-year total for 2025, China’s National Development and Reform Commission said last month.
Most of the Chinese innovative drugs licensed to overseas partners, however, are currently not first-in-class, Huang noted.
China’s push to build a world-leading biotech industry could also face geopolitical barriers, as the effort requires the country to have direct access to developed markets, according to Huang.
Yang Huang, head of China healthcare research at JPMorgan, pictured at the Grand Hyatt Hong Kong in Wan Chai on Tuesday. Photo: Warton Li
Chinese biotech firms currently rely on overseas partners to develop and commercialise their drugs under the dominant out-licensing business model, but a few industry leaders “could consider doing things by themselves”, he said.
Building this independence, however, remained a long-term goal stretching beyond the next three to five years and could be contingent on factors including the global geopolitical landscape, Huang added.
Washington has ramped up its scrutiny of cross-border biopharmaceutical collaboration amid China’s rise in the industry.
The US Treasury Department last month proposed new rules under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (Coins) Act, which, if approved, would curb US biotech investments in certain nations including China.
The Biosecure Act, meanwhile, will prohibit entities that receive federal funding and contracts from doing business with “biotechnology companies of concern”, with a list of blacklisted companies expected to be released by the end of this year.
Such geopolitical risks remained a focal point for many investors watching China’s healthcare sector, Huang said, describing the investment bank’s 2027 outlook for the sector as “cautiously optimistic”.
“The best approach for Chinese healthcare companies is to remain patient while continuing to strengthen their research and development capabilities,” Huang said.
Still, the Chinese sector offered high growth potential and could serve as a defensive play for investors looking to rotate their exposure away from artificial intelligence and hardware, he added.
By Xinmei Shen

title_en: Flags, fists and an extra 5 minutes: Manila reveals a confident but tired Trump
content_en:
The US leader may be saving his energy for Shenzhen’s ‘main event’ with Xi and Putin, but maintains post-midterm dominance on world stage.
US President Donald Trump arrives at Manila’s Ninoy Aquino international airport on Tuesday. Photo: AFP
The fist came before the flags. As US President Donald Trump stepped off Air Force One in Manila on Tuesday evening, he raised a clenched fist towards the cameras, accepted miniature American and Philippine flags from a child and waved them down the red carpet.
Roughly 20 hours later, as he departed Manila for Shenzhen in southern China, Trump again raised his fist towards the cameras.
Experts said the sequence which opened his first foreign trip since Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections read as a deliberate signal that Trump intended to continue projecting strength and command on the international stage.
According to some observers, the president looked tired after the long flight from Washington. Others assumed he was simply saving his energy for China, the main event of the Asia trip.
Barely an hour later, the same pattern was observed at the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) photo opportunity with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japan’s Sanae Takaichi and Australia’s Anthony Albanese.
Standing with the three leaders, Trump turned what was meant to be a brief group shot into a five-minute press opportunity. While the others waited largely silent, he fielded questions on domestic issues and the Nvidia controversy.
“Shall we move,” the Indian leader asked at one point and tried to edge the group forward. Trump stayed put, kept answering and then pointed to his counterparts, calling Modi “a very tough man” and Takaichi “even tougher”.
US President Donald Trump unexpectedly extended a photo opportunity with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, India’s Narendra Modi and Australia’s Anthony Albanese in Manila on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
The moment quickly drew online attention as an awkward extension of what was meant to be a brief moment for the cameras, with the other leaders left looking non-committal as they stood beside the US president.
Former Indian foreign secretary Kanwal Sibal called the scene “most disrespectful towards the other three leaders”, saying they “stood there like props” while Modi maintained a “stern” expression.
The Sydney Morning Herald described Modi gesturing as if to ask what was happening, Albanese frowning and fidgeting with his suit button, and Takaichi holding a tight, poker-faced smile as Trump “held court”.
Some social media commenters said Trump looked pale and tired as he waved the flags on the tarmac after the long flight. Others focused on the Quad photo-op, describing it as Trump turning the moment into a personal monologue while the other leaders stood by.
Observers noted a more subdued demeanour from the moment Trump stepped off the plane. “All of a sudden, it seems like a long time,” he remarked at an Asean dinner later that evening.
The energy behind the performance appeared thinner than usual even as he continued to project control, they said.
According to Aubrey Immelman, associate professor of psychology at the College of Saint Benedict and St. John’s University, Trump looked “somewhat disengaged” in the two sets of images.
Immelman said it appeared to him that Trump was just “going through the motions” and really was focused on the “main event” – his trilateral with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.
There was also an alternative explanation, he noted: “a combination of the 80-year-old Trump not being well rested and suffering from jet lag after the long flight from Washington to Manila.”
[embedded media]
Immelman, who has published extensive assessments of Trump’s personality and leadership style, also observed that the other Quad leaders “looked pretty unexpressive and non-committal themselves”.
He added that he “didn’t see much display of interpersonal warmth, but maybe that’s only because it was really just a photo op”.
Despite Trump’s statements that the US would catch up with China on critical minerals and that there was “no better partner for Asean than the US”, Immelman found him “more low-key and less boastful than we’ve seen him on his home turf in recent times, where he would typically rattle off a long list of his achievements in office”.
He concluded that this too “[could] be accounted for by the simple fact that Trump was tired and that he was saving his energy for China”.
According to observers, Manila offered only a partial picture of Trump’s post-midterms demeanour on the world stage. The clearer test will come in Shenzhen, where he will take part in the Apec leaders’ summit as well as sit down for three-way talks with Xi and Putin.
[embedded media]
Christopher Ulrich, a body language expert and political analyst who has advised senior US officials, described the broader trip as staged political theatre of the type that has become familiar.
The domestic timing is hard to ignore. Trump reaches Shenzhen at a moment when his standing at home is under open question and the summit offers him a high-profile world stage.
“We’ll see whether and how that shows up in his dynamics with Putin and Xi,” Ulrich said.
“Some news reports of his engagements at the Manila summit suggest he’s been relaxed and getting on well, so that may serve as a possible baseline to look at for Shenzhen. Yet we won’t know until we see their interactions,” he said.
“Then compare how he engages with Xi and Putin against how he handles allies like Japan and Australia. With allies, we’ve seen the pat on the arm and the first-name warmth.”
Ulrich added that changes in body language with Xi and Putin will be closely watched, as will who opens any joint remarks, how the leaders are positioned and who has the last word.
“Look at what isn’t there as much as what is,” he said.
By Khushboo Razdan

title_en: Chinese spaceplanes’ global reach, a study on erectile dysfunction: 7 science highlights
content_en:
From brain gene-editing attempt gone wrong to high-speed torpedo tech, here are some highlights from SCMP’s recent science reporting.
A photograph of China’s reusable Shenlong spaceplane docked to another spacecraft, taken by Vantor’s WorldView-3 satellite. Photo: Vantor
We have put together stories from our coverage on science from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing.
1. 40 Chinese spaceplanes could hit any target on Earth in minutes: study
A newly released photograph in a US intelligence report has offered a rare glimpse of what is widely believed to be China’s secret Shenlong spaceplane in orbit, showing its payload bay doors open.
2. ‘10,000-tonne level talent’ biologist Zhao Yingming leaves Chicago for Hangzhou
Leading biologist Zhao Yingming, who was the Louis Block Professor in the Ben May Department for Cancer Research at the University of Chicago, has just joined Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, according to sources.
3. Chinese scientists fired after child dies in first brain gene-editing attempt
Investigators in China say Qiu Zilong of Shanghai Jiao Tong University accepted cash and gifts worth about 1.06 million yuan (US$159,000), including high-end liquor and electronic devices. Photo: Xinhua
The world’s first attempt to edit genes inside a child’s brain, which killed a six-year-old girl in Shanghai last year, has led to the firing of scientists following an official investigation that found they had broken research rules and taken money from her family.
4. China holds 80% of world’s underwater data centre patents as energy demands grow
China owns 80 per cent of the world’s underwater data centre patents, giving it a decisive lead in critical technologies, according to a two-decade study of global patents in the field.
5. Chinese engineers reduce cargo ship fuel use by 5% with high-speed torpedo tech
The second-generation intelligent Bubble Lubrication System has been installed on a newly built 50,000-tonne product and chemical tanker. Image: Xinhua
Bubble-lubrication technology allows torpedoes and other projectiles to travel at extreme speeds under water in a gas-filled cavity.
6. China eyes new grip on EV sector with high-performance rare-earth rubber
China’s high-performance rare-earth rubber faces a commercial test as manufacturers seek to expand its use in electric vehicle (EV) and heavy-duty tyres, with market data suggesting it commands a higher price than conventional synthetic rubber.
7. Wearing briefs boosts erectile dysfunction risk, 26,000-man study in China finds
Large-scale Chinese study finds that tight briefs can affect sperm count, semen quality and sexual function. Photo: Shutterstock
From A-list underwear campaigns to everyday wardrobe staples, tight briefs are often hailed as the ultimate symbol of masculine appeal. However, a major new study out of China suggests that choosing tight underwear over classic boxer shorts could lead to higher rates of erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation and prostatitis.
By SCMP

title_en: From war games to crisis planning: Manila’s bid for a ‘Squad’ command hub
content_en:
A joint centre with the US, Japan and Australia could boost intelligence sharing, though analysts say it falls short of a mutual pact.
From left: Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth leave after posing for photos ahead of their quadrilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu in October. Photo: AFP
As the Philippines eyes a coordination hub with defence partners to bolster its regional security shield, analysts say Manila stands to gain greater stability – even if closer military ties do not guarantee allied intervention in a crisis.
The strategy hinges on a proposed Combined Coordination Centre (CCC) with “Squad” partners the United States, Japan and Australia. The hub is expected to give the Philippines faster access to intelligence, improved maritime surveillance and a more unified response to China’s growing regional footprint.
Coupled with a new defence pact with Canberra, the initiative underscores Manila’s push to secure more dependable backing from its partners amid a long-standing South China Sea territorial row with Beijing that has escalated into violent clashes at sea.
[embedded media]
But observers say the hub’s effectiveness could depend on the trajectory of US-China relations, highlighting Manila’s delicate balancing act between strengthening deterrence and avoiding the crosshairs of superpower rivalry.
The Philippines’ Department of National Defence announced plans to establish the CCC in a statement on November 10. Philippine National Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr discussed the move with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles in Cebu on October 28, on the sidelines of the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus.
According to Manila, Squad leaders committed to establishing the hub to synchronise defence investments and expand the scope and frequency of joint military drills. The department has not yet released details on the centre’s location, organisational structure, timeline or specific functions.
Rachel Vandenbrink, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), said the centre would institutionalise coordination and allow the four nations to respond more rapidly to crises. Vandenbrink said the hub was expected to be housed at Camp Aguinaldo – the main headquarters of the Philippine military – and “staffed continuously”, adding that it could facilitate real-time intelligence sharing, maritime surveillance, contingency planning and more coordinated public messaging.
Philippine soldiers march during a military parade marking the 89th anniversary of the Armed Forces of the Philippines at Camp Aguinaldo in Manila in December 2024. Photo: AFP
Vandenbrink noted that the initiative built on expanding joint drills, including Japan’s participation in Balikatan – the largest annual US-Philippines military exercise – and Manila’s growing role in Australia’s Exercise Pitch Black.
She added that the hub complemented the Australia-Philippines Defence Cooperation Arrangement signed on Sunday during the Asean summit, which commits both sides to mutual consultations during contingencies.
“The two developments are complementary, with the [arrangement] providing a framework for bilateral political consultation and the [centre] a platform for multilateral operational coordination,” Vandenbrink said.
Lucas Myers, assistant director at the University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy, said the hub strengthened Manila’s deterrence by upgrading its crisis-response mechanisms.
“By more directly integrating Australian, Japanese and US maritime forces, it signals to Beijing that coercion against Manila will draw a coordinated response from the other Squad countries as well,” Myers said, adding that Manila saw the CCC as “stabilising and reassuring” amid daily Chinese pressure and “a real risk of armed conflict”.
In September, a China coastguard vessel collided with a Philippine fisheries boat about 54 nautical miles off Palawan.
Timothy Heath, founder and principal researcher at defence consultancy Perceptum, said the hub could provide equipment and intelligence Manila would otherwise lack, giving it “a better picture of the situation in the South China Sea”.
While the US, Japan and Australia would have a mechanism to cooperate with Manila against major Chinese aggression, Heath stressed that the arrangement fell short of a Nato-style mutual defence treaty, as Tokyo, Manila and Canberra hold formal alliances only with Washington, not each other.
“However, they do have friendly ties and could cooperate with each other in a serious military crisis,” he added.
Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Social Science, said the hub reinforced the Defence Cooperation Council, a framework launched by Squad nations at Singapore’s Shangri-La Dialogue at the end of May to transition their security ties from ad hoc cooperation into an enduring structure.
“It further anchors the US in the region, thus helping to dispel uncertainty over [American] commitment vis-a-vis its regional allies and partners,” Maslow said.
However, with Sino-US diplomacy gaining momentum, Maslow warned that Washington might refrain from amplifying the Squad’s role. “The sustainability of such defence cooperation initiatives is dependent on the overall trajectory of US-China relations,” he said, adding that Squad partners would weigh their investments in arrangements like Squad carefully around this week’s Apec summit and next month’s G20 gathering.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Apec summit, marking their fourth in-person meeting in roughly a year.
US President Donald Trump (right) and Chinese President Xi Jinping pose in the Grand Foyer of the White House in Washington in September. Photo: TNS
Beijing has pushed back sharply against the minilateral grouping. Responding to joint US, Japanese and Australian air and maritime patrols near the Philippines earlier this year, Chinese Defence Ministry spokesman Zhang Xiaogang accused outside powers of travelling thousands of kilometres to “flex their muscles” and stoke tensions, warning that the Chinese military remained on high alert.
On Thursday, China’s nationalistic tabloid Global Times argued the CCC would turn the Philippines into “a geographic hub for external forces seeking to jointly intervene in Southeast Asian affairs, further placing the country at the centre of geopolitical tensions”. The commentary claimed Washington wanted to “weaken” China in its neighbourhood, Tokyo hoped to ease East China Sea pressure while Canberra aimed to obstruct Beijing’s South Pacific ties – concluding that “none of these calculations have anything to do with the Philippines’ interests”.
David Dutton, a senior resident fellow at ASPI, said the hub would strengthen Manila’s operational effectiveness and sovereignty through a network of international partnerships.
“The Philippines already faces sustained Chinese pressure in the South China Sea,” Dutton said, adding that its alliances are essential to preserving its sovereignty. “The Squad can contribute to regional stability by helping create a stable balance.”

title_display: From war games to crisis planning: Manila’s bid for a ‘Squad’ command hub
content_display:
A joint centre with the US, Japan and Australia could boost intelligence sharing, though analysts say it falls short of a mutual pact.
From left: Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth leave after posing for photos ahead of their quadrilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu in October. Photo: AFP
As the Philippines eyes a coordination hub with defence partners to bolster its regional security shield, analysts say Manila stands to gain greater stability – even if closer military ties do not guarantee allied intervention in a crisis.
The strategy hinges on a proposed Combined Coordination Centre (CCC) with “Squad” partners the United States, Japan and Australia. The hub is expected to give the Philippines faster access to intelligence, improved maritime surveillance and a more unified response to China’s growing regional footprint.
Coupled with a new defence pact with Canberra, the initiative underscores Manila’s push to secure more dependable backing from its partners amid a long-standing South China Sea territorial row with Beijing that has escalated into violent clashes at sea.
[embedded media]
But observers say the hub’s effectiveness could depend on the trajectory of US-China relations, highlighting Manila’s delicate balancing act between strengthening deterrence and avoiding the crosshairs of superpower rivalry.
The Philippines’ Department of National Defence announced plans to establish the CCC in a statement on November 10. Philippine National Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr discussed the move with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles in Cebu on October 28, on the sidelines of the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus.
According to Manila, Squad leaders committed to establishing the hub to synchronise defence investments and expand the scope and frequency of joint military drills. The department has not yet released details on the centre’s location, organisational structure, timeline or specific functions.
Rachel Vandenbrink, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), said the centre would institutionalise coordination and allow the four nations to respond more rapidly to crises. Vandenbrink said the hub was expected to be housed at Camp Aguinaldo – the main headquarters of the Philippine military – and “staffed continuously”, adding that it could facilitate real-time intelligence sharing, maritime surveillance, contingency planning and more coordinated public messaging.
Philippine soldiers march during a military parade marking the 89th anniversary of the Armed Forces of the Philippines at Camp Aguinaldo in Manila in December 2024. Photo: AFP
Vandenbrink noted that the initiative built on expanding joint drills, including Japan’s participation in Balikatan – the largest annual US-Philippines military exercise – and Manila’s growing role in Australia’s Exercise Pitch Black.
She added that the hub complemented the Australia-Philippines Defence Cooperation Arrangement signed on Sunday during the Asean summit, which commits both sides to mutual consultations during contingencies.
“The two developments are complementary, with the [arrangement] providing a framework for bilateral political consultation and the [centre] a platform for multilateral operational coordination,” Vandenbrink said.
Lucas Myers, assistant director at the University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy, said the hub strengthened Manila’s deterrence by upgrading its crisis-response mechanisms.
“By more directly integrating Australian, Japanese and US maritime forces, it signals to Beijing that coercion against Manila will draw a coordinated response from the other Squad countries as well,” Myers said, adding that Manila saw the CCC as “stabilising and reassuring” amid daily Chinese pressure and “a real risk of armed conflict”.
In September, a China coastguard vessel collided with a Philippine fisheries boat about 54 nautical miles off Palawan.
Timothy Heath, founder and principal researcher at defence consultancy Perceptum, said the hub could provide equipment and intelligence Manila would otherwise lack, giving it “a better picture of the situation in the South China Sea”.
While the US, Japan and Australia would have a mechanism to cooperate with Manila against major Chinese aggression, Heath stressed that the arrangement fell short of a Nato-style mutual defence treaty, as Tokyo, Manila and Canberra hold formal alliances only with Washington, not each other.
“However, they do have friendly ties and could cooperate with each other in a serious military crisis,” he added.
Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Social Science, said the hub reinforced the Defence Cooperation Council, a framework launched by Squad nations at Singapore’s Shangri-La Dialogue at the end of May to transition their security ties from ad hoc cooperation into an enduring structure.
“It further anchors the US in the region, thus helping to dispel uncertainty over [American] commitment vis-a-vis its regional allies and partners,” Maslow said.
However, with Sino-US diplomacy gaining momentum, Maslow warned that Washington might refrain from amplifying the Squad’s role. “The sustainability of such defence cooperation initiatives is dependent on the overall trajectory of US-China relations,” he said, adding that Squad partners would weigh their investments in arrangements like Squad carefully around this week’s Apec summit and next month’s G20 gathering.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Apec summit, marking their fourth in-person meeting in roughly a year.
US President Donald Trump (right) and Chinese President Xi Jinping pose in the Grand Foyer of the White House in Washington in September. Photo: TNS
Beijing has pushed back sharply against the minilateral grouping. Responding to joint US, Japanese and Australian air and maritime patrols near the Philippines earlier this year, Chinese Defence Ministry spokesman Zhang Xiaogang accused outside powers of travelling thousands of kilometres to “flex their muscles” and stoke tensions, warning that the Chinese military remained on high alert.
On Thursday, China’s nationalistic tabloid Global Times argued the CCC would turn the Philippines into “a geographic hub for external forces seeking to jointly intervene in Southeast Asian affairs, further placing the country at the centre of geopolitical tensions”. David Dutton, a senior resident fellow at ASPI, said the hub would strengthen Manila’s operational effectiveness and sovereignty through a network of international partnerships.
“The Philippines already faces sustained Chinese pressure in the South China Sea,” Dutton said, adding that its alliances are essential to preserving its sovereignty. “The Squad can contribute to regional stability by helping create a stable balance.”

title_en: Bahrain and Kuwait repel drone attacks after US strikes Iranian island
content_en:
Gulf air defences intercepted incoming fire following raids on a Revolutionary Guards missile site on Qeshm.
Smoke rises on Iran’s Qeshm Island following a US air strike on November 17. Photo: Social media via Reuters
Bahrain and Kuwait said Wednesday that they had repelled air attacks launched against them following US strikes on an Iranian island, as Gulf nations face retaliatory bombardment in the Middle East war.
The conflict – which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February – has spilled over to Gulf states that host US military facilities.
The Iranian army said Wednesday its drones “targeted Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms belonging to the terrorist US military at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait”, in a statement carried by state television IRIB.
Kuwait’s military said Wednesday its air defences were “responding to hostile drone threats”, urging its public to follow security and safety advice.
While Bahrain said its air defences intercepted attacks from Iran early Wednesday, a day after Tehran’s Revolutionary Guards said they attacked a base used by Washington.
The United States and Iran are in a stand-off over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran’s attempts to close the waterway.
A surge in tanker attacks since October threatens to further strain global oil supplies. On Tuesday, a crew abandoned a liquefied petroleum gas tanker off Oman’s Khasab.
Iran’s official IRNA news agency cited a regional official as saying the United States had hit Qeshm Island in the Hormuz strait without causing serious damage.
Smoke rises on Iran’s Qeshm Island following a US air strike on November 17. Photo: Social media via Reuters
US fighter jets “used precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island”, an American official said on condition of anonymity, adding that the strike was in response to Iranian “aggression targeting US personnel and assets”.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said on Wednesday it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Iran-backed group towards the Riyadh area.
Explosions boomed across Bahrain’s capital on Tuesday as a mobile phone alert warned residents to seek safety.
Bahrain’s armed forces said they “confronted, intercepted and destroyed a number of treacherous Iranian aerial attacks today … before they could achieve their objectives”, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they targeted a US-operated radar system.
“Combat drones belonging to the Revolutionary Guards carried out a precision operation this morning, targeting a radar system operated by US forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain,” the Guards’ Sepah news website said.
[embedded media]
The attack was in response to the “repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones”, it added. The Guards also said they had intercepted and captured a US drone south of Qeshm.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, was heavily targeted earlier in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, but had not been hit for weeks until Iranian drone attacks on Friday and Sunday.
Despite Washington and Tehran holding back from a full resumption of hostilities, the sides have traded fire and accusations.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday he was taking “very seriously” reports that Iran was developing plans to use a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington.
CNN cited seven anonymous US officials as saying Iran was plotting how to target senior administration figures with a bomb laced with chemical or radioactive material, though they stopped short of saying Iran planned to carry out such an attack.
“If there is (such a threat), they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before,” Trump said, adding: “I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy”.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the report and called it “Iraq War-style propaganda”.
The violence came as the United States moved the USS Theodore Roosevelt into the region, bringing the number of American carrier strike groups in the region to three.
The deployment adds to an already large US naval presence, which includes two other supercarriers – the George H W Bush and the George Washington – and more than a dozen destroyers.
Iranian drone attacks have resumed ahead of this week’s unprecedented trilateral summit between Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts.
Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will discuss “world peace” at the talks in Shenzhen, according to Beijing. Trump has said he plans to discuss the Iran war at the meeting.
Additional reporting by Reuters
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Thailand’s businesses fret over Trump’s zero tariff on US goods, farmers comment
content_en:
The US president says Thailand is set to ‘eliminate all tariffs on US exports’ and a farm deal will make ‘our farmers very happy’.
US President Donald Trump and Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul show signed documents at a ceremony in Manila on Tuesday. Photo: AP
Thai farmers and industries have been left pondering what the preliminary trade framework signed late on Tuesday by US President Donald Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul means for them, especially regarding market access and the standards of American agricultural products.
The two leaders signed a “joint statement on reciprocal trade” on the sidelines of the Asean summit in Manila. It is not a binding trade deal. Trump nonetheless presented it as a win for US businesses, including the country’s large farming sector.
Bangkok “will eliminate all tariffs on US exports … and remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry”, said Trump, who also attended the final day of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.
He claimed Thailand had agreed to buy an estimated US$2.6 billion of US agricultural products “that makes our farmers very happy”, adding that a few weeks of negotiations remained before a full deal could be signed.
Anutin said at his meeting with Trump that “we have reached a substantial conclusion in our negotiations”, adding that “there is still a little more to do, but I’m confident the agreement will be ready for us to sign real soon”.
On Wednesday, Bangkok clarified that the tariff schedules were still pending a final legal text, with Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun saying that legal drafting alone would take about two months, followed by cabinet review, public consultations and parliamentary approval.
In a post by Thailand’s Government House on social media, Anutin said import tariffs on US goods had not been eliminated and that the joint statement with Trump “prioritises Thai people, farmers and entrepreneurs”.
Farmers harvest rice in a field in Chainat province. Thailand’s farming lobbies are concerned about Bangkok’s ongoing trade talks with Washington, particularly on agricultural products. Photo: Reuters
Analysts say Bangkok’s statement appears to temper Trump’s claims. Thailand, like other US trading partners, continues to contend with US tariffs and Trump’s hardball negotiating style.
Trump threatened Thailand with a 36 per cent import tariff last year, later reduced to 19 per cent, before a US Supreme Court ruling in February invalidated his emergency duties. Non-exempt Thai goods now face an additional 12.5 per cent US tariff imposed in July, which Bangkok wants cut to 10 per cent to match regional competitors.
The United States is Thailand’s largest export market, buying almost a quarter of its exports in the first nine months of this year. According to US trade data, the US trade deficit with Thailand widened to US$71.7 billion last year.
Some analysts attribute that widening, at least in part, to the transshipment of Chinese goods through the Southeast Asian nation.
“Thailand’s choice is essentially between reaching an agreement and having no agreement at all,” said Nonarit Bisonyabut, a research fellow at the Thailand Development Research Institute. “Without a deal, Thailand would have no way to bring that [tariff] rate down.”
Regional rivals including Malaysia, Indonesia and Cambodia have already signed trade deals with the US, which Nonarit said would leave Thailand at a competitive disadvantage.
“However, an agreement does not come for free,” he added. “Thailand would have to open its market, accept US standards for certain products, potentially allow some higher-risk imports and purchase more US goods. It is still unclear which sectors would be opened under the agreement and how many sensitive products would be affected.”
Containers piled up in a cargo terminal at the Bangkok Port. Analysts say Thailand may have to allow some higher-risk imports and purchase more US goods under the agreement. Photo: AP
Farmers’ objections
Thai farming groups have complained about what they call lower food standards in the US, including the use of certain feed additives in pigs that US law permits but Thailand bans.
“In the previous round, after the trade negotiations took place, the outcome was that we imported their corn instead of their pork. But the corn quality was not OK,” said Worawut Siripun, deputy secretary general of the Swine Raisers Association of Thailand.
“This time, the [Thai] government and the Chamber of Commerce have not talked with our association at all about what issues will be negotiated with the US,” he said.
He said the association’s position was “non-negotiable”, adding: “We do not accept any form of pork products from the US because we are still concerned about their use of ractopamine”.
Ractopamine, which is widely used in the US livestock industry to bulk up pigs and cattle, is banned in many countries over potential risks to human health.
Thai farmers already struggle with rising costs, as the US-Israel war on Iran has pushed up energy and commodity prices, raising prices for everything from transport to fertilisers.
Floods and a looming drought linked to a strengthening El Nino weather phenomenon threaten crops and livestock. The country’s influential agriculture sector also fears growing competition from China as well as the US.
[embedded media]
A full-fledged trade deal could carry political risks for Anutin, who is contending with a small but significant protest movement against his government.
Nonarit said he expected “considerable opposition within Thailand” to opening up its market to US goods across industries.
“One concern is public health,” he said. “Even when US products meet American regulatory standards, differences in consumption habits mean their risks may need to be assessed differently for Thai consumers.”
He noted that Thais typically ate more offal than Americans did, adding that offal in the two countries might also contain different residual levels of the additives fed to livestock.
Opening Thailand’s market up would also affect businesses that had long been protected from competition, he said. “Some will argue that certain sectors should be reserved for Thai operators, while some academics may favour greater liberalisation on efficiency grounds.”
By Aidan Jones

title_en: Malaysians lose US$1.6 billion to scams since 2023, love fraud ranks lowest
content_en:
Fake investments caused the most losses as the home ministry urged victims to report scams quickly.
Malaysians lost US$1.6 billion to online scams since 2023, with fake investments causing the most losses. Photo: Shutterstock
Online scammers have siphoned off 6.95 billion ringgit (US$1.6 billion) from victims in Malaysia between 2023 and August 2026, with non-existent investment schemes accounting for the biggest financial losses, according to the home ministry.
In a parliamentary written reply dated Monday, the ministry said police data recorded 181,750 online scam cases over the period, including 45,683 cases involving losses of 1.18 billion ringgit in the first eight months of 2026 alone.
Annual losses have climbed steadily, rising from 1.22 billion ringgit in 2023 to 1.57 billion ringgit in 2024 before surging to 2.97 billion ringgit in 2025.
By modus operandi, non-existent investments caused the steepest losses at 3.28 billion ringgit, followed by telecommunications-related crimes at 2.03 billion ringgit, while love scams recorded the lowest losses at 169.72 million ringgit. In terms of case volume, however, telecommunications scams topped the list with 69,195 cases, followed by e-commerce scams (47,221) and love scams (3,540).
The figures were provided in response to lawmaker Mohd Hasnizan Harun (PN-Hulu Selangor), who asked for the latest 2026 scam statistics and the ministry’s plans to introduce a shared liability framework holding banks, telecommunications companies and digital platforms accountable for system weaknesses.
In a separate parliamentary reply on the same day to MP Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh), the ministry attributed the surge in losses to increasingly sophisticated syndicates exploiting digital technology, fake identities, social media and psychological manipulation.
[embedded media]
To improve fund recovery rates, the ministry stressed the importance of the “golden hours” immediately following a scam, urging victims to call the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) hotline at 997 within the first 24 hours so authorities can trace and block stolen funds before they are withdrawn or transferred.
Between January and August 2026, the NSRC received 159,728 calls involving 250.35 million ringgit in losses. Of that amount, 9.14 million ringgit was seized and 6.67 million ringgit, or 73 per cent of the seized funds, was successfully returned to victims.
Addressing efforts to rescue Malaysians trapped in overseas job scam syndicates, the ministry said it was working closely with the foreign affairs ministry, Malaysian diplomatic missions and host-country authorities.
Upon receiving a report, intelligence is shared immediately to facilitate local rescue operations, while diplomatic missions handle consular help, documentation and repatriation, alongside ongoing regional cooperation and public awareness campaigns against lucrative but suspicious overseas job offers.
This story was first published by The Star

By modus operandi, non-existent investments caused the steepest losses at 3.28 billion ringgit, followed by telecommunications-related crimes at 2.03 billion ringgit, while love scams recorded the lowest losses at 169.72 million ringgit. In terms of case volume, however, telecommunications scams topped the list with 69,195 cases, followed by e-commerce scams (47,221) and love scams (3,540).
The figures were provided in response to lawmaker Mohd Hasnizan Harun (PN-Hulu Selangor), who asked for the latest 2026 scam statistics and the ministry’s plans to introduce a shared liability framework holding banks, telecommunications companies and digital platforms accountable for system weaknesses.
In a separate parliamentary reply on the same day to MP Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh), the ministry attributed the surge in losses to increasingly sophisticated syndicates exploiting digital technology, fake identities, social media and psychological manipulation.
[embedded media]
To improve fund recovery rates, the ministry stressed the importance of the “golden hours” immediately following a scam, urging victims to call the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) hotline at 997 within the first 24 hours so authorities can trace and block stolen funds before they are withdrawn or transferred.
Between January and August 2026, the NSRC received 159,728 calls involving 250.35 million ringgit in losses. Of that amount, 9.14 million ringgit was seized and 6.67 million ringgit, or 73 per cent of the seized funds, was successfully returned to victims.
Addressing efforts to rescue Malaysians trapped in overseas job scam syndicates, the ministry said it was working closely with the foreign affairs ministry, Malaysian diplomatic missions and host-country authorities.
Upon receiving a report, intelligence is shared immediately to facilitate local rescue operations, while diplomatic missions handle consular help, documentation and repatriation, alongside ongoing regional cooperation and public awareness campaigns against lucrative but suspicious overseas job offers.

title_en: Xi and Putin say they will seek fairer global order, ahead of trilateral meeting with Trump
content_en:
‘Russian-Chinese foreign policy coordination is working steadily and positively,’ Russian president says.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (left) listens to Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: AP
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin pledged to maintain stable bilateral ties and advance a multipolar world amid mounting global uncertainties during their meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday, ahead of their landmark trilateral summit with the United States.
Highlighting the resilience of bilateral relations, Xi said China-Russia ties “stand as firm as a mountain amid wind and rain” and called for taking a long-term strategic view to inject greater stability and certainty into the world.
“Russian-Chinese foreign policy coordination is working steadily and positively,” Putin said.
“Amid a complex geopolitical situation, we remain committed to constructive approaches to building a fairer multipolar world order.”
[embedded media]
Putin touched down in Shenzhen shortly before 2am on Wednesday, where he was greeted on the tarmac by Cai Qi, China’s fifth-ranking official.
It was the highest-level airport reception for any foreign leader attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit so far.
Xi also noted that Wednesday’s sit-down marked the 50th time he and Putin had met since 2013, counting both in-person and virtual talks.
Putin echoed Xi’s call to strengthen bilateral ties, saying the two countries “will work back to back for the benefit of both peoples”.
The Russian leader said bilateral trade had exceeded US$200 billion for several consecutive years and continued to show strong growth momentum.
Progress could also be seen in scientific research, innovation and people-to-people exchanges, including tourist flows that were up 43 per cent, he added.
Putin’s sit-down with Xi comes a day ahead of a landmark trilateral summit between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia on Thursday.
According to Russian media reports, Putin has a packed itinerary in Shenzhen that includes the inaugural Russia-China-US leaders’ meeting, Apec summit sessions and a visit to Shenzhen MSU-BIT University.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (right) attends a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: Reuters
Ties between the two countries have warmed significantly in recent years, accelerated by Russia’s strategic pivot to the east following its invasion of Ukraine.
Trade has surged to record levels, underpinned by reciprocal visa-free policies aimed at boosting tourism and business exchanges.
In May, just four days after US President Donald Trump’s state visit to Beijing, the Russian leader made his 25th trip to China.
That visit concluded with a package of agreements – spanning transport, energy, science, education and global governance – as both sides described relations as having reached an “unprecedented level”.
Although Beijing has repeatedly insisted that it was not providing support for Russia’s war against Ukraine, some Chinese firms have been hit with Western sanctions for reportedly supplying the Kremlin’s military-industrial complex or buying Russian oil.
While Beijing has sought to diversify its energy supplies, regular imports from Russia have provided an important buffer against global geopolitical shocks, including disruptions caused by the US-Israel war in Iran.
The two sides are also working to reach an agreement on the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which is designed to transport natural gas from the Russian Arctic through Mongolia into northern China.
However, progress has repeatedly stalled over the past two decades. Moscow said in May that the two sides were close to agreeing terms, but Beijing has avoided making public commitments on price and supply volume.
By Carol Yang

title_en: Huawei calls US prosecution’s case ‘fictionalised portrait’ in closing arguments
content_en:
Chinese tech giant’s lawyer ‘sets the record straight’ and criticises ‘lack of evidence’ in five-hour address to the court.
Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial before US District Judge Ann Donnelly at Brooklyn Federal Court in New York on Tuesday. Illustration: Reuters
A US federal court in New York spent another long day on Tuesday hearing closing arguments from Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies in the final stage of a high-profile trial that once inflamed tensions between Washington and Beijing.
The case has dragged on for nearly eight years, and the trial has been under way since September, with prosecutors commencing closing arguments on Monday.
Huawei and three affiliated companies face 12 criminal counts, including racketeering conspiracy, which US federal prosecutors allege involved an agreement to reinvest proceeds from a pattern of crimes into the business.
Other charges include conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and obstruction of justice.
Representing Huawei, Brian Heberlig from the law firm Steptoe attacked what he called the government’s “fictionalised portrait” of the company.
[embedded media]
In a five-hour closing argument, he praised Huawei’s hard work and innovation while criticising what he said was a lack of evidence. “I am here to set the record straight,” he told jurors. “Huawei didn’t steal its way to success, it earned it.”
Huawei is one of the world’s largest technology companies, reporting revenue of US$126 billion in 2025 and employing about 213,000 people worldwide.
Heberlig’s central strategy was to portray the alleged incidents as isolated acts by individual employees that did not represent the company as a whole. By contrast, prosecutors have presented them as evidence of a companywide culture of criminal conduct.
Prosecutors allege Huawei took source code from Cisco and a component from T-Mobile’s smartphone-testing robot, known as Tappy, while an employee is accused of photographing Fujitsu equipment at a trade show.
They argue that these incidents, alongside a bonus programme rewarding employees for obtaining competitors’ confidential information, demonstrate a broader pattern of theft.
Heberlig countered that the incidents highlighted by prosecutors were “cherry-picked” from decades of operations at a company with hundreds of thousands of employees.
He said employees involved in the Cisco, Fujitsu and T-Mobile incidents had been fired or disciplined, while other conduct cited by prosecutors amounted to ordinary business activity. There was no pattern of criminal activity to support the racketeering charge, he argued.
Heberlig dismissed a 2013 memo encouraging employees to obtain competitors’ confidential information as the mistake of a low-level manager, who was subsequently fired, he said.
He also spent considerable time arguing that Huawei had never concealed its Iranian business from banks or lied to them.
One of the most contentious moments concerned Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, and statements she made under the agreement that secured her release from Canada.
Meng was arrested in Canada in December 2018 at Washington’s request. In 2021, she reached a deferred prosecution agreement in which she admitted misleading HSBC about Huawei’s business in Iran.
She returned to China after spending nearly three years under house arrest. A judge ruled in June that her statements could be used as evidence against Huawei. The charges against Meng were subsequently dismissed and she is not a defendant in the current trial.
[embedded media]
Heberlig told jurors that Meng had made the statements to the best of her knowledge and belief, arguing this did not mean she intentionally lied. Prosecutors objected twice to his interpretation of her statements. Judge Ann Donnelly sustained both objections.
Robert Pollack, a prosecutor who began the government’s rebuttal against Huawei, mocked Heberlig for pounding the table and shouting as he interpreted Meng’s statements, suggesting he did so because the facts and the law were against him. Heberlig had occasionally raised his voice during his closing arguments.
On the obstruction charge, which centres on allegations that Huawei moved employees out of the United States to evade investigators, Heberlig said the departures were part of routine downsizing of the company’s US operations.
The two-month trial saw prosecutors call 61 witnesses, while Huawei called 15 witnesses in its defence.
The case has drawn international attention since Meng’s arrest, which further strained already tense relations between Beijing and Washington.
Following her arrest, China detained two Canadians who were finally freed in 2021, within hours of Meng’s departure from Canada. US officials said their release was not part of the Meng agreement.
Huawei has been effectively barred from selling its telecommunications equipment to US carriers since 2019. If convicted, the company could face substantial fines and forfeiture of proceeds from the alleged crimes.
The government’s rebuttal was expected to continue on Wednesday. Donnelly will then instruct the jury on the law, with deliberations expected to begin that day.
By Han Li

title_en: Democrats flip Alaska seat to seal 56-44 US Senate majority
content_en:
Mary ⁠Peltola defeats Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a tight race, giving her party its largest upper-chamber margin since 2009.
Democrat Mary Peltola at an election night event in Anchorage, Alaska, on November 3. Photo: AP
Democrat Mary ⁠Peltola won Alaska’s US Senate ⁠race on Tuesday, projections from US ⁠media showed, defeating Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and giving her party its ninth flip of the midterm elections and a commanding 56-44 Senate majority.
Peltola won 50 per cent of first-place votes to Sullivan’s 46 per cent, enough to clear the 50 per cent threshold and avoid additional rounds under Alaska’s ‌ranked-choice voting system.
Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but voter frustration with the high cost of living and the state’s strong independent political streak put it back in play for Democrats.
Peltola will be just the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate. The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014.
Her historic victory makes her one of the first two Native American women ever to be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on ⁠corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Peltola said on X after media projected her victory. “Thank you, ‌Alaska. Let’s get to work.”
Alaska’s isolated communities can make its election counts unusually lengthy. The race was further complicated by allegations that Democrats helped recruit an independent candidate ‌as a spoiler.
Two other candidates were on the general-election ballot: Republican Gerry Heikes, a ⁠drywall contractor, and ⁠Dan J. Sullivan Jnr, a retired teacher running as an independent.
[embedded media]
Republicans alleged that Sullivan Jnr was recruited to confuse voters who ‌supported the incumbent senator and unsuccessfully sought to remove him from the ballot, arguing he was not a “good faith” candidate. Alaska’s Supreme Court rejected ‌that argument.
Just ‌before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign had helped recruit Sullivan ‌Jnr into the race. Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement. Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation into ⁠the allegations and has said it was examining anything that could “resemble perjury”.
The Justice Department also launched a ⁠criminal investigation into possible wrongdoing. US Attorney General Todd Blanche has described the reported recruitment effort as “fraud”.
The department has sent more than 140 subpoenas, letters and notices in its investigation, ‌Reuters previously reported, though those actions ‌do not indicate guilt.
The contest was the final uncalled race in the Senate. Peltola’s win gives Democrats their largest majority since 2009 which, combined with securing the House of Representatives, sets up two years of possible deadlock between Congress and President Donald Trump.
Additional reporting by Associated Press and Agence France-Presse
By Reuters

title_en: The big test facing the Middle East’s emerging security autonomy
content_en:
The question is whether states can turn overlapping relationships into arrangements that restrain force, protect commerce and include rivals.
Illustration: Mario Cameira
Gulf governments are building collective defences while exploring security arrangements with the very country many of those defences are designed to deter.
On November 5, Turkey’s parliament approved a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Five days later, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) agreed to establish a military command in Kuwait. In between, Iran’s foreign minister contacted 12 regional counterparts, calling for security arrangements without outside powers.
These are competing responses to the same insecurity. Regional governments are gaining ways to organise protection and diplomacy, yet disagree over whether Iran belongs inside the system they are building. The challenge is to reconcile military commitments with political accommodation.
In July, I described three overlapping paths to a post-war order: US-led security partnerships, China-supported reconciliation and a regional-autonomy track involving Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey and Pakistan. The third track has now become more prominent. It is acquiring institutions, drawing in additional countries and negotiating its relationship with the other two.
The “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”, signed in August, commits Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to regard an attack on one as an attack on all. Turkey’s parliamentary approval advances ratification, although troop deployments and joint operations require further decisions. The GCC’s Kuwait command decision adds to its long-standing military coordination. Neither yet proves governments will delegate meaningful operational authority.
Meanwhile, regional diplomacy is growing. Last month, senior officials from the three Mecca pact signatories visited Tehran to discuss de-escalation. Earlier, foreign ministers from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan met their counterparts from Germany, France, Italy and Britain to discuss regional security. Last week, Saudi Arabia and Qatar also held a consultation with the four European countries.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei meet Saudi Arabia’s Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al-Saud, Pakistan’s army chief General Syed Asim Munir and Turkey’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin in Tehran on October 26. Photo: Iranian Presidency/AFP
Oman offers a different model. In a speech last month, Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi proposed reviving a dialogue between the six-member GCC, Iran and Iraq with a non-aggression pact as the goal.
The expanded network shows why autonomy cannot be measured by distance from foreign powers. Saudi Arabia participates in the GCC command structure and the Mecca pact while retaining American security links and opening talks with Tehran. Pakistan brings its own channels to Iran and Washington; Turkey brings Nato membership and European diplomacy.
The real test is whether governments use those connections to coordinate negotiating positions, mobilise resources or establish rules others will observe.
The United States remains integral. Gulf states still depend heavily on American military capabilities, and the war with Iran has underscored both their value and the risks of hosting US forces. The G7 statement on November 11 supported US mine-clearing and civilian-vessel escorts through the Strait of Hormuz while recognising a separate French-British defensive initiative.
European involvement therefore expands regional options without necessarily weakening the American security framework. On November 12, US President Donald Trump said Washington did not need an Iran deal, days after meeting Qatar’s prime minister to discuss diplomacy. Such reversals encourage Gulf capitals to keep alternative channels open.
US President Donald Trump arrives at a multilateral meeting with leaders from the Gulf Cooperation Council, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 22. Photo: Reuters
China has a different contribution. The 2023 Saudi-Iranian agreement it brokered preserved a channel across a major regional divide. In March, China and Pakistan jointly proposed steps for ending hostilities, protecting civilian infrastructure and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
In September, Xi called for a regionally shaped security framework, underpinned by development. On November 2, Foreign Minister Wang Yi separately met Saudi and Iranian security officials in Beijing while Oman’s sultan visited President Xi Jinping. China subsequently sent an envoy to Iran and Oman, supporting discussion of a new regional security architecture.
The significance of these contacts lies in the convergence between China’s reconciliation diplomacy and initiatives originating within the region. The China-Oman joint statement couples support for diplomacy and safe navigation with trade, investment and development cooperation. Beijing can encourage dialogue and supply economic incentives, although it cannot replace American military guarantees or settle regional rivalries on its own.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq attend a welcoming ceremony at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on November 2. Photo: AFP
Iran exposes the limits of regional autonomy. Tehran calls for an architecture free of interference, while Gulf countries fear its missiles, drones and armed partners. Its foreign minister’s outreach to 12 counterparts shows diplomatic interest; reported Iranian attacks on navigation facilities on an Omani island and on Kuwait and Bahrain underline the distrust that persists. An arrangement labelled regional can still intensify the region’s security dilemma.
The Strait of Hormuz provides the clearest practical test. Oman and Iran have discussed a temporary shipping corridor, mine clearance and traffic management. On November 11, Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the two coastal states should determine navigation rules.
Oman has publicly stressed applicable international law; the G7 opposes tolls and unlawful restrictions. China, too, needs dependable passage for energy and trade. Agreement on navigation procedures, monitoring and dispute resolution would reveal whether the three tracks can produce usable common rules.
[embedded media]
This disagreement reaches beyond the Gulf. A coastal-state arrangement that restricts lawful transit would face resistance from Asian energy importers and Western navies alike. A settlement dictated by outside powers would also struggle to gain the confidence of Iran and its neighbours.
A workable compromise would respect coastal-state rights and internationally recognised navigation freedoms, specify transparent shipping and mine-clearance procedures, and establish ways to investigate breaches. Even limited technical cooperation could build confidence for broader security talks.
Regional autonomy will be measured by such outcomes. Governments may deepen joint defence, invite Chinese diplomatic support and continue relying on Western military assets. The question is whether they can turn these overlapping relationships into arrangements that restrain force, protect commerce and include rivals.
The Middle East has more regional initiatives than before. Countries’ ability to govern shared risks will decide whether greater agency brings greater security.
By Hao Nan
