Gulf governments are building collective defences while exploring security arrangements with the very country many of those defences are designed to deter.
On November 5, Turkey’s parliament approved a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Five days later, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) agreed to establish a military command in Kuwait. In between, Iran’s foreign minister contacted 12 regional counterparts, calling for security arrangements without outside powers.
These are competing responses to the same insecurity. Regional governments are gaining ways to organise protection and diplomacy, yet disagree over whether Iran belongs inside the system they are building. The challenge is to reconcile military commitments with political accommodation.
In July, I described three overlapping paths to a post-war order: US-led security partnerships, China-supported reconciliation and a regional-autonomy track involving Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey and Pakistan. The third track has now become more prominent. It is acquiring institutions, drawing in additional countries and negotiating its relationship with the other two.
The “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”, signed in August, commits Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to regard an attack on one as an attack on all. Turkey’s parliamentary approval advances ratification, although troop deployments and joint operations require further decisions. The GCC’s Kuwait command decision adds to its long-standing military coordination. Neither yet proves governments will delegate meaningful operational authority.
Meanwhile, regional diplomacy is growing. Last month, senior officials from the three Mecca pact signatories visited Tehran to discuss de-escalation. Earlier, foreign ministers from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan met their counterparts from Germany, France, Italy and Britain to discuss regional security. Last week, Saudi Arabia and Qatar also held a consultation with the four European countries.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei meet Saudi Arabia’s Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al-Saud, Pakistan’s army chief General Syed Asim Munir and Turkey’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin in Tehran on October 26. Photo: Iranian Presidency/AFP
Oman offers a different model. In a speech last month, Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi proposed reviving a dialogue between the six-member GCC, Iran and Iraq with a non-aggression pact as the goal.
The expanded network shows why autonomy cannot be measured by distance from foreign powers. Saudi Arabia participates in the GCC command structure and the Mecca pact while retaining American security links and opening talks with Tehran. Pakistan brings its own channels to Iran and Washington; Turkey brings Nato membership and European diplomacy.
The real test is whether governments use those connections to coordinate negotiating positions, mobilise resources or establish rules others will observe.
The United States remains integral. Gulf states still depend heavily on American military capabilities, and the war with Iran has underscored both their value and the risks of hosting US forces. The G7 statement on November 11 supported US mine-clearing and civilian-vessel escorts through the Strait of Hormuz while recognising a separate French-British defensive initiative.
European involvement therefore expands regional options without necessarily weakening the American security framework. On November 12, US President Donald Trump said Washington did not need an Iran deal, days after meeting Qatar’s prime minister to discuss diplomacy. Such reversals encourage Gulf capitals to keep alternative channels open.
US President Donald Trump arrives at a multilateral meeting with leaders from the Gulf Cooperation Council, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 22. Photo: Reuters
China has a different contribution. The 2023 Saudi-Iranian agreement it brokered preserved a channel across a major regional divide. In March, China and Pakistan jointly proposed steps for ending hostilities, protecting civilian infrastructure and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
In September, Xi called for a regionally shaped security framework, underpinned by development. On November 2, Foreign Minister Wang Yi separately met Saudi and Iranian security officials in Beijing while Oman’s sultan visited President Xi Jinping. China subsequently sent an envoy to Iran and Oman, supporting discussion of a new regional security architecture.
The significance of these contacts lies in the convergence between China’s reconciliation diplomacy and initiatives originating within the region. The China-Oman joint statement couples support for diplomacy and safe navigation with trade, investment and development cooperation. Beijing can encourage dialogue and supply economic incentives, although it cannot replace American military guarantees or settle regional rivalries on its own.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq attend a welcoming ceremony at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on November 2. Photo: AFP
Iran exposes the limits of regional autonomy. Tehran calls for an architecture free of interference, while Gulf countries fear its missiles, drones and armed partners. Its foreign minister’s outreach to 12 counterparts shows diplomatic interest; reported Iranian attacks on navigation facilities on an Omani island and on Kuwait and Bahrain underline the distrust that persists. An arrangement labelled regional can still intensify the region’s security dilemma.
The Strait of Hormuz provides the clearest practical test. Oman and Iran have discussed a temporary shipping corridor, mine clearance and traffic management. On November 11, Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the two coastal states should determine navigation rules.
Oman has publicly stressed applicable international law; the G7 opposes tolls and unlawful restrictions. China, too, needs dependable passage for energy and trade. Agreement on navigation procedures, monitoring and dispute resolution would reveal whether the three tracks can produce usable common rules.
[embedded media]
This disagreement reaches beyond the Gulf. A coastal-state arrangement that restricts lawful transit would face resistance from Asian energy importers and Western navies alike. A settlement dictated by outside powers would also struggle to gain the confidence of Iran and its neighbours.
A workable compromise would respect coastal-state rights and internationally recognised navigation freedoms, specify transparent shipping and mine-clearance procedures, and establish ways to investigate breaches. Even limited technical cooperation could build confidence for broader security talks.
Regional autonomy will be measured by such outcomes. Governments may deepen joint defence, invite Chinese diplomatic support and continue relying on Western military assets. The question is whether they can turn these overlapping relationships into arrangements that restrain force, protect commerce and include rivals.
The Middle East has more regional initiatives than before. Countries’ ability to govern shared risks will decide whether greater agency brings greater security.

title_en: As Apec puts Shenzhen in the spotlight, will foreign restaurants benefit?
content_en:
The summit could offer a chance to reach new customers amid cautious domestic spending, business owners say.
Storefront of HH Bagels in Shekou district,
Shenzhen, China. Photo: Handout
As Shenzhen welcomes political and business leaders from across the Asia-Pacific region for a major international summit, foreign restaurant owners in the southern Chinese tech hub hope the event will bring more customers and new business opportunities. But they continue to grapple with fierce competition and cautious consumer spending.
For New Yorker Matt Klein, who has run HH Bagels in Shenzhen’s Shekou district for nearly 14 years, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings could offer a rare opportunity to raise the profile of his business at what he described as its most difficult time.
Klein hopes the summit will introduce his New York-style bagel store to a wider international audience and open doors to new business.
The Apec CEO Summit, held on Tuesday and Wednesday, brought together more than 2,000 political and business representatives from all 21 member economies and beyond, ahead of the Economic Leaders’ Meeting on Wednesday and Thursday.
The gathering is one of the region’s most prominent economic forums, giving Shenzhen a chance to showcase its growing international influence and reinforce its status as a global tech and commercial centre.
But behind the city’s wider ambitions, some foreign business owners said the local consumer market remained challenging.
Klein, who moved to Shenzhen in 2010 and opened HH Bagels with his wife two years later, said business had become considerably tougher since the Covid-19 pandemic.
“People are more concerned about how much they spend,” he said, citing worries about jobs and household finances, as well as a shift towards cheaper meals and spending on experiences rather than dining out.
The growth of food delivery platforms has intensified pressure on international restaurants, while cheaper options at convenience stores and retailers such as Sam’s Club and Costco have also added to the pressure.
“Right now, this is the most difficult time we’ve had since we opened,” Klein said.
[embedded media]
The shop’s customer base has also changed dramatically. When it first opened, foreigners made up more than 90 per cent of customers; today, they account for about 20 per cent, he said.
He added that long-term foreign residents had become less common in Shekou since the pandemic, even as international tourists and short-term business travellers had grown.
His account reflects broader challenges facing China’s consumer economy, where household demand has remained subdued despite continued economic growth.
China’s consumer price index rose 0.7 per cent year on year in October, while retail sales increased by just 0.4 per cent, according to official figures released this month. In Shenzhen, retail sales grew 2.3 per cent in the first nine months, well below the city’s 6 per cent economic growth over the same period.
Beijing has moved to curb excessive price competition, introducing measures to regulate food-delivery subsidies and stop platforms from pressuring restaurants to join discount campaigns.
Serkan, manager of Doors Lounge Turkish Restaurant in Shekou’s Sea World district, offered a more optimistic view. He acknowledged that cautious consumer spending and competition over prices were major challenges, but said the restaurant, which is owned by his brother, had attracted more customers every year.
“Customers are more careful with their spending and there’s a lot of competition on price, so every guest’s experience matters more than ever,” he said.
Shenzhen was attracting more international tourists, not just business travellers, Serkan said – a trend he hoped Apec would support.
“A major event like Apec makes Shenzhen more memorable in the eyes of the world,” Serkan said, adding that the summit could create new opportunities for restaurants to welcome international visitors.
By Mia Nurmamat

title_en: Tencent profit dips as sixfold increase in AI infrastructure spending sacrifices margin
content_en:
Capital expenditure jumped 527 per cent during the quarter as the company expanded its computing capacity.
The Tencent logo is seen at the company’s headquarters in Shenzhen on April 17. Photo: Reuters
Tencent Holdings ramped up capital spending more than sixfold in the third quarter to above US$12 billion, weighing on profit and free cash flow as the Chinese tech giant poured money into computing power to catch up in the country’s cutthroat artificial intelligence race.
Adjusted net income for the three months ended September 30 fell 6 per cent year on year to 66.5 billion yuan (US$10 billion), matching the consensus estimate of analysts polled by Bloomberg. Revenue rose 8 per cent to 207.3 billion yuan, missing market expectations of 210.5 billion yuan.
Tencent’s capital expenditure reached 81.4 billion yuan, up 527 per cent from a year earlier and 54 per cent from the second quarter. The infrastructure outlay pushed the company into a negative free cash flow of 69.1 billion yuan.
Excluding compute procurement payments for AI initiatives, free cash flow would have been a positive 16.9 billion yuan, the Shenzhen-based company said on Wednesday.
“Our recent significant achievements across models and applications have accelerated Tencent’s evolution for the new AI era,” co-founder and CEO Pony Ma Huateng said in a statement.
The results underscore how Tencent, which operates the world’s largest video game business by revenue and China’s ubiquitous WeChat super app, is sacrificing near-term margins to defend its turf amid fierce domestic AI rivalry and mounting investor scrutiny over returns on spending.
A bright spot from that investment was its cloud business. Revenue from its fintech and business services division climbed 9 per cent to 63.7 billion yuan, driven by a 35 per cent surge in cloud computing revenue as it ramped up compute supply in the quarter.
Marketing services revenue, encompassing Tencent’s fast-growing online advertising business, rose 19 per cent to 43 billion yuan on the back of AI-powered ad-targeting upgrades.
Video game sales, traditionally the Shenzhen-based company’s largest revenue pillar, increased 11 per cent domestically to 47.6 billion yuan but dropped 9 per cent internationally to 18.9 billion yuan against a high base.
Tencent has stepped up the release of foundation models and agentic AI tools, including WorkBuddy, to capture enterprise and developer adoption, both at home and abroad.
“We believe WorkBuddy has grown to become the largest AI application in China, measured by total daily large language model token consumption by users,” Ma said.
Meanwhile, WeChat, known as Weixin on the mainland, recorded 1.45 billion monthly active users as of September. Tencent said it expanded the beta testing of Xiaowei, an AI assistant built into the super app, in the past quarter.
On Monday, the firm rolled out Hy4 Flash, a lightweight model with 224 billion parameters priced at 7 US cents per million input tokens.
Billed as Tencent’s most cost-effective Hy model to date, the flash variant arrived less than two weeks after the debut of its flagship Hy4 model, which the company ranked among the world’s top-tier open-weight releases.
“Hy4 has achieved China state-of-the-art AI model status, and Hy4 flash brings down [inference costs] to deliver cost performance for real-world use cases,” Ma said.
The earnings release follows a stark internal warning from senior executives last week at an event marking Tencent’s 28th anniversary. Management told employees that the AI wave represented a matter of “survival and death”, cautioning that the company risked disruption if it failed to adapt proactively.
“With intense domestic competition and the extremely difficult monetisation of AI, we need more than ever to bring our leading position and insights into our core business,” executives said in speech excerpts made public on Monday, adding that the company would swiftly reorganise to dismantle internal silos.
“The wave is already charging right at us.”
Management added that half of the workforce should focus on building AI-native businesses and exploring new growth frontiers, while the remaining 50 per cent should defend core operations and drive efficiency.
Tencent’s Hong Kong-listed shares fell 0.85 per cent to HK$372.80 on Wednesday ahead of the earnings release.
By Iris Deng

title_en: Returning the favour, Xi personally welcomes Trump ahead of high-stakes Apec talks
content_en:
In greeting the US president on the tarmac in Shenzhen, Chinese leader reciprocates rare welcome he received in Washington in September.
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump upon his arrival at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport on Wednesday ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. Photo: EPA
US President Donald Trump received a historic red-carpet welcome from Chinese President Xi Jinping upon arriving in Shenzhen on Wednesday as the leaders prepare for high-stakes talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
Xi personally greeted Trump on the tarmac on Wednesday afternoon, reciprocating the rare welcome the Chinese leader received upon arriving in Washington for a state visit in September.
Wednesday’s welcome marked the first time in nearly seven decades that China’s top leader personally greeted a visiting foreign head of state upon arrival. The last such instance was in 1959, when Mao Zedong welcomed Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.
In 1986, then Chinese president Li Xiannian welcomed Queen Elizabeth of Britain at the airport in Beijing. The queen then met China’s paramount leader, Deng Xiaopeng.
[embedded media]
Xi highlighted the reciprocal gesture and mentioned the welcome afforded to him in Washington in September by the US first couple, according to a read-out released by state news agency Xinhua.
“China is a land of etiquette with a tradition of reciprocity,” the Chinese leader was quoted as saying.
Xi looked forward to having in-depth exchanges with Trump on “major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape” while advancing the constructive strategic stability of bilateral ties, Xinhua said.
Beyond Xi’s personal appearance, the welcome ceremony for Trump was significantly more elaborate than those held for other state leaders arriving in Shenzhen.
It featured nearly twice as many Chinese young people waving bouquets and national flags on the tarmac, as well as a military band playing both countries’ national anthems.
[embedded media]
In addition, a formation of five Chinese J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, trailing red, yellow and blue smoke across the sky to welcome Trump.
When Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen earlier on Wednesday, he was greeted by China’s fifth-ranked official, Cai Qi.
For other state leaders, such as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, no national flags were waved upon their arrivals.
In May, Trump received a lavish welcome ceremony when he arrived in Beijing for a state visit, greeted by Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng at the airport as more than 100 young people dressed in blue-and-white uniforms waved national flags.
The reception in May was more formal in protocol than Trump’s 2017 trip to Beijing, when he was received at the airport by then state councillor Yang Jiechi.
By Fan Chen

title_en: For the Thai prime minister, Apec in Shenzhen is almost home ground
content_en:
Anutin Charnvirakul has family links to southern China and is at ease expressing himself in Cantonese.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has family links to southern China. Photo: ifeng.com
The Apec summit in Shenzhen is something of a homecoming for Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.
Anutin can trace his family roots back to southern China, and when he was asked on Wednesday how it felt to be in Guangdong province, he burst out laughing and replied in Cantonese.
“Hou hoi sam!” he said in Cantonese, which means “so happy”.
In a video published by state news agency China News Service, Anutin likened China and Thailand to siblings, saying their ties went beyond an ordinary partnership.
“I think 90 per cent of Thai people have the roots from China back hundreds of years ago,” he said. “We cannot live without each other.”
Anutin was born in Bangkok and goes by the Chinese name Chen Xiyao. His parents and all four grandparents came from China, he told Chinese state broadcaster CCTV in an interview in 2023.
“My family spoke Cantonese at home every day,” he said.
[embedded media]
The ancestral home of Anutin’s father’s family is in Huafeng, a village in Jiangmen’s Xinhui district in the western Pearl River Delta, according to the district government.
His father, Chavarat Charnvirakul, who was briefly Thailand’s acting prime minister in 2008, visited the village in 1998 and donated money to build a road.
Anutin became prime minister in September 2025 and made his first official visit to China in that role in July, when he met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shanghai.
Xi described China and Thailand as “one family” and called for closer ties between the two countries.
On Friday, Anutin hosted Chinese Premier Li Qiang for talks in Bangkok. The two leaders discussed the China-Thailand railway and witnessed the signing of agreements covering the car industry, agriculture and customs.
Anutin arrived at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport on Wednesday morning with his wife and delegation.
He returned a salute as he stepped off the plane, then applauded the group welcoming him as he walked along the red carpet.
By Eve Qiao

His father, Chavarat Charnvirakul, who was briefly Thailand’s acting prime minister in 2008, visited the village in 1998 and donated money to build a road.
Anutin became prime minister in September 2025 and made his first official visit to China in that role in July, when he met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shanghai.
Xi described China and Thailand as “one family” and called for closer ties between the two countries.
On Friday, Anutin hosted Chinese Premier Li Qiang for talks in Bangkok. The two leaders discussed the China-Thailand railway and witnessed the signing of agreements covering the car industry, agriculture and customs.
Anutin arrived at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport on Wednesday morning with his wife and delegation.
He returned a salute as he stepped off the plane, then applauded the group welcoming him as he walked along the red carpet.

title_en: Field of fire: Chinese scientists develop drone gun that can plant rice more efficiently
content_en:
Researchers develop pump system that uses jets to plant seeds more efficiently than randomly scattering them in the field.
The drone could help improve crop yields. Photo: Handout
For years, engineers around the world have experimented with mounting guns on drones to boost battlefield firepower.
But a new study by Chinese researchers shows that unmanned vehicles could be used to shoot a very different kind of ammunition – rice.
In a paper published last month, the researchers detailed an optimised pump system that could use precise, high-pressure jets to plant rice rather than randomly scattering the seeds.
“This study proposes a seed-metering pump designed for a drone-based, pulsed-jet rice seeding system,” the researchers wrote in the Chinese-language journal Transactions of the Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering.
After testing several pump methods, the team – from South China Agricultural University and Guangdong-based laboratories specialising in agricultural equipment, aviation and artificial intelligence – settled on a system that overcame hurdles such as poor flow rates, seed damage, clogging and weak ejection pressure.
In field tests, a drone using the optimised pump system planted seeds in neat, evenly spaced clusters – straying less from the target line and maintaining more consistent spacing between clusters than a commercially available pump.
The resulting yield of the planted rice reached an average of around 6,730kg per hectare (6,000lb per acre), compared with around 6,040kg per hectare using the conventional method.
Drones have become a major modern weapon of war used to carry out precision strikes. China and other countries have also tested ways of using guns mounted on drones for close-quarters combat.
However, drones are also being used for civilian purposes, including agriculture.
In China, they are already being used for tasks such as spraying pesticides and water, as well as carting harvested crops.
China is one of the world’s biggest producers of rice, accounting for nearly 27 per cent of global production, second only to India, which accounts for just over 28 per cent, according to the latest figures by the United States Department of Agriculture.
In 2020, a drone-based direct seeding system made by robotics firm XAG was made commercially available.
The company said at the time that rice farming could not rely on large machinery such as automated tractors because they were not compatible with the terrain and size of many rice farms in Asia.
Conventional drone-based rice planting scatters the seeds randomly across fields, but the team behind the new system said this method suffered from several drawbacks including “the susceptibility of seeds to interference from rotor-generated airflow, a lack of control over seed placement and poor uniformity in distribution”.
“These issues lead to inconsistent crop density, inadequate ventilation and light penetration, an increased risk of pests and diseases and unstable crop yields,” the study said.
Pulsed-jet rice seeding uses a specialised pump that ejects a mixture of liquid and germinated rice to shoot seeds into fields in uniform rows or clusters.
While orderly planting can boost efficiency, raise yields and cut costs, the team wrote that conventional pumps designed for liquids fell short of the technical demands for rice seeding.
“Consequently, there is a need to develop a specialised seed-metering pump tailored for pulsed-jet rice seeding,” they said.
To achieve organised row and cluster seeding, the team said the initial ejection velocity of the rice seeds needed to be increased to minimise the impact of rotor airflow on the seeds’ trajectory.
To address this, the researchers tested three different pump configurations to determine the optimal design.
“In terms of its superior seeding performance, the semi-open impeller pump was selected as the seeding pump configuration,” they wrote.
They then conducted field tests using a prototype pump, including tests at a site in Guangzhou’s Zengcheng district where they compared its performance with that of a commercially available pump.
The rice was soaked and germinated before being incorporated into a mixture containing cellulose powder, bentonite clay and water.
[embedded media]
During the experiment, the drones flew at a speed of 2 metres per second (6.6 feet per second) and operated 2 metres above the ground, with row spacing set to 1.5 metres.
The team’s pump system planted rice in evenly spaced clusters, with a standard deviation of 2cm (0.8 inches) off the target row line, compared with 2.9cm for the commercially available pump.
The average variation for the centre-to-centre distance between adjacent seed clusters was also lower for the experimental system.
A few months later, in November, the team measured the harvest using a random sampling method, finding that the average yield from their system outperformed conventional drone seeding.
The team said these results indicated the seeding pump increased the exit velocity of the rice, limiting the impact of rotor airflow on the descent trajectory of the seeds.
“This facilitates orderly, row-based and pocket-specific seeding, confirming the feasibility of a drone-mounted, pulsed-jet rice seeding device based on a semi-open impeller pump,” they wrote.
However, the researchers emphasised that the system still warranted further exploration, including its high power consumption during operation and the difficulty of precisely controlling how deeply the seeds penetrated into the ground.

title_en: Malaysia’s Pardons Board minutes expose legal rift over Najib’s house arrest
content_en:
The declassified minutes show the king allowed Najib to serve the rest of his jail term at home despite the attorney general’s objections.
Former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak waves as prison officers escort him at the Kuala Lumpur High Court complex on November 10. Photo: AP
Malaysia’s attorney general objected to former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest, saying it had no legal basis – but the king approved the arrangement, newly disclosed Pardons Board minutes showed, fuelling a debate over the limits of royal clemency powers.
Attorney General Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar warned against setting a precedent during the September 18 meeting, according to declassified minutes published by local news outlet Malaysiakini on Wednesday.
“[Dusuki] said that the move would have implications on political stability, the country’s image at the international level, investments and the economy. He stressed that the prisoner should continue serving his sentence,” read the Malay-language minutes of the meeting, chaired by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar.
Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh also reportedly objected to the proposal.
However, the king granted Najib a conditional pardon at the meeting, allowing the former leader to serve the remainder of his prison term at home until his scheduled release in August 2028, upon settlement of a 50 million ringgit (US$12.1 million) fine.
[embedded media]
Najib was convicted of misappropriating 42 million ringgit from SRC International, a former subsidiary of scandal-plagued state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad.
The 73-year-old was sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined 210 million ringgit in 2020, but a conditional royal pardon in 2024 halved his prison term and reduced the fine. He was moved to his home on November 10, after his party, Umno, paid the fine.
The minutes were declassified for court purposes in response to the Malaysian Bar Council’s legal challenge against the house arrest order.
In court documents filed on November 10, the council said that Article 42 of the constitution provides only for pardons, reprieves and respites, and does not extend to creating a new form of detention.
Its members asked the court to suspend implementation of the house arrest order pending the outcome of the judicial review.
Legal vs constitutional
Senior constitutional lawyer Mohamed Haniff Khatri Abdullah argued that the king’s constitutional power of mercy overrode ordinary legislation and did not require a separate legal framework for house arrest.
“Pardon is a constitutional power, the prerogative of the king. It is above any other law, which means that there is no need for a law to exist, because pardon is a power of mercy, nothing to do with law,” Haniff said.
He cited the royal pardon granted to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in 2018 as an example of how the king’s powers could override ordinary provisions governing imprisonment.
“There is no need for any rules or regulations when it comes to the power of mercy,” he said.
The absence of specific legislation governing house arrest did not invalidate the king’s decision, he said.
The attorney general was entitled to offer his legal opinion during the meeting, but such advice did not override the king’s final decision, he added.
“To be fair to the AG, he did not mention that he is disputing the pardon, because he knows he can only give his opinion when requested, but his opinion does not override the final decision of the king.”
A car carrying jailed former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak arrives at his residence, where will serve his house arrest sentence, on November 10. Photo: Reuters
Another law expert said while Dusuki’s objections were legally significant, they did not automatically invalidate the king’s decision.
Senior constitutional lawyer Jahaberdeen Mohamed Yunoos said under Article 42(9) of the Federal Constitution, the Pardons Board was required to consider the attorney general’s written opinion but not obliged to accept it.
“Therefore, proceeding despite the AG’s objections does not, by itself, render the decision unconstitutional,” Jahaberdeen said.
However, he drew the distinction between challenging the merits of a royal pardon and questioning whether a house arrest was constitutionally authorised in the absence of specific legislation.
“The courts should be able to examine whether Article 42 provides a lawful basis for house detention,” he said. “Such an examination would not involve questioning the wisdom of royal pardon, but determining whether the power exercised falls within constitutional limits.”
The Bar Council’s latest judicial review application could give the courts an opportunity to clarify the issue, he said – although it remained uncertain whether judges would consider the challenge given the earlier ruling on the limits of judicial review.
“Ultimately, judicial scrutiny of these limits should not be seen as an affront to the monarchy, but as a safeguard of its dignity and integrity,” he said.
This Week in Asia has contacted the Attorney General Chambers for comments.
By Ushar Daniele

title_en: EU proposes new US$49 billion Ukraine loan for 2027
content_en:
The funding would go two-thirds of the way towards filling a €70 billion black hole Kyiv is facing next year.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attends a press conference on EU financial and military support for Ukraine at the European Commission in Brussels, Belgium, on Wednesday. Photo: EPA
The European Union on Wednesday proposed member states give Ukraine an extra €45 billion (US$49 billion) loan to plug Kyiv’s 2027 budget shortfalls as Russia’s war drags on.
The funding would go two-thirds of the way towards filling a €70 billion black hole Kyiv is facing next year – with Brussels looking to incentivise other Ukraine backers to do the rest.
“Five years since the start of this war of aggression, Europe stands united. We are as committed as ever to support Ukraine in war and in peace,” European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said.
“We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiation table, and Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”
EU leaders will discuss the loan at a summit in Brussels next week in the hope of reaching a deal.
The EU is currently paying out a €90 billion loan to Kyiv that it hoped would see the country through to the end of next year.
But as Russia has intensified its attacks, it has become clear that those funds would not be enough.
A firefighter works at the site of a market hit by a Russian drone strike in the town of Zlatopil in the Kharkiv region, Ukraine, on Wednesday. Photo: Press service of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Kharkiv region/Handout via Reuters
The new loan would follow the same format as the current one and be borrowed against headroom in the EU’s central budget.
It would also be linked to Kyiv pressing on with reforms.
While the aim is to forge agreement next week, the issue of the funding has now become wrapped up with broader fraught negotiations over the EU’s next central budget.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has insisted that all of the EU must settle the financing and all 27 member states must be involved before a deal can be reached on the budget.
That has rankled several of the EU’s least pro-Ukraine countries who want to be left out of backing the loan, such as Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia.
Last time round, Budapest, Bratislava and Prague managed to get themselves exempted from having to help cover the financing.
Von der Leyen insisted the aim this time remains to get all countries on board.
Beyond the bloc, Brussels is pushing other allies of Ukraine – such as Britain, Canada and Japan to fill in the rest of Kyiv’s needs next year.
Similar pleas have previously fallen short.
In a bid to incentivise them this time, Brussels says others could provide guarantees to help bolster the loan or use the interest on frozen Russian assets in the EU to cover their own financing.
The proposal for a new loan means that the EU for now will not try to look into the thorny issue of directly tapping over €200 billion of frozen Russian central bank assets held in the bloc to fund Ukraine.
That plan was shot down in 2025 by Belgium – where most of the assets are held – and the position of its government has not shifted.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: How low tech exposure turned India into a haven during Asia’s chip sell-off
content_en:
After a two-year lull, foreign funds have poured record cash into Mumbai stocks as strong earnings and IPO momentum fuel a broad rebound.
A live screen on the facade of the Bombay Stock Exchange building in Mumbai, India, in May 2025. Photo: AP
India is emerging as an unlikely winner in Asia’s artificial intelligence-driven market rout following the Nvidia fallout, as tighter US chip curbs and falling oil prices steer investors towards Indian equities – even as observers question how long the rally will last.
The boost to India’s markets comes after a two-year hiatus, with global investors shifting capital towards non-AI sectors and crude oil prices dipping since the US midterm elections eased fears of an escalation in the Middle East conflict.
India’s benchmark BSE Sensex has risen by around 6.65 per cent since the November 3 US midterm election, contrasting with sharp drops across South Korea’s Kospi, Taiwan and Singapore amid concerns over stricter US congressional scrutiny of domestic AI data centre expansion and a broader tech sell-off.
“We expect concerns about the sustainability of AI-related capital expenditure and earnings to prompt a rotation away from East Asian markets such as South Korea and Taiwan, while encouraging foreign investors to return to India after a two-year absence,” said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at Union Bancaire Privé.
Separately, the Trump administration moved to tighten export curbs late on Monday, with the US Department of Commerce filing new rules targeting several routes through which Chinese firms have accessed advanced American chips and computing power. These new restrictions will affect data centre investment across Southeast Asia, according to a report by UK-headquartered Capital Economics on Wednesday.
An AI data centre reference architecture display at the Wiwynn booth during Computex in Taipei in June. Concerns over the sustainability of AI capital expenditure and tighter US chip curbs have prompted investors to shift away from Taiwanese and South Korean tech stocks. Photo: AFP
“I would expect the United States to maintain close scrutiny of access to advanced AI chips and other strategically sensitive technologies, particularly where national security concerns arise,” said John Quelch, executive vice-chancellor and distinguished professor of social science at Duke Kunshan University in China. “However, the more immediate policy direction appears to be tighter enforcement of existing export controls and greater scrutiny of potential diversion through third-country intermediaries,” he added.
India’s markets – which had cooled over the past two years as global capital chased AI and semiconductor booms in Taiwan and South Korea – have stood out in recent days amid the broader uncertainty prevailing across most of Asia.
“If this dynamic reverses, India could see renewed foreign inflows,” Casanova said, noting that foreign investor sentiment towards India had previously weakened due to high share valuations and a surge in oil prices that weighed on the rupee against the US dollar. A decline in oil prices, expected through next year, could provide an additional tailwind for Indian equities, he added.
Historically, more than 80 per cent of oil and natural gas transiting the Strait of Hormuz via Iran and Oman has been destined for Asian markets. Energy prices have plunged since the US election, with Brent crude dropping roughly 16 per cent from a high of US$110 per barrel on October 16 to around US$92.44 on Monday.
Pump jacks operate at the South Belridge Oil Field in Kern County, California, in February 2022. Global crude prices have fallen roughly 16 per cent since mid-October as Middle East tensions eased, relieving pressure on the rupee and boosting Indian equities. Photo: AFP
“We have seen a return of foreign flows into Indian equities in the recent three weeks. Nevertheless, it is unclear how long this rotation trade will sustain,” said Cameron Systermans, head of multi-asset for Asia at Marsh.
He noted that earnings growth for South Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers is likely to remain strong in the near term despite recent market jitters, underpinned by sustained AI capacity expansion. “Nonetheless, we are cognisant that the diversification theme has been gaining attention recently, with the likes of India and other emerging markets with lower tech exposure providing a good hedge against the tail risk of the AI theme suddenly losing steam,” he added.
“Foreign investors have already started to move into markets that are less exposed to AI. In Asia, the most obvious ones are India and Indonesia,” said Mali Chivakul, emerging markets economist at Bank J. Safra Sarasin, referring to index provider MSCI’s October proposal to downgrade Indonesia to stand-alone status over governance concerns. “Indonesia has been mired with the MSCI potential downgrade over its governance issues, so the main beneficiary so far has been India.”
Foreign investors have net purchased US$9.61 billion in Indian shares so far in November, surpassing the previous monthly record set in November 2020, according to market data reported by Indian daily The Economic Times.
IPO prospects
Pranav Haldea, managing director of market data firm Prime Database, said that while long-term concerns remain over how AI adoption will affect India’s traditional billable-hour software services firms, market sentiment has turned positive – at least for now.

title_display: How low tech exposure turned India into a haven during Asia’s chip sell-off
content_display:
After a two-year lull, foreign funds have poured record cash into Mumbai stocks as strong earnings and IPO momentum fuel a broad rebound.
A live screen on the facade of the Bombay Stock Exchange building in Mumbai, India, in May 2025. Photo: AP
India is emerging as an unlikely winner in Asia’s artificial intelligence-driven market rout following the Nvidia fallout, as tighter US chip curbs and falling oil prices steer investors towards Indian equities – even as observers question how long the rally will last.
The boost to India’s markets comes after a two-year hiatus, with global investors shifting capital towards non-AI sectors and crude oil prices dipping since the US midterm elections eased fears of an escalation in the Middle East conflict.

Separately, the Trump administration moved to tighten export curbs late on Monday, with the US Department of Commerce filing new rules targeting several routes through which Chinese firms have accessed advanced American chips and computing power. These new restrictions will affect data centre investment across Southeast Asia, according to a report by UK-headquartered Capital Economics on Wednesday.
An AI data centre reference architecture display at the Wiwynn booth during Computex in Taipei in June. Concerns over the sustainability of AI capital expenditure and tighter US chip curbs have prompted investors to shift away from Taiwanese and South Korean tech stocks. Photo: AFP

A decline in oil prices, expected through next year, could provide an additional tailwind for Indian equities, he added.

Energy prices have plunged since the US election, with Brent crude dropping roughly 16 per cent from a high of US$110 per barrel on October 16 to around US$92.44 on Monday.

title_en: Hong Kong’s Tsim Sha Tsui remains Asia’s priciest retail district as New York leads globally
content_en:
New York’s Upper Fifth Avenue has also claimed the top spot this year, while Shanghai’s West Nanjing Road ranked first in mainland China.
Tourists shop in a luxury store on Canton Road in Tsim Sha Tsui. Photo: Jelly Tse
Hong Kong’s Tsim Sha Tsui is still the Asia-Pacific region’s most expensive retail district this year, despite a 6 per cent annual decline in rents to €13,016 (US$14,318) per square metre, according to property consultancy Cushman & Wakefield’s latest report.
New York’s Upper Fifth Avenue (49th to 60th Streets), meanwhile, climbed two places to become the world’s most expensive retail district, overtaking London’s New Bond Street, which was last year’s leader. The findings come from the consultancy’s 36th annual “Main Streets” report released on Wednesday.
The shopping strip in the Big Apple saw annual rents surge 35 per cent to €24,998 per square metre, while those in the British capital’s trendy shopping district were unchanged at €20,642, according to the report. Milan’s Via Montenapoleone ranked third globally.
“While rental growth has moderated globally, competition for space in the world’s most established retail destinations remains intense,” said Dominic Brown, head of international research at Cushman’s global think tank.
“The return of Fifth Avenue to the top of the rankings demonstrates how quickly rents can accelerate when strong retailer demand meets limited availability,” Brown said.
“We are seeing similar dynamics across major global markets, where retailers continue to prioritise locations that offer international visibility, strong consumer spending and long-term brand value.”
Tsim Sha Tsui, a popular tourist and shopping district also known as TST, last topped the global ranking in 2021, when it edged out Causeway Bay. This year it ranked fourth worldwide.
In the Asia-Pacific ranking, Causeway Bay’s main street shops took second place this year, even as rents dropped 3 per cent to €12,301 per square metre. It also ranked second last year.
Central, meanwhile, slipped one place to eighth, with main street rents unchanged at €6,686 per square metre. Tokyo’s Ginza and Omotesando ranked third and fourth, respectively.
Shanghai’s West Nanjing Road was the highest-ranked district in mainland China, placing 12th in the Asia-Pacific region. Annual rents slipped 1 per cent to €5,044 per square metre.
Sona Aggarwal, Cushman & Wakefield’s managing director and head of retail sales and strategy for the Asia-Pacific region, said the region continued to offer a dynamic retail landscape with diverse growth paths across different countries.
“Whether driven by domestic spending, tourism or retailer expansion, opportunities exist across a diverse range of locations,” Aggarwal said.
“Retailers that understand the unique demand drivers within each market and have a clear expansion strategy will be best positioned to identify and capture growth opportunities as they arise, both in established hubs and in emerging retail districts.”
By Cheryl Arcibal

title_en: Takaichi makes low-key arrival in Shenzhen after South Korea’s Lee is greeted by dancers
content_en:
As tensions simmer between Tokyo and Beijing, Japanese leader’s welcome contrasts sharply with that for the South Korean president.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi arrives in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: Kyodo via Reuters
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit amid strained ties between Beijing and Tokyo.
The low-key arrival marking the first China visit by a Japanese leader in seven years contrasted sharply with the warm welcome given to South Korean President Lee Jae Myung earlier in the day.
On the tarmac, Takaichi was met by retired Chinese diplomat Zhang Qiyue and Japanese ambassador to China Kenji Kanasugi before she nodded briefly to the ground crew.
A video released by Takaichi’s office showed an honour guard welcoming her.
Earlier, when South Korean leader Lee and first lady Kim Hea Kyung arrived, an honour guard stood to attention while more than 100 dancers in white shirts and pink skirts lined both sides of the red carpet.
Holding two bouquets of flowers each, they jumped, danced and chanted “Warm welcome, warm welcome!”
Dancers welcome South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and first lady Kim Hea Kyung at the airport. Photo: Xinhua
Meanwhile, when US President Donald Trump touched down soon after Takaichi, he was personally greeted on the tarmac by Chinese President Xi Jinping – echoing Trump’s own personal reception for Xi in Washington in September.
During diplomatic encounters, the details of official ceremonies can often convey political messages. Ahead of the trip, Tokyo has sought Beijing’s assurance that Takaichi would be treated equally with other visiting state leaders, according to media reports.
The last Japanese prime minister to visit China was Shinzo Abe, Takaichi’s political mentor, who travelled to Chengdu in December 2019 for a trilateral summit with Chinese and South Korean leaders.
When Abe arrived in Beijing for the 2014 Apec summit, he walked straight off his plane and into a waiting car without an official welcome ceremony.
When Xi met him on the sidelines of that summit the two leaders shook hands without smiling, and neither country’s flag appeared in the background. Relations were strained at the time over the disputed Diaoyu Islands – known as the Senkakus in Japan – and Abe’s December 2013 visit to the Yasukuni Shrine that commemorates the country’s war dead.
[embedded media]
When Abe arrived for the 2016 Group of 20 summit in Hangzhou, he was greeted on the tarmac by Chinese officials and presented with flowers by a young girl, though his subsequent meeting with Xi remained low-key, with neither country’s flag displayed.
It was a warmer greeting for Abe during his formal visit in 2018, when then premier Li Keqiang hosted a welcome ceremony with an honour guard and a 19-gun salute.
But relations between China and Japan have again deteriorated, since Takaichi said in November last year that a crisis in the Taiwan Strait could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, potentially paving the way for military intervention.
Beijing demanded that she retract the remarks, which it said undermined the political foundation of bilateral relations. She has refused to do so.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Japan, like most countries, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state.
[embedded media]
The diplomatic dispute has since strained political and economic ties between the two countries.
There have nevertheless been some signs of continued engagement between Beijing and Tokyo.
In September, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng met former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya and a delegation of about 50 Japanese business leaders in Beijing.
Wang described bilateral relations as being in a “grave situation”, saying they had yet to return to normal ahead of the 55th anniversary of diplomatic normalisation next year.
Earlier this month, Beijing again said that responsibility for the serious difficulties in bilateral relations lay entirely with Tokyo, urging Takaichi to correct her Taiwan remarks.
By Cao Jiaxuan

title_en: US panel proposes tougher AI chip export rules ahead of Xi-Trump talks
content_en:
Exporters would have to show that sales to China would not divert chipmaking capacity from US customers.
Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips are at the centre of a US congressional commission’s proposal to tighten export restrictions on China. Photo: Handout
A bipartisan US commission urged Congress on Wednesday to require companies exporting advanced artificial intelligence chips to China to certify that the shipments would not divert manufacturing capacity from the US market, adding a new proposal to the debate over chip controls ahead of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a bipartisan panel created by Congress to assess the national security implications of US-China economic ties, said exporters should submit data that the US Commerce Department can audit to show how they allocate capacity for advanced chip fabrication, high-bandwidth memory and packaging. False certifications could carry criminal penalties under the proposed changes to the Export Control Reform Act.
The Commerce Department already requires companies seeking licences to ship certain chips, including Nvidia’s H200, to certify that the sales would not divert global foundry capacity from US customers.
The commission wants Congress to put a broader requirement into law and make it harder to waive. Any move to waive or narrow the requirement would need a national security determination submitted to Congress for 30 days of review.
At a briefing on Tuesday, commissioner Leland Miller said chips destined for China could compete for the same factory capacity and components as chips sought by US companies.
[embedded media]
“There should be no export of chips to China if the fabrication capacity is being used for those chips instead of being used for chips that American firms need,” Miller said.
The proposal comes as lawmakers from both parties weigh adding chip controls to the annual defence bill, including a measure that would give Congress a greater role in reviewing export decisions.
Miller said he saw signs that Congress and the administration were beginning to work together on export controls. The commission’s vice-chair, Mike Kuiken, was more sceptical. He said Congress generally steps in when lawmakers have reached a bipartisan consensus and believe the executive branch “is doing a bad job”.
The debate has intensified since Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive last week amid scrutiny of his ties to a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company under investigation for possible US export-control violations.
The Commerce and Justice departments said in a joint statement this week that Commerce opened its inquiry in 2024 and that Nvidia put Megaspeed on its internal list of companies it would not sell to in June 2025.
Asked at Tuesday’s briefing whether the Nvidia controversy would have changed the commission’s findings, chair Randall Schriver said the panel had long studied “China’s approach to acquiring advanced technologies, including advanced chips”. He said the commission did not know what had happened in the Megaspeed case, which was still under investigation.
On Monday, the Commerce Department issued a separate rule restricting Chinese companies’ remote access to advanced US chips through overseas data centres.
The annual report follows the commission’s first official visit to mainland China since 2019. The delegation travelled to Beijing, Hangzhou and Shanghai, where its discussions covered AI, advanced technology and economic security, among other issues.
The report, approved unanimously by all 10 sitting commissioners, ranked a proposed American Data Initiative as its top recommendation.
The panel urged Congress to make federal data easier to use, including by creating data sets for AI development.
It also proposed requiring data brokers to obtain Americans’ consent before selling or sharing their personal information and barring transfers to firms or individuals under the jurisdiction of China or other designated foreign adversaries, even with consent.
“Data is literally the lifeblood of every frontier artificial intelligence model that exists today,” Kuiken said at Tuesday’s briefing. He said the United States should make better use of the data the federal government has collected over generations.
The panel also called for companies to disclose when products or services offered in the United States use AI models developed by Chinese companies. It said the Federal Trade Commission should be able to take action against companies that fail to disclose their use.
A separate recommendation would restrict new deployments of Chinese open-weight models, whose underlying parameters are publicly available, in sensitive applications such as systems that run critical infrastructure or process large volumes of sensitive personal data.
Deploying the models in those settings would require a time-limited authorisation based on an independent evaluation of the safeguards.
By Teresa Elena Frontado

title_en: Former Malaysian minister calls on Indonesia to pay US$3 billion for haze losses
content_en:
Alternatively, Jakarta should form a cross-border task force allowed to enter Indonesian forests to combat fires, ex-finance minister says.
Visitors look out at the hazy Kuala Lumpur skyline on October 16. Photo: AP
Malaysia’s former finance minister Lim Guan Eng called on Indonesia to compensate the country for economic and welfare losses – estimated at 13 billion ringgit (US$3 billion) – arising from this year’s haze crisis, or agree to form a permanent transboundary task force to tackle future fires.
Malaysia should accept Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s apology for the prolonged haze to maintain good relations and Asean solidarity, Lim said on Tuesday, according to the Malay Mail newspaper.
But it could still ask its neighbour for compensation.
Citing a study commissioned by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers, Lim said Malaysia had suffered 8 billion ringgit in welfare losses and 5 billion ringgit in economic losses as a result of the haze, the Malay Mail newspaper reported.
A child walks among volunteers fighting a fire that reignited behind an elementary school at Alalak village in Barito Kuala Regency, South Kalimantan on October 28. Photo: AFP
The health-related welfare losses reflected the economic cost associated with premature mortality risks and were linked to an estimated 1,700 premature deaths among Malaysians, he said.
The second figure was calculated based on economists’ prediction that severe air pollution could reduce international visitor arrivals by up to 8 per cent, resulting in losses of up to 5 billion ringgit in tourism-related GDP and economic spillovers. This posed a threat to the Visit Malaysia 2026 campaign, Lim said.
He also proposed a 1,000 ringgit tax rebate for air purifier purchases to help protect vulnerable groups, particularly children and senior citizens, noting that air purifiers were essential in the haze.
If Jakarta could not offer compensation, Lim said it should establish a permanent cross-border task force with the authority to enter Indonesian forests immediately to combat wildfires. Such a team was necessary to prevent annual recurrence and strengthen the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ ability to tackle transboundary haze, he added.
Lim urged Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan to represent the interests of all Malaysians and convey the proposal to Indonesia.
At the Asean summit in Manila on Sunday, Prabowo apologised to Malaysia and Singapore for the haze. However, he maintained that the forest fires were not Indonesia’s fault, and his government had done its best to contain them.
[embedded media]
Jakarta has deployed 71,000 firefighters to combat the months-long fires, with 16 of them losing their lives during operations, CNA reported. Indonesia might need 350 years to recover land burnt in this year’s fires, a team of academics wrote in The Conversation news and analysis network on Wednesday.
An expert says Prabowo’s apology does little to signal Jakarta’s commitment to Asean cooperation.
Prabowo kept saying Asean was important but “doesn’t walk the talk”, Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate professor of international relations at Jenderal Achmad Yani University in Cimahi, told This Week in Asia.
“The problem is not a lack of Asean rhetoric. It is the lack of convincing evidence that this rhetoric translates into sustained political commitment.”
Late last month, Indonesia and Singapore established a joint task force to hold companies suspected of contributing to the wildfires accountable by sharing information, The Straits Times reported.
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said at the regional summit on Sunday the task force “doesn’t have to be a bilateral platform” and should cover all Asean members, according to CNA.
“If anyone is caught doing this, across Asean, we will share information, we will take action, and we will hold companies responsible. I think that is something we should strive to do as part of Asean.”

title_en: UK inflation hits 12-month high of 3.6% on soaring fuel, tobacco costs
content_en:
The headline rate of inflation, which rose from 3.5 per cent in September, marks the fourth consecutive monthly increase.
Customers fill their tanks at a petrol station in London, Britain. Photo: EPA
UK inflation has risen to its highest level for a year after being pushed up by petrol and diesel costs and tobacco duty changes, according to new figures.
The rate of Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation was 3.6 per cent in October, up from 3.5 per cent in September, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Wednesday.
The reading was in line with predictions from economists and it marks the fourth consecutive monthly increase.
It moves inflation further away from the Bank of England’s 2 per cent target, amid warnings from the bank earlier this month that inflation could keep rising to a peak of about 5 per cent next year.
A person fills a car with petrol. UK inflation rose to 3.6 per cent in October, marking the fourth consecutive monthly increase. Photo: dpa
ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said: “Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate.
“Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively.”
The latest figures showed that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (6.8 US cents) per litre between September and October, as tensions in the Middle East continued to push oil prices higher.
Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per litre in October to an average price of 199.5 pence per litre – the highest since ONS records began in 1996.
Nevertheless, petrol and diesel prices have both eased back in November as oil prices moved lower following the US midterm elections.
Another driver of inflation was higher tobacco costs for smokers after duty rates were increased at the start of the month.
The duty rise added around £1.21 to an average pack of 20 cigarettes, according to HMRC data.
Tobacco prices rose 5.2 per cent for the month and were 12.4 per cent higher year-on-year as a result, marking the highest inflation rate for almost two years.
The increase in inflation also came after the Ofgem energy price cap increased by 4 per cent in October, while changes in the calculation of the cap contributed higher household gas costs.
A customer pays for fruit at a market in London, Britain. Statisticians say food price inflation has eased to 0.2 per cent. Photo: EPA-EFE
Elsewhere, food and non-alcoholic drink inflation slowed further to its lowest level for more than five years, at 0.8 per cent.
Statisticians said food price inflation eased to 0.2 per cent, highlighting a contribution from cheaper chocolate as prices in the category dipped by 2.9 per cent.
Experts said this was potentially linked to both falling cocoa prices and increased discounting from retailers.
The latest consumer price inflation data comes after separate ONS figures released on Tuesday showed that regular earnings growth eased back to 3.5 per cent in the three months to September.
It suggests that the rising cost-of-living is on track to surpass wage growth in the coming months.
“The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world,” said Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the treasury.
“The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”
By dpa

title_en: CUHK council could dismiss leaders without inquiry under proposed rule change
content_en:
Lawmakers suggest amendments to the leading university’s legislative structure and provisions are urgently needed.
The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) campus in Sha Tin, where proposed rule changes would allow the governing council to directly dismiss senior leaders. Photo: Jelly Tse
A leading university in Hong Kong has proposed to skip the legislation process when changing its governance rules and empower its council to dismiss top management without a formal inquiry.
The proposal, part of reforms launched recently by the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), was submitted on Wednesday to the Legislative Council (Legco) by four lawmakers who also sit on the institution’s governing council.
“The CUHK Ordinance and the Statutes set out in Schedule 1 have remained largely unchanged since 1976,” the lawmakers said in a paper addressed to the Legco education panel chairman.
“Their structural framework and provisions have increasingly fallen behind the practical developmental needs of CUHK, creating an urgent need for amendment,” they added.
The paper, which detailed legislative amendments to the university’s governing by-laws, will be discussed by the panel on December 4.
The four lawmakers who are also members of the CUHK council are Jonathan Leung Chun, Chan Han-pan, Tang Ka-piu and Nicholas Chan Hiu-fung.
Under the proposal, the Statutes, regarded as the by-laws or governing regulations of CUHK, would no longer be treated as subsidiary legislation, which must be introduced and vetted at the Legco.
If the proposal went ahead, the governing council would need only to meet the vote thresholds required at council meetings to change the rules governing CUHK’s student union, senate, colleges and other matters. This would mean these changes would no longer need the Legco’s scrutiny and approval.
The council would also become CUHK’s top body, with a proposed amendment adding “supreme” before its description as “governing and executive body of the University”.
Under the proposals, the Legislative Council would no longer need to be consulted or give formal approval for changes to CUHK’s governing statutes. Photo: Jelly Tse
The original preamble in the ordinance defined CUHK as “a University with a federal constitution”. Under the amendment, “federal constitution” would be removed and the colleges’ role would be described as supporting the university in enriching students’ learning experience.
Under the proposals, the power and duties of the university senate, which is the highest academic governing body of an institution, would be subject to “direction by the council”, instead of “review by the council” as before.
The council would also have the power to directly dismiss the vice-chancellor, pro-vice-chancellors, college heads or faculty deans on grounds including misconduct, incompetence and inefficiency, by meeting the vote threshold.
Under the current rules, the council must, if requested to do so by the individual or by any three council members, appoint a committee of council and senate members to investigate and report the allegations before removing a senior officer or professor.
The draft bill would also make it a criminal offence, punishable by a HK$10,000 (US$1,280) fine, to form or join any organisation using the CUHK name without the council’s written consent
In a separate paper, the council secretariat said the proposed changes were to ensure the CUHK Ordinance remained current and was aligned with overall national development and the university’s future developmental needs.
It added that a task force had been set up to review the changes, noting that the university’s stakeholders had “expressed broad support for the proposed revisions to the CUHK Ordinance”.
The proposed amendments followed a 2023 private member’s bill by three legislators who were also members of the CUHK governing council. Those proposals downsized the council and raised the bar for appointing or removing the vice-chancellor.
The push for reform was fuelled by clashes in 2022 between CUHK’s management and the council, including the latter’s decision to renew vice-chancellor Rocky Tuan Sung-chi’s term before a new chairman took office and the launch of a redesigned emblem without councillors being consulted.
The sponsors of the 2023 bill, including Tommy Cheung Yu-yan, cited incidents during and after the 2019 campus protests, which saw CUHK called a “riot university”, as proof of systemic governance failures.
The South China Morning Post has contacted students and alumni for comments.
By William Yiu, Kristen Cheung

title_en: Will Xi get his wish for the butterflies, and bilateral ties, to ‘fly even better’?
content_en:
South Korean leader says emblem of Gyeongju Apec has made the journey to Shenzhen and he hopes the two nations can take a ‘new leap forward’.
Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting with his South Korean counterpart in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: AFP
The butterflies that enchanted the South Korean and Chinese leaders at last year’s Apec summit in Gyeongju have been revived in Shenzhen as a symbol of the growing momentum in bilateral ties.
Butterflies were the emblem of the Gyeongju summit, and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Wednesday suggested they had made the journey to China.
Lee made the remarks in a social media post soon after he arrived in Shenzhen and held his third bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping since taking office in June 2025.
In the post – written in Korean and Chinese – Lee said the butterflies of Gyeongju had finally flown to Shenzhen, echoing Xi’s earlier wish that they could “fly even better, and perhaps even sing” in China’s tech hub.
Lee added that he hoped the two countries could take a “new leap forward” as they mark 35 years of diplomatic relations.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attends talks with Xi. Photo: Alex Plavevski/EPA POOL via AP
The reference dates back to the October 31 welcome dinner at last year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Gyeongju, which featured a performance titled “Journey of Butterfly: Together, We Fly”.
Lifelike robotic butterflies danced across the stage alongside video projections of illuminated butterflies in flight, according to South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency.
Lee, who hosted the dinner, said at the time that the emblem symbolised the spirit of connectivity among Apec members.
The performance clearly left an impression on Xi. At the summit’s closing ceremony the next day, Xi revealed that Lee had urged him to bring the butterflies to the 2026 gathering in China and make them fly just as beautifully.
“I hope this beautiful butterfly will fly to Shenzhen, and that it will fly even better, and perhaps even sing,” Xi said at the time.
Recalling the exchanges on Wednesday, Lee said momentum towards a “full restoration” of bilateral ties – which both leaders pledged to pursue a year earlier – was now firmly established.
[embedded media]
Regional security, particularly North Korea, remains another critical area where Seoul hopes to secure Beijing’s cooperation. During talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on November 13, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun urged China to play a constructive role in bringing Pyongyang back to the negotiating table, according to a South Korean readout.
Cho also outlined Seoul’s efforts towards denuclearisation and peace on the Korean peninsula, while Wang reiterated that China’s policy on the peninsula remained unchanged.
The diplomatic push comes amid heightened speculation over North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s travel plans. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump signalled that he might meet Kim in China, while Kim’s two-day inspection of a tourism development in the North Korean city of Samjiyon, near the Chinese border, over the weekend has further stoked rumours of an impending visit.
By Cao Jiaxuan

title_en: Carney hails ‘real progress’ in China-Canada ties but suggests US has no need to worry
content_en:
The Canadian prime minister said he had shared his views on AI governance in his meeting with President Xi Jinping the previous day.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addresses the media in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: AFP
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Wednesday that ties with China were “growing on every front” after the two countries agreed to ease trade restrictions, but brushed off suggestions that it was a threat to the United States.
Carney also said he had raised the global governance of artificial intelligence when he met Chinese President Xi Jinping the previous day, setting out Canada’s “model for how this governance can be developed”.
Relations between the two countries have been improving as Ottawa seeks to manage its growing trade tensions with Washington.
After Carney’s meeting with Xi on Tuesday – held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen – the two sides agreed to expand existing tariff reliefs, further opening the Chinese market to Canadian agricultural and seafood exports.
The agreement will cover around C$400 million (US$280 million) worth of Canadian goods, including frozen pork, fish and seafood. Canada will in return extend tariff exemptions on some Chinese steel and aluminium products for another two years.
The agreement follows Beijing’s pledge earlier this month not to raise tariffs on Canadian canola, peas, lobsters and crabs until the end of 2028.
In a press conference on Wednesday, the Canadian leader said: “There’s some real progress in the bilateral relationship in trade, travel, learning, cultural exchange … Our relationship is growing on every front.”
He added that easing trade curbs would bring “new orders … better prices … [and] greater certainty”, framing it as part of a push to build a “dense web of reliable partnerships” and reduce reliance on any one market.
[embedded media]
Asked whether closer ties with China could be seen as a threat to the US, Carney replied: “We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork, we are exporting halibut.
“These are not cutting-edge semiconductors. These are not the types of trade relationship that the United States has with China.”
He added that, relative to the size of its economy, Canada’s trade with China was on a much smaller scale compared with the US.
Relations between the North American neighbours suffered another blow when trade talks collapsed in August and the US imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, triggering counter-tariffs from Ottawa.
Carney said the US had “fundamentally changed its trading objectives” but added that he would hold talks with US President Donald Trump later on Wednesday.
According to a statement from the Canadian prime minister’s office, Carney and Xi “agreed on the importance of strengthening cooperation on the global governance of artificial intelligence” and on the need to promote the safe and responsible development of AI use.
[embedded media]
On Wednesday, Carney told reporters that there were “enormous risks” that came with AI, and it was “past time to develop global governance frameworks”.
He added: “I took the opportunity in the discussions with President Xi yesterday to share our views on a model for how this governance can be developed, and for us, with respect to China, that is that is the principal area of cooperation.”
Both China and the US are competing to dominate the technology and have been pushing other countries to cooperate with them.
Canada has not signed up to either Pax Silica, the Trump administration’s drive to China-proof AI and chip supply chains, or the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation, Beijing’s rival attempt to shape global AI governance.
By Dewey Sim

title_display: Carney hails ‘real progress’ in China-Canada ties but suggests US has no need to worry
content_display:
The Canadian prime minister said he had shared his views on AI governance in his meeting with President Xi Jinping the previous day.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addresses the media in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: AFP
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Wednesday that ties with China were “growing on every front” after the two countries agreed to ease trade restrictions, but brushed off suggestions that it was a threat to the United States.
Carney also said he had raised the global governance of artificial intelligence when he met Chinese President Xi Jinping the previous day, setting out Canada’s “model for how this governance can be developed”.
Relations between the two countries have been improving as Ottawa seeks to manage its growing trade tensions with Washington.
After Carney’s meeting with Xi on Tuesday – held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen – the two sides agreed to expand existing tariff reliefs, further opening the Chinese market to Canadian agricultural and seafood exports.
The agreement will cover around C$400 million (US$280 million) worth of Canadian goods, including frozen pork, fish and seafood. Canada will in return extend tariff exemptions on some Chinese steel and aluminium products for another two years.
The agreement follows Beijing’s pledge earlier this month not to raise tariffs on Canadian canola, peas, lobsters and crabs until the end of 2028.
In a press conference on Wednesday, the Canadian leader said: “There’s some real progress in the bilateral relationship in trade, travel, learning, cultural exchange … Our relationship is growing on every front.”
He added that easing trade curbs would bring “new orders … better prices … [and] greater certainty”, framing it as part of a push to build a “dense web of reliable partnerships” and reduce reliance on any one market.
[embedded media]
Asked whether closer ties with China could be seen as a threat to the US, Carney replied: “We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork, we are exporting halibut.
“These are not cutting-edge semiconductors. These are not the types of trade relationship that the United States has with China.”
He added that, relative to the size of its economy, Canada’s trade with China was on a much smaller scale compared with the US.
Relations between the North American neighbours suffered another blow when trade talks collapsed in August and the US imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, triggering counter-tariffs from Ottawa.
Carney said the US had “fundamentally changed its trading objectives” but added that he would hold talks with US President Donald Trump later on Wednesday.
According to a statement from the Canadian prime minister’s office, Carney and Xi “agreed on the importance of strengthening cooperation on the global governance of artificial intelligence” and on the need to promote the safe and responsible development of AI use.
[embedded media]
On Wednesday, Carney told reporters that there were “enormous risks” that came with AI, and it was “past time to develop global governance frameworks”.
He added: “I took the opportunity in the discussions with President Xi yesterday to share our views on a model for how this governance can be developed, and for us, with respect to China, that is that is the principal area of cooperation.”
Both China and the US are competing to dominate the technology and have been pushing other countries to cooperate with them.
Canada has not signed up to either Pax Silica, the Trump administration’s drive to China-proof AI and chip supply chains, or the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation, Beijing’s rival attempt to shape global AI governance.

title_en: Philippine police file criminal complaints against Thomas Markle
content_en:
Police say the complaints accuse ‌Markle ‌of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation ‌of children.
Thomas Markle in a jail booking photograph after cutting off an electronic ankle monitor he was ordered to wear. Photo: Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office via Reuters
Philippine police said on Wednesday that ⁠criminal complaints ⁠had been filed against Thomas ⁠Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, over alleged online child sexual abuse offences.
The filing of the complaints will enable prosecutors to examine ‌evidence and decide whether charges should be filed in court.
It came less than two weeks after US authorities arrested Thomas Markle in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage ⁠girls.
Thomas Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the ‌claims were untrue and describing them as “sick lies”.
Philippine police said complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s ‌office in Cebu province on Monday following an investigation last ⁠month into ⁠the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials.
A private security guard stands beside a lit window outside Maravida Senior Living, where Thomas Markle was staying, in Lakeland, Florida, on November 6. Photo: AFP
Markle had lived in ‌Cebu for a period before returning to the United States.
Police said the complaints accuse Markle ‌of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation ‌of children.
Forensic examination of the remaining devices surrendered in the Philippines ⁠by Markle’s son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr, was ongoing and ⁠could yield further evidence to support the case or lead to additional charges, if warranted, police said.
Meghan, an American ‌actor, has been ‌estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles’ younger son, Harry, in 2018.
She has said she is “deeply distressed” over the matter.
By Reuters
